code.title: Operator admin key compared with non-constant-time string equality (timing oracle)
code.description: The admin gate at endpoints.go:61 `if h.operatorKey != "" && r.Header.Get("Authorization") != "Bearer "+h.operatorKey` uses Go's `!=` string comparison, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. Every /admin/ledger/* endpoint (summary, providers, reconcile) is protected only by this comparison. There is no constant-time compare (no crypto/subtle).
code.recommendation: Replace with `subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(authHeader), []byte("Bearer "+h.operatorKey)) == 1` after a length-independent guard, or hash both sides and compare the hashes. Also consider requiring the key be set (reject when operatorKey=="").
code.evidence: Confirmed endpoints.go:61 uses native string `!=` for the bearer comparison; grep for `crypto/subtle`/`subtle.ConstantTime` across internal/billing and internal/auth returns nothing, so no constant-time path exists — the factual claim is accurate. Downgraded to LOW because: (1) the target is the remote `coordinator.streamvc.live`, where network jitter dwarfs the single-digit-nanosecond per-byte timing signal of Go string compare, making byte-recovery impractical; (2) the secret is a high-entropy operator key, not a short PIN, so the search space defeats even a perfect oracle; (3) the gated endpoints are admin-only and read-mostly (summary/providers at endpoints.go:68-147) plus a reconcile that only writes a benign reconciliation_runs row (endpoints.go:199-212), not fund movement. The separate `operatorKey==""` open-access path (endpoints.go:61 short-circuits when empty) is real but config.go:399 enforces `auth.operator_key must be set`, making the empty case unreachable in production. Real hardening item, but LOW.

code.title: Unbounded growth of per-provider rate-limiter map (memory leak / DoS amplifier)
code.description: `handler.lastEarnings map[string][]time.Time` (endpoints.go:38) is keyed by providerID and only ever read, appended to, or in-place compacted (`kept := h.lastEarnings[providerID][:0]` at endpoints.go:430). A map entry is created on the first /providers/{id}/earnings call for any providerID that passes token validation, but entries are never deleted even when a provider's slice becomes empty. The handler lives for the process lifetime.
code.recommendation: Evict empty entries: after compaction, `if len(kept)==0 { delete(h.lastEarnings, providerID) }` before returning, or run a periodic sweep. Alternatively bound the map size or use an LRU.
code.evidence: Confirmed: lastEarnings declared at endpoints.go:38, initialized once in Handlers (endpoints.go:26) on a process-lifetime handler, and allowEarnings (endpoints.go:423-441) never calls `delete`, so empty-slice entries persist. Mechanism is real. Downgraded to LOW: (1) the attacker cannot mint arbitrary providerID keys — endpoints.go:332-339 validates the bearer token via tokenStore.ValidateToken then requires `subject == providerID`, so each distinct map key needs a distinct VALID provider token subject, bounding key cardinality to legitimately issued provider identities (provider-scale, not request-scale); (2) each entry is tiny (a string key plus a []time.Time slice that is compacted to <= earningsRateLimitPerMin entries every call at endpoints.go:431-435). For a POC/early-network coordinator with tens-to-hundreds of providers, total footprint is kilobytes and grows only with the real provider population. Genuine housekeeping gap with a correct one-line fix, but not a medium DoS on the provider-bounded keyspace.

code.title: N+1 query: admin providers endpoint runs a per-row sub-query for pending payout credits
code.description: Inside the row loop of `providers()` (endpoints.go:123-145), each provider row triggers a separate `h.sum(ctx, 'SELECT SUM(provider_credits) FROM ledger_payout_ready WHERE provider_id=? AND status=\'ready\'', providerID)` (endpoints.go:139). With limit up to 200 providers per page this is up to 200 extra round-trips per request on top of the main grouped scan, while the main query is held open via `rows` (defer rows.Close at endpoints.go:120).
code.recommendation: Compute pending_payout_credits for the whole page in one query (e.g. a LEFT JOIN against an aggregated ledger_payout_ready subquery keyed by provider_id) instead of one sum() per row.
code.evidence: Confirmed exactly as described. endpoints.go:123 opens `for rows.Next()` over the grouped provider scan (QueryContext at endpoints.go:103, deferred Close at endpoints.go:120), and endpoints.go:139 calls `h.sum(...)` once per emitted row, up to `limit` (capped at 200 via endpoints.go:93-95) extra round-trips; h.sum -> sumErr -> QueryRowContext on the same h.store.db (endpoints.go:404-420). Verdict stays LOW with two mitigations grounded in code: (a) endpoint is admin-only behind the operator-key gate, not attacker-reachable at volume; (b) the sub-query hits `ledger_payout_ready` which has covering index `idx_lpr_provider_status ON ledger_payout_ready(provider_id, status, window_end_utc)` (store.go:119), so each call is an index lookup, not a table scan. The concurrent-statement concern is not a correctness bug — database/sql hands QueryRowContext a separate pooled connection. Real, low, worth folding into a single LEFT JOIN.

code.title: operator_share_bps = 10000 - ProviderShareBps can violate CHECK and abort hot-path billing if a stale/invalid config carries bps>10000
code.description: insertOperatorCreditTx (hotpath.go:230-248) writes `operator_share_bps` as `10000 - result.ProviderShareBps` (hotpath.go:242). ledger_operator_credits enforces `CHECK(operator_share_bps BETWEEN 0 AND 10000)` (store.go:90). The finding posits that if a config snapshot ever held provider_share_bps > 10000, the subtraction would go negative and abort the WriteHotPath transaction, silently dropping billing.
code.recommendation: Clamp/validate ProviderShareBps to [0,10000] at the boundary where it enters ComputeCredits, and/or fail the request explicitly with a clear fault rather than via a CHECK-constraint abort. Defense-in-depth only.
code.evidence: Mechanics confirmed: hotpath.go:242 writes `10000-result.ProviderShareBps` and store.go:90 CHECKs operator_share_bps in [0,10000]; a negative value would fail the insert and roll back via BEGIN IMMEDIATE/ROLLBACK (hotpath.go:37-45). BUT the premise is refuted by the schema. The only write path into ledger_config_snapshots is InsertConfigSnapshot (snapshot.go:38-44), whose destination column is itself `provider_share_bps INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(provider_share_bps BETWEEN 0 AND 10000)` (store.go:152). The legacy rebuild migration recreates the table with the identical CHECK (store.go:236) and re-validates every row via INSERT...SELECT (store.go:241-247). So a value >10000 can never be persisted, hence snapshotAt() (snapshot.go:64-83) can never read one back, hence 10000-bps can never go negative from the snapshot path. The other source, ParseShareBps(cfg.ProviderShare), is fed by config validated to [0.0,1.0] at config.go:515, yielding bps in [0,10000]. ParseShareBps lacks an internal clamp, but the DB CHECK on the snapshot table is the binding guard making the >10000 scenario unreachable. Downgraded to INFO: reasonable defense-in-depth hardening, no reachable revenue-loss path today.

code.title: Dead/unreachable code in hot-path attempt_n derivation
code.description: hotpath.go:56 enters the block only when `derived := requestCount-1; derived > in.AttemptN`. The nested guard at hotpath.go:57 `if in.AttemptN != derived` is therefore always true (derived > AttemptN implies derived != AttemptN), so the inner branch always executes and returns at hotpath.go:85. Consequently hotpath.go:87 `in.AttemptN = derived` is unreachable dead code. Logic is correct but the structure is misleading.
code.recommendation: Drop the always-true `if in.AttemptN != derived` wrapper and remove the unreachable `in.AttemptN = derived` at line 87, or restructure so derived-attempt handling is expressed once.
code.evidence: Confirmed by reading hotpath.go:55-88. Outer guard at line 56 establishes `derived > in.AttemptN` (strict), so the nested guard at line 57 `if in.AttemptN != derived` is tautologically true. The inner-if body always reaches `return err` at line 85 (after COMMIT at line 83), making line 87 `in.AttemptN = derived` unreachable. `go vet ./internal/billing/` returns exit 0 (no diagnostic) because vet does not do this value-range reasoning — precisely why human review is warranted. Severity correctly LOW: no behavioral defect (line 58 already sets in.AttemptN=derived before the work, so the dead line 87 would have been a no-op anyway), purely a maintainability/clarity hazard on the billed path.

code.title: ParseMultiplierPPM/ParseShareBps lack overflow/clamp guards on operator-supplied floats
code.description: ParseMultiplierPPM (formula.go:46-48) returns int64(math.Round(v*1e6)) and ParseShareBps (formula.go:50-52) returns int64(math.Round(v*1e4)) with no bounds check. GlobalMultiplier is validated only as >0 (no upper bound) at config.go:518, so a very large multiplier could overflow the int64 conversion. Downstream checkedMul guards the actual credit computation, so a corrupted multiplier degrades to the null-error/zero-credit path rather than producing wrong money.
code.recommendation: Add an explicit upper bound on GlobalMultiplier in config validation and clamp/validate the PPM and bps values to sane ranges before persisting a snapshot.
code.evidence: Confirmed and correctly self-rated INFO. ParseMultiplierPPM (formula.go:46-48) and ParseShareBps (formula.go:50-52) both do `int64(math.Round(v*denom))` with no bounds check, and config.go:518 validates GlobalMultiplier only as `> 0` (vs ProviderShare bounded to [0,1] at config.go:515). The finding's harmless-by-design reasoning holds against the code: (1) the persisted global_multiplier_ppm column is `CHECK(global_multiplier_ppm >= 0)` (store.go:153/60), rejecting only negatives; (2) ComputeCredits routes the multiplier exclusively through checkedMul at formula.go:158, and checkedMul (formula.go:180-191) returns ok=false on `a > math.MaxInt64/b`, sending the row to the null-error/zero-credit path (formula.go:159-162 -> zeroCredits) rather than emitting wrong money. The only undefined-ish step is the int64(float64) conversion for a float beyond MaxInt64, but that value is operator-controlled config, not attacker input, and any garbage PPM is still caught by checkedMul before corrupting credits. Confirmed at INFO — real missing upper-bound worth adding for defense-in-depth, no reachable money-corruption path today.

code.title: Raw-HTTP streaming path misclassifies buyer disconnect as a provider breaker fault (false fault + wrong billing)
code.description: In forwardStreaming (the non-WS, raw-HTTP SSE path), the read loop reads upstream SSE lines via reader.ReadBytes('\n') on resp.Body. attemptCtx is derived from r.Context() (line 1607-1611), so when the BUYER disconnects, r.Context() is canceled, which cancels attemptCtx and causes the in-flight provider read to fail with a context error. The code does NOT check r.Context().Err() before classifying: on any non-EOF read error it unconditionally logs 'provider disconnected during streaming', emits a buyer-facing SSE error, returns wsForwardProviderDisconnectedCommitted, and tags the request-log/billing attempt with billing.FaultBreakerQualifying (line 1691). Every other forwarding path guards this exact case (forwardWSStreaming 1559-1561, forwardWSNonStreaming 1411-1413, non-streaming HTTP 1622-1624). The raw-HTTP streaming path is the lone path missing the guard.
code.impact: A buyer that cancels mid-stream causes the request to be recorded as a provider disconnect and billed with FaultBreakerQualifying, which zeroes the provider's credits for work it actually performed.
code.recommendation: Mirror the WS paths: before the disconnect classification at line 1686, add `if r.Context().Err() != nil { return wsForwardCancelled, 0, progressAttempt("Buyer disconnected during streaming", billing.FaultNone) }`. Check this on the non-EOF read-error branch so a canceled buyer context is never attributed to the provider.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED as a correctness/billing bug, with one correction to the stated impact. Verified at server.go:1607-1611 attemptCtx = r.Context() (then WithTimeout of r.Context()), so buyer disconnect cancels the upstream read. server.go:1682-1691: the io.EOF branch (1682) returns clean; the fall-through (1686-1691) unconditionally logs 'provider disconnected during streaming', writes an SSE provider_disconnected error, and returns progressAttempt(..., billing.FaultBreakerQualifying) with NO r.Context().Err() check. Contrast verified: forwardWSStreaming server.go:1559-1561 and 1493-1495 both gate on r.Context().Err(); forwardWSNonStreaming 1411-1413; non-streaming-HTTP request-error branch 1622-1624. Billing impact verified WORSE than 'wrong billing' implies: billing/formula.go:112-114 `if row.FaultFlag == FaultBreakerQualifying { return row }` returns a row with GrossCredits/ProviderCredits unset (zero), so the provider is paid 0 for a clean buyer cancel. CORRECTION to the finding's breaker-poisoning claim: the raw-HTTP path at 1691 sets only the requestLogAttempt.FaultFlag and does NOT call s.recordBreakerFault; the circuit breaker is incremented solely via s.recordBreakerFault->s.pool.RecordBreakerFault (server.go:2050-2051), which this path never invokes. So this specific path does NOT directly trip the breaker (unlike the WS paths at 1562/1573 which call recordBreakerFault in addition to setting the flag). The 'clients can poison provider reputation / remove honest providers from the pool' part of the impact is therefore overstated for this code path. Kept at high because the confirmed harm — denying an honest provider all payment and writing a false provider-disconnect record on a routine buyer cancel (stop button / closed tab), with high confidence and trivial to trigger — is itself a real money/correctness defect on the trusted billing record.

code.title: Public /v1/pool/check rate-limiter is keyed on spoofable X-Forwarded-For and never evicts (unbounded-memory DoS + rate-limit bypass)
code.description: /v1/pool/check is registered on the PUBLIC buyer Handler() (line 335). Its only protection is allowPoolCheck (617-627), which throttles to 1 req/sec PER KEY using s.poolCheckLast (a sync.Map). The key is clientIP(r) (629-641), which returns the first comma-segment of the attacker-controlled X-Forwarded-For header verbatim when present, with no validation that it is a real IP or that the request arrived through a trusted proxy. The map is only ever written via s.poolCheckLast.Store(ip, now) with no Delete, Range-based sweep, or TTL eviction, so distinct keys accumulate forever; and because the bucket is per spoofed key, an attacker rotating X-Forwarded-For bypasses the 1-req/sec limit AND inserts a permanent map entry per request.
code.impact: An unauthenticated attacker hitting the public endpoint with a unique X-Forwarded-For per request grows poolCheckLast without bound (OOM of the coordinator) while defeating the rate limiter so each spoofed identity drives a full pool.Snapshot() scan.
code.recommendation: (1) Do not trust X-Forwarded-For unless the request came from a known trusted proxy hop; prefer r.RemoteAddr or a configured trusted-proxy depth for keying. (2) Bound poolCheckLast via a background janitor / evict-on-read / fixed-size LRU.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED on both halves. server.go:335 registers GET /v1/pool/check on the public Handler() router (alongside /v1/chat/completions); the only auth-bearing routes are on InternalHandler() (340-345), so this endpoint is unauthenticated. server.go:617-627 allowPoolCheck keys on clientIP(r); the only mutation is s.poolCheckLast.Store(ip, now) at 625 — no expiry. server.go:629-641 clientIP returns strings.TrimSpace(forwarded[:i]) (first comma segment of X-Forwarded-For) verbatim with zero validation and no trusted-proxy gate, only falling back to RemoteAddr when the header is absent. Confirmed via grep that poolCheckLast appears at exactly 3 sites: server.go:72 (sync.Map field declaration), 620 (.Load), 625 (.Store) — no .Delete/.Range/.LoadAndDelete/janitor anywhere, and the struct has no associated TTL field. So distinct spoofed keys accumulate permanently and each rotated key both bypasses the per-key 1s throttle and drives handlePoolCheck's s.pool.Snapshot() scan (server.go:593). Unbounded-memory DoS + rate-limit-bypass on an unauthenticated public endpoint of the money-authority process; high is justified.

code.title: Global providerhttp.Client.Timeout caps total streaming duration, killing healthy long non-WS SSE streams and misreporting them as provider disconnects
code.description: forwardStreaming issues the upstream SSE request via the shared providerhttp.Client.Do (line 1619). That client is constructed with http.Client{Timeout: TimeoutS} (providerhttp/client.go:16-21), default 300s (config.go:254). Go's http.Client.Timeout covers the ENTIRE exchange including reading the streamed response body, so for a long non-WS completion the body read in the loop (reader.ReadBytes at 1665) fails once the wall-clock timeout elapses, and the code takes the 1686-1691 branch: emits 'Provider disconnected during streaming', records FaultBreakerQualifying.
code.impact: Legitimate long generations over the raw-HTTP streaming fallback could be truncated at the global timeout and mis-attributed as provider faults, compounding finding #1. Limited because most providers route via the WS-tunneled path so this fallback is comparatively rare.
code.recommendation: Use a dedicated streaming client without a whole-request Timeout (rely on attemptCtx / request-scoped deadlines), or set Transport.ResponseHeaderTimeout/IdleConnTimeout instead of Client.Timeout. Also add the r.Context().Err() guard from finding #1.
code.evidence: The mechanism is REAL but the binding-constraint claim does not hold in the default config, so I lower medium->low. Verified providerhttp/client.go:16-17 Init sets http.Client{Timeout: time.Duration(timeoutS)*time.Second}; Go's Client.Timeout does include response-body reads, so it can in principle abort a healthy stream. main.go:37 calls providerhttp.Init(cfg.ProviderHTTP.TimeoutS); config.go:254 ProviderHTTP.TimeoutS default = 300. BUT the per-attempt deadline that actually wraps the read is attemptTimeout(r) (server.go:1040 -> 1271-1276), which returns either retryPerAttemptTimeout (default 60s, server.go:316) or requestTimeout (server.go:313 default 300s, but config.go:240 RequestTimeoutS default = 280, wired at main.go:98). In every default configuration the per-attempt context deadline (60s or 280s) is <= the 300s client timeout, so attemptCtx fires FIRST and the client.Timeout is not the binding constraint; the finding's central assertion that 'the hard client.Timeout sits underneath it and fires independently [first]' only materializes if an operator sets RequestTimeoutS strictly greater than ProviderHTTP.TimeoutS (e.g. >300). It is still a genuine latent footgun (two independent ceilings, and whichever fires routes to the un-guarded 1686-1691 branch and bills FaultBreakerQualifying), but with the default 280<300 ordering it does not bite, the path is the rarely-used non-WS fallback, and the underlying mis-classification is already captured by finding #1. Low is the appropriate adjusted severity.

code.title: stickyStore LRU eviction does an O(n) full-map scan while holding the global sticky mutex on every insert once capacity is reached
code.description: When len(s.sticky) >= s.stickyMaxEntries (default 10000), stickyStore performs a full linear scan over the entire map under s.stickyMu (a plain sync.Mutex) to find the single oldest entry to evict (2415-2431). stickyLookup, purgeStickyAccount, and stickyStore all contend on this same mutex, so once the map saturates every subsequent pinned request pays an O(n) scan inside the critical section.
code.impact: Under sustained sticky load at capacity, routing latency on the hot path degrades and stickyMu contention rises. Not a correctness bug — bounded and self-limiting — but a throughput cliff at scale.
code.recommendation: Use an amortized structure (container/list-backed LRU or sharded map with per-shard locks) so eviction is O(1), or batch-evict a chunk of stale entries per scan. At minimum skip the scan when the prior sweep already dropped the map below capacity.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED, severity correctly LOW; the finding's worst-case framing is slightly pessimistic but the core concern is real. Verified server.go:2413-2431: s.stickyMu.Lock() (a plain sync.Mutex at server.go:63, shared with stickyLookup and purgeStickyAccount at 2440), then `if len(s.sticky) >= s.stickyMaxEntries` (default 10000, server.go:318) runs `for k, entry := range s.sticky` — a full-map scan under the lock. Mitigation the finding underweights: lines 2419-2422 delete ALL TTL-expired entries (now.Sub(entry.LastUsedAt) > stickyTTL, 30min default per server.go:317) during the same pass, so it is not strictly one-eviction-per-insert; the single-oldest delete at 2428-2430 only fires when, after purging expired entries, the map is still >= capacity. Thus the 'saturated map pays the full scan on essentially every pinned request' only holds when 10000+ entries are simultaneously within their 30-min TTL. The O(n)-under-a-plain-Mutex serialization of all sticky ops at saturation is a genuine throughput concern; low severity stands.

code.title: estimateTokens uses raw-byte/4 over the entire JSON envelope, over- and under-estimating context for capacity/preflight gating
code.description: estimateTokens returns len(raw)/4 over req.raw, the full serialized request body including JSON structural overhead (keys, braces, quotes, tool schemas, base64 image payloads). This value gates context-capacity rejection (p.MaxContextTokens < estimatedTokens at 2123/2620 -> 413 context_exceeds_capacity) and preflight (estimatedTokens <= s.preflightThreshold at 2642). Because structural bytes inflate the count, requests can be rejected as exceeding context when the real prompt-token count is well under the provider's window.
code.impact: Buyers may receive spurious 413 context_exceeds_capacity rejections (or unnecessary preflight round-trips) for prompts that actually fit, especially tool-heavy or multi-message requests. No security impact; affects routing acceptance accuracy.
code.recommendation: Estimate over message content only (sum of decoded content string lengths) rather than the full raw envelope, or raise the divisor margin / add a tolerance margin before issuing a hard 413.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED, low/info severity appropriate. server.go:2999-3005 estimateTokens = len(raw)/4 over the full json.RawMessage (min 1). Consumers verified: server.go:2073 estimatedTokens := estimateTokens(req.raw) in selectProviderExcluding; server.go:2123 `if p.MaxContextTokens < estimatedTokens { hasRoutableContextMiss = true }` (general routing); server.go:2620-2621 `if p.MaxContextTokens < estimatedTokens` -> http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge code context_exceeds_capacity (pinned path, a hard 413 with no tolerance margin); server.go:2642 `if estimatedTokens <= s.preflightThreshold` gates preflight (threshold 4096, server.go:306). The estimate is biased HIGH (structural JSON overhead inflates len(raw)), so the realistic failure mode is exactly the spurious 413 the finding describes. It is intentionally a rough heuristic, but it is indeed the sole gate for the pinned-provider hard 413 with no margin, so the finding is accurate; severity stays low.

code.title: Provider-supplied routing metrics (slots_free, slots_total, max_concurrency, max_context_tokens, ram_gb) are never bounds-checked
code.description: requireInt() only checks JSON-unmarshal success; it imposes no non-negativity or sanity bound. The parsed values flow unvalidated into pool.Provider via prepareProviderAdmission (server.go:519-522, where SlotsFree/SlotsTotal are initialized to hello.MaxConcurrency) and via ApplyHeartbeat (pool/provider.go:427-430) and ApplyStateUpdate. By contrast ParseDrainStatus DOES validate InflightRequests>=0 and EstimatedDrainSeconds>=0 (messages.go:577-582), showing the codebase knows to do this but omits it for the routing-critical fields. No check enforces slots_free<=slots_total either.
code.impact: A malicious/untrusted provider can advertise slots_free=2147483647 and max_context_tokens=2147483647. The buyer scheduler sorts least-loaded by SlotsFree (buyer/server.go:2255-2284) and gates routing on MaxContextTokens>=estimatedTokens (buyer/server.go:2123, 2620, 2663) and SlotsFree>0 (pool/provider.go:107). The attacker thus wins routing for every request and for arbitrarily large contexts it cannot actually serve, degrading the network and starving honest providers. Negative values are also accepted and could produce surprising comparisons elsewhere.
code.recommendation: Validate these integers at parse time in ParseHello / ParseHeartbeat / parseAuthInitial: reject negative values, reject slots_free>slots_total, and clamp/reject implausibly large max_context_tokens / max_concurrency to a configured ceiling. Mirror the existing pattern in ParseDrainStatus.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED that the input-validation gap exists: requireInt (messages.go:448-450) only does json.Unmarshal and never bounds-checks, unlike requireString (which rejects empty) and ParseDrainStatus (messages.go:577-582) which explicitly rejects InflightRequests<0 and EstimatedDrainSeconds<0. The unvalidated ints flow straight into pool.Provider at server.go:519-522 (SlotsFree/SlotsTotal=hello.MaxConcurrency, MaxContextTokens=hello.MaxContextTokens) and ApplyHeartbeat at provider.go:427-430 — no bounds anywhere in that path. So the core 'never bounds-checked' claim is real. HOWEVER the headline impact is partly INCORRECT: the default-objective sort (buyer/server.go:2280-2285) is `candidates[i].SlotsFree < candidates[j].SlotsFree`, i.e. ASCENDING, and selection iterates from index 0 returning the first preflight pass (2188-2192). Lowest SlotsFree is therefore selected first, so an attacker advertising slots_free=MAX_INT ranks LAST, not first — the 'wins routing for every request via slots_free' mechanism is inverted. The genuinely exploitable vector is MaxContextTokens: the exclusion gate `p.MaxContextTokens < estimatedTokens` (2123, 2620, 2663) lets a liar advertising max_context_tokens=MAX_INT stay eligible for arbitrarily large contexts it cannot serve, and in the 'balanced' objective the normalized ctx component carries 0.2 weight (balancedScores, server.go:2304) so a huge value inflates the score. The RoutingEligible gate (provider.go:103-107) requires SlotsFree>0, so negative slots_free fails closed (no exploit there). Net: a real, untrusted-provider input-validation gap with genuine routing impact via MaxContextTokens, but no money/pinned impact and the slots_free amplification claimed is not achievable; severity reduced from medium to low.

code.title: WebSocket upgrade completes before token validation, allowing unauthenticated connection setup
code.description: handleProvider() calls gobwas.UpgradeHTTP(r, w) FIRST (line 169) and only afterward calls validateProviderToken(r) (line 174). On auth failure it writes a close frame and schedules conn.Close() via time.AfterFunc(100ms) (line 177). The 101 Switching Protocols handshake, socket allocation, and a 100ms-lived timer are therefore granted to any unauthenticated client before the bearer token is checked.
code.impact: An attacker with no valid provider token can repeatedly drive full WS upgrades plus a 100ms-pending close timer, a modest connection/timer-churn amplification. No protocol state beyond the raw conn is reached, so impact is limited, but it weakens the 'auth before resource commitment' principle on an internet-reachable endpoint.
code.recommendation: Validate the Authorization bearer token from the *http.Request before calling UpgradeHTTP; on failure return an HTTP 401 without upgrading. The token is already available pre-upgrade (validateProviderToken only needs r), so the reorder is mechanical.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED exactly as described. server.go:169 calls gobwas.UpgradeHTTP(r, w) unconditionally first; server.go:174 calls s.validateProviderToken(r) afterward; on failure server.go:176-178 writes a close frame and schedules `time.AfterFunc(100*time.Millisecond, func(){ _ = conn.Close() })`. validateProviderToken (server.go:183-209) reads only r.Header.Get('Authorization') and r.Context() — it never touches the upgraded conn — so the reorder-before-upgrade is mechanically possible as the recommendation states. The impact characterization is accurate and conservative: no protocol/session state is reached before the token check (handleConn at 211 only runs after `ok`), so this is a low-severity auth-ordering / minor amplification issue. Severity low is justified; kept.

code.title: RefundRequest pops the most-recent window timestamp regardless of which request actually failed
code.description: TryReserveRequest appends now() to requestWindows[providerID] and increments rec.TotalRequestsServed. RefundRequest unconditionally drops the LAST element of the window (window[:len(window)-1]) and decrements TotalRequestsServed. With concurrent in-flight requests for the same provisional provider, the refunded slot may correspond to a different (newer, still-in-flight) request than the one that failed, because the slice is LIFO rather than keyed to the specific reservation. The refund is also only triggered on a subset of failure results (buyer/server.go:1326-1334: ProviderDisconnected / QueueFull), so quota can drift.
code.impact: Provisional per-hour quota accounting can drift up or down under concurrency, letting a provider slightly exceed its ProvisionalQuotaPerHour or be under-charged. Bounded by the quota size and provisional-only; no money or pinned-provider impact.
code.recommendation: Make reservations refundable by identity: have TryReserveRequest return a token/timestamp and have RefundRequest remove that specific entry, or remove the oldest expired-then-matching entry rather than blindly the last.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED. TryReserveRequest (admission.go:140-145) appends `now` to requestWindows[providerID] and increments rec.TotalRequestsServed (147). RefundRequest (admission.go:160-163) unconditionally drops the last element: `a.requestWindows[provider.ProviderID] = window[:len(window)-1]` with only a `len(window) > 0` guard — it is NOT keyed to the failed request's timestamp, so under concurrent in-flight reservations it removes whichever entry happens to be last, exactly the LIFO mismatch described. The subset-of-failures trigger is also confirmed at buyer/server.go:1326-1327 (refund only on wsForwardProviderDisconnected for streaming) and 1332-1333 (only wsForwardQueueFull / wsForwardProviderDisconnected for non-streaming). Both operations hold a.mu (admission.go:137-138, 158-159) so there is no slice corruption or race on the data structure itself — only the accounting picks the wrong (still-valid) entry. Impact is correctly scoped: provisional-tier only (early return at 134-135 / 155-156), bounded by ProvisionalQuotaPerHour, no money/pinned impact. Low severity is justified; kept.

code.title: warmup-fallback timer keyed only by providerID can race a reconnect and is not cleaned on disconnect
code.description: markDegradedForWarmup stores a time.AfterFunc timer in s.timers keyed by providerID only (line 1187). handleDisconnect (1190-1210) clears the warmup gate and session but never deletes s.timers[providerID]. The timer's own callback eventually self-deletes (1179/1185) and its MarkState call is guarded by assignedID (pool/provider.go:225), so a stale timer cannot resurrect a replaced session — but until it fires, a disconnected/reconnected provider leaves a dangling timer, and a reconnect under the same providerID with a different assignedID relies entirely on the assignedID guard inside MarkState to avoid acting on the wrong session.
code.impact: Minor: a short-lived dangling timer per disconnect during the warmup window; no incorrect state transition because MarkState validates assignedID. Becomes a (small, self-healing) timer accumulation only under rapid connect/disconnect churn.
code.recommendation: In handleDisconnect, do s.timers.LoadAndDelete(providerID) and Stop() the timer, mirroring the cleanup done for warmups. Optionally key the timer by sessionKey(providerID, assignedID) for symmetry with sessions.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED. markDegradedForWarmup stores the AfterFunc timer keyed by providerID only: `s.timers.Store(providerID, timer)` (server.go:1187). handleDisconnect (server.go:1190-1210) calls clearWarmupGate, closes/deletes the session, and MarkState/RemoveIfSession — but contains NO s.timers delete for providerID, confirming the missing cleanup. The self-healing claim is also verified: the timer callback deletes itself at server.go:1179 and 1185, and its state mutation goes through MarkState which returns false unless `p.AssignedID == assignedID` (pool/provider.go:225), so a stale timer cannot flip a replaced session to Ready. Net effect is exactly as described — a short-lived dangling timer per warmup-window disconnect, self-healing, no incorrect state transition, accumulation only under rapid churn. Correctly rated low; kept.

code.title: send() silently drops control messages on write-buffer backpressure
code.lines: 118-130 (send); used at server.go:1048 DrainAll, server.go:1123 warm_up, admin_endpoints.go:104 reject-drain, relay.go:195 cancel_request
code.description: providerSession.send does a non-blocking channel send and returns ErrRelayBackpressure when writeCh (default cap 64, WS.WriteBufferSize) is full. Several control-plane callers ignore that error: cancelActive (relay.go:194-195) does `_ = ps.send(b)` for the cancel_request, and handleAdminReject (admin_endpoints.go:104) does `_ = session.send(...)` for the drain. If the buffer is saturated by inference chunks, a cancel or drain can be dropped with no retry.
code.impact: Under write-buffer saturation a cancellation or drain instruction may never reach the provider, so the provider can keep generating (and the buyer keeps being relayed/charged) after the buyer cancelled, or a blacklisted provider may not drain promptly. DrainAll and handleBlacklist DO surface the error (they log / report drain_sent), so impact is confined to the ignored callers.
code.recommendation: Treat backpressure on control frames as significant: log it and, for cancel/drain, fall back to closing the connection (conn.Close) so the provider stops, rather than silently dropping. At minimum stop discarding the error in cancelActive and handleAdminReject.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED with a partial mitigation worth noting. send() (relay.go:118-130) does a non-blocking `select { case ps.writeCh <- payload: return nil; default: return ErrRelayBackpressure }`; writeCh is `make(chan []byte, bufferSize)` (relay.go:93) where bufferSize = s.cfg.WS.WriteBufferSize (server.go:603), consistent with the cited default cap. The asymmetry is real: cancelActive ignores the error with `_ = ps.send(b)` for cancel_request (relay.go:195), and handleAdminReject ignores it with `_ = session.send([]byte(`{"type":"drain"}`))` (admin_endpoints.go:104) — whereas DrainAll surfaces it (`if err := session.send(...); err != nil { log.Warn(...); continue }`, server.go:1048-1051) and the warm_up caller logs it (server.go:1123-1125). MITIGATION the finding understates: the admin-reject path immediately schedules `time.AfterFunc(200*time.Millisecond, ...)` that calls s.close(session.conn,...) and session.conn.Close() (admin_endpoints.go:106-109), so a dropped drain frame is followed by a forced connection close 200ms later — the provider IS stopped on that path even if the drain frame is lost. cancelActive (relay.go:189-203) has NO such fallback close, so a dropped cancel_request is the genuinely unmitigated case (provider keeps generating/charging after buyer cancel). Real reliability issue requiring buffer saturation to trigger; low severity is justified; kept.

code.title: Inconsistent blocking vs non-blocking sends to active.errs (NAK fallback path)
code.description: Every other writer to active.errs uses a non-blocking `select { case errs<-err: default: }` (failActive:170, cancelActive:197, failAll:227). The NAK fallback path at line 609 instead does a bare blocking send `active.errs <- ErrRelayNAKFallback`. It is currently safe because removeActive (line 608) atomically takes sole ownership of the active and errs is buffered(1) and empty at that point, so the send cannot block. But the asymmetry is a latent hazard: any future change that pre-populates errs or reuses the active would deadlock the single per-connection read loop (handleNAK runs inline under readProviderLoop).
code.impact: No current deadlock. Latent risk: if invariants change, a blocking send here would stall the provider read loop and wedge that provider's session.
code.recommendation: Use the same non-blocking select/default pattern at line 609 as the other errs writers, for consistency and defense-in-depth.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED. relay.go:609 is a bare blocking send `active.errs <- ErrRelayNAKFallback`, whereas failActive (relay.go:170-173), cancelActive (relay.go:197-200), and failAll (relay.go:227-230) all use the non-blocking `select { case ...errs <- err: default: }` pattern — the asymmetry is exactly as described. The 'currently safe' reasoning is verified: errs is created as `make(chan error, 1)` (relay.go:149, buffered 1), and line 608 calls session.removeActive(nak.InReplyTo) which under activeMu deletes the entry from ps.active and returns it (relay.go:155-162), giving sole ownership; at that point errs is empty, so the buffered-1 send at 609 cannot block. So there is no current deadlock, only a latent inconsistency: if a future change ever pre-fills errs or shares the active, this blocking send would stall the inline readProviderLoop handler. Info severity is appropriate (style/defense-in-depth, no live bug); kept.

code.title: Pillar-D output-size cap off-by-one: stream prematurely closed when output exactly equals the cap
code.description: In capChoiceContent, when content fits within the cap (contentBytes <= remaining) the code adds the bytes and then checks `if g.outputBytes >= capBytes { g.capClosed = true; return true }`. Returning true here signals 'truncated' even though NO truncation occurred — the content was fully preserved and exactly filled the budget. enforceOutputCap then reports truncated=true, and CheckStreamingChunk sets stop=true, does `events = events[:i+1]`, and appends an extra `data: [DONE]`. Verified empirically: a single 32-byte content chunk under OutputSizeCapBytes=32 returns stop=true and an injected [DONE], even though the legitimate output was complete and within budget. The same path also blanks any further content (line 285, container[key]="") if more arrives after capClosed flips at the exact boundary.
code.impact: A provider whose legitimate completion exactly equals the configured cap (or whose first chunk exactly fills it) has its SSE stream truncated one chunk early with a spurious [DONE], and any subsequent legitimate chunks in the same response are blanked. The buyer receives a complete-looking but prematurely terminated response. No money-loss or security bypass; a reliability/correctness defect that silently drops valid output at the exact-cap boundary.
code.recommendation: Change the boundary test so reaching the cap exactly is not treated as a truncation. Either use `if g.outputBytes > capBytes` (effectively dropping the early-close on the <= branch) or restructure capChoiceContent to return false when content was fully emitted and only return true when bytes were actually dropped. Keep capClosed=true so that a *later* chunk is what triggers truncation, rather than closing on a chunk that fit exactly. Add a regression test for the exact-cap boundary.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED the logic but downgraded low->info. pillar_d.go:296-302: when `contentBytes <= remaining`, it does `g.outputBytes += contentBytes; if g.outputBytes >= capBytes { g.capClosed = true; return true }`. The `>=` (not `>`) means an exact-cap fill returns truncated=true with no bytes dropped. enforceOutputCap (line 263-273) propagates that true; CheckStreamingChunk (lines 106-117) then does `events = events[:i+1]; stop = true; break`, and renderSSEDataEvents (lines 238-240) appends `data: [DONE]\n\n` when stop. The guard is constructed ONCE per request (buyer/server.go:1432, outside the loop) and CheckStreamingChunk is called per-chunk via writeChunk (line 1459), so outputBytes/capClosed persist across chunks and a `stop=true` triggers relay.Cancel("tier2_output_truncated") (line 1486) ending the stream — so the early-close is real. HOWEVER the impact is overstated: pillar_d_test.go:33-58 (TestPillarDACD1StreamingASCIIExactCap, cap=32) asserts stop=true and the [DONE] suffix as the INTENDED contract for a chunk that hits the cap, so this is designed behavior at the cap boundary, not an accidental regression. config.go:285 sets OutputSizeCapBytes default 0 (feature disabled) and config.go:287 DefaultOutputSizeCapBytes default 1048576 (1 MiB). A legitimate completion landing byte-exact on a 1 MiB cap is vanishingly improbable, and blanking content after the cap is the cap doing its job. The genuine defect is the cosmetic spurious-[DONE]/one-chunk-early-close precisely at the boundary, which is info-severity, not a behavior that meaningfully drops valid output in practice.

code.title: Empty challenge makes the attestation replay/freshness binding a no-op (defense-in-depth gap)
code.description: VerifyAttestationToken computes `wantChallenge := base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(challenge)` and rejects unless `token.Challenge == wantChallenge`. When the caller passes an empty challenge ([]byte{} or nil), wantChallenge is the empty string, so any token carrying an empty Challenge field passes the replay check, and (for the mock path) yields AttestationStatusAttested. Verified empirically: BuildMockAttestationToken with an empty challenge + VerifyAttestationToken with empty challenge returns `attested`. The function does not assert len(challenge) > 0. The production WS caller (ws/server.go:329 randomBytes(32) -> :382) always supplies 32 random bytes, so this is NOT currently exploitable in the live handshake — but the public API contract permits a caller to silently disable replay protection by passing an empty nonce.
code.impact: Not exploitable through the current WS path (challenge is always 32 random bytes). As a latent contract defect: any future or alternate caller (e.g. a tool, test harness, or refactor) that passes an empty challenge silently removes the per-session replay/freshness binding, allowing a captured attestation token with an empty Challenge to be replayed/accepted. This is the component's primary anti-replay control, so a hard guard is warranted.
code.recommendation: Reject empty challenges explicitly at the top of VerifyAttestationToken when attestation is being evaluated (e.g. `if len(challenge) == 0 { return AttestationStatusFailed }`, or require a minimum length such as 16 bytes), so the replay binding cannot be silently disabled by a caller. Document the non-empty-challenge precondition on the exported function.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED as a latent contract defect; severity low is correct. pillar_c.go:119-123: `wantChallenge := base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(challenge); if token.Challenge != wantChallenge { ... return AttestationStatusStale }`. For challenge=nil/[]byte{}, EncodeToString returns "", so a token with Challenge=="" passes. There is no `len(challenge)==0` guard anywhere in the function (read lines 83-157). I enumerated ALL non-test callers via grep: exactly two besides the definition — ws/server.go:382 and cmd/tier2-mda-artifact/main.go:599. ws/server.go:329 generates `challengeBytes, err := randomBytes(32)` and passes those exact bytes at line 382, so the live handshake is safe. The artifact CLI at main.go:514-519 decodes the challenge and then explicitly enforces `if len(challengeBytes) != 32 { return error }` before calling VerifyAttestationToken at line 599 — so the second caller is also safe. The empty-challenge path is reachable only by direct library/test use. This is therefore a real but non-exploitable defense-in-depth gap on the exported API; low severity unchanged.

code.title: Certificate chain verification uses ExtKeyUsageAny, disabling EKU enforcement on the MDA chain
code.description: verifyAttestationCertificateChain calls certs[0].Verify with `KeyUsages: []x509.ExtKeyUsage{x509.ExtKeyUsageAny}`, which tells crypto/x509 to accept the leaf regardless of its Extended Key Usage. The only structural constraints enforced are chaining to an operator-configured root plus validity period; all attestation-specific assurance then rests on the downstream MDA extension checks (freshness, device property, CSR key binding, binding signature). Any certificate the configured root (or an intermediate it trusts) issued for a different EKU would also satisfy the chain step.
code.impact: Weakens the chain check to 'issued by the trusted root, any purpose'. For Apple MDA leaf certs this is likely intentional (they may not carry a coordinator-specific EKU), and the MDA extension + binding-signature checks still gate the positive Attested result, so a non-MDA cert from the same root would fail those later checks. The risk is that the structural trust decision is broader than necessary and relies entirely on the extension checks being complete and the operator root being narrowly scoped to MDA issuance.
code.recommendation: Confirm against Apple MDA cert profiles whether a specific EKU or a required MDA leaf marker OID can be asserted; if so, replace ExtKeyUsageAny with the specific EKU or add an explicit leaf-marker check. If MDA leaves genuinely carry no usable EKU, document the rationale in a code comment so the broad setting is not mistaken for an oversight, and ensure operator docs require the configured root be MDA-issuance-scoped.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED the code (pillar_c.go:675 `KeyUsages: []x509.ExtKeyUsage{x509.ExtKeyUsageAny}` inside certs[0].Verify) but downgraded low->info. The chain check is only ONE of seven sequential gates that must ALL pass before a positive AttestationStatusAttested is returned — verifyProductionMDAChainShape (lines 196-233) runs, in order: verifyAttestationCertificateChain (196), verifyMDALeafPublicKey (200, requires ECDSA P-256/P-384), verifyMDAFreshness (204, ConstantTimeCompare of a SHA-256 freshness digest against the device-attest token at lines 268-274), verifyMDADeviceProperties (208), verifyMDACSRKeyBinding (212, CSR signature check + RawSubjectPublicKeyInfo equality at lines 303-307), and verifyAttestationBindingSignature (228) — only then line 232-233 returns Attested. A non-MDA cert issued by the same root would pass the EKU-any chain step but fail freshness/CSR-binding/binding-signature. The finding text itself concedes ExtKeyUsageAny is 'likely intentional' for Apple MDA leaves. With low confidence and the broad setting being a documentation/scoping observation rather than a defect (Apple MDA leaves plausibly carry no coordinator EKU), info is the justified severity.

code.title: Device-property check passes on the first non-blank recognized OID rather than asserting required properties
code.description: verifyMDADeviceProperties iterates the recognized MDA device-property OIDs and returns success ('') as soon as it finds the first one present and non-blank; it only fails if none are present or the first-found one is blank. mdaExtensionValueBlank returns false (i.e. 'not blank' -> treated as valid) for any value that is non-empty and does not ASN.1-decode to an empty string/octet-string, so arbitrary non-empty extension bytes count as a valid device property. There is no assertion that any *specific* property (e.g. OS version, SIP status, secure boot, third-party kext status) is present, nor that values are well-formed.
code.impact: A provider with a genuine root-anchored MDA leaf could include a single arbitrary non-empty recognized extension and satisfy the device-property gate without the coordinator validating which security-relevant properties (SIP enabled, secure boot, no third-party kexts) are actually attested. This narrows the integrity signal the gate provides. Requires a validly-chained MDA leaf, so impact is bounded; flagged as a hardening observation rather than a bypass.
code.recommendation: Confirm against the intended SPEC-008 policy which device properties are mandatory and, if specific ones are required (e.g. secure boot / SIP status), check those OIDs explicitly and validate their decoded values against an allowed-state policy rather than accepting the first present-and-non-blank recognized OID. Tighten mdaExtensionValueBlank to validate the expected ASN.1 type per OID.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED at info severity (unchanged). pillar_c.go:281-293: verifyMDADeviceProperties loops `for _, oid := range mdaRecognizedDevicePropertyExtensions`, skips OIDs not present (continue at line 285), and on the FIRST present OID immediately `return ""` (success) at line 290 unless mdaExtensionValueBlank is true; it only returns the failure reason 'mda_device_property_missing' (line 292) if NONE of the recognized OIDs are present. The recognized set (lines 44-54) includes SIP status, secure boot status, and third-party kernel extensions OIDs, but none is individually required — any one present-and-non-blank OID (e.g. just the serial number, mdaOIDSerialNumber line 45) satisfies the gate. mdaExtensionValueBlank (lines 485-498) returns true only for empty bytes, ASN.1 empty string, or ASN.1 empty octet-string; otherwise returns false (line 497), so arbitrary non-empty bytes that don't decode to one of those count as 'not blank' = valid, with no per-OID type/value-state validation. The reading is accurate. This still requires a fully root-chained MDA leaf that passes all other gates (freshness, CSR binding, binding signature per lines 200-231), so it is a bounded hardening observation, not a bypass — info is correct.

code.title: request_log table has no retention/pruning — unbounded growth and indefinite buyer-IP (PII) retention
code.description: The requestlog Store only ever INSERTs into request_log (insert() at lines 144-188; migrate() at 85-115). A repo-wide search for DELETE/prune/retention/cleanup/expire/VACUUM against request_log returns nothing — there is no scheduled prune, no max-row cap, and no TTL. Every buyer chat-completion writes one row per attempt (internal/buyer/server.go:830 logRowWithBilling), and each row stores buyer_ip (store.go schema line 100, populated from buyerIP(r.RemoteAddr) at server.go:841), pref_header, provider_header, model, and error text. On a production money-moving coordinator this table grows without bound for the life of the deployment.
code.impact: Two coupled failures: (a) disk/DB growth is unbounded; (b) buyer IP addresses (PII) are retained indefinitely with no expiry, and are readable via the operator API (SessionDetail) for the life of the deployment.
code.recommendation: Add a retention job (e.g. periodic DELETE FROM request_log WHERE ts_utc < ? for a configurable cutoff, then PRAGMA wal_checkpoint/incremental VACUUM) driven by a config value analogous to config.go ProvisionalRetentionDays. Separately, consider not persisting raw buyer_ip beyond a short window (or storing a truncated/hashed form).
code.evidence: CONFIRMED that no retention exists: grep -rniE 'DELETE FROM request_log|prune|retention|cleanup|expire|VACUUM|wal_checkpoint' over internal/ returns zero request_log-related hits (all matches are session/catalog/token expiry in tier2, pool, ws — unrelated). store.go has exactly one write path: insert() (lines 144-188) does INSERT INTO request_log; migrate() (85-115) only CREATEs the table + two indexes; no DELETE/prune method exists on Store. buyer_ip is `buyer_ip TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''` (store.go:100), populated in buyer/server.go:841 `BuyerIP: buyerIP(r.RemoteAddr)` where buyerIP (server.go:2851) returns the host part of RemoteAddr. SessionDetail (store.go:65) selects buyer_ip into the operator-API response. So both sub-claims (unbounded growth + indefinite PII) are factually correct. I DOWNGRADE high->medium because: (1) it is a SQLite single-file store keyed by an indexed ts_utc/id, and explorer window scans are bounded by parseWindow max-window enforcement (handlers.go:495-497) + LIMIT (capped 200, handlers.go:460-462) — query latency degrades gradually with row count, not catastrophically; (2) RemoteAddr on a coordinator behind a tunnel/proxy is frequently the proxy/tunnel address rather than a true end-buyer IP, weakening the PII-severity claim; (3) this is operational/compliance hygiene with no integrity, fund-loss, or availability break and no remote trigger beyond ordinary traffic. Real and worth fixing, but not HIGH.

code.title: Single-event lookup /activity/{id} only scans the first page within the default window, returns spurious 404
code.description: handleActivity computes a window (default ActivityDefaultWindowHours), fetches one page (limit, capped at 200 via windowAndLimit), federates+truncates to `limit` via federatedActivityPage (line 345), and only THEN, when eventID != "", linearly scans that single truncated page for source_id/request_id == eventID (lines 346-352). If the matching event is real but sorts beyond the first `limit` rows, or is older than the default window, the loop never finds it and the handler returns 404 (line 353). The lookup never issues an ID-targeted query against the DB.
code.impact: An operator deep-linking to /activity/{id} for an event not in the most recent ~50-200 events of the default window gets 'not found' for an event that exists in request_log; the same event is retrievable via /sessions/{request_id}.
code.recommendation: For the eventID branch, query the row directly by request_id/source_id (the store already supports request_id lookups, cf. SessionDetail) instead of scanning a paginated page, or at minimum widen the lookup to the full configured max window. Add a regression test that requests /activity/{id} for an event beyond page one.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED mechanically: handleActivity (handlers.go:290) calls windowAndLimit with ActivityDefaultWindowHours (cfg default 24h, config.go:331) and ActivityMaxWindowDays (default 7, config.go:330); limit defaults to 50, capped at 200 (handlers.go:451-462). It calls store.Activity once (line 318) for the current window, then federatedActivityPage truncates to `limit` (line 345). The eventID branch (lines 346-354) iterates ONLY over that truncated `items` slice and returns 404 (line 353) if not found — there is genuinely NO id-targeted DB query in this path (store.go has no GetActivityByID; only Activity() windowed scans and SessionDetail by request_id). So the bug is real. I DOWNGRADE medium->low because: (1) the request defaults are caller-controllable — /activity/{id}?window_hours=...&limit=200&from=...&to=... lets the operator widen the window and page size up to the 7-day/200-row maxima, so it is not an unconditional failure; (2) the dashboard cross-view links it claims to break: TestDashboardCrossViewLinkWiring (handlers_test.go:632-645) only asserts sessions/buyers/providers/settlements deep-links in dashboard.js — it does NOT assert an /activity/{id} deep-link, and grep of dashboard.js shows no activity/${id} navigation, so the stated user-facing trigger (operators deep-linking events) is not actually wired in the shipped UI; (3) the same data is fully retrievable via /sessions/{request_id} (store.go:61 SessionDetail) and via /activity paging, so it is a convenience/correctness gap with a workaround, not data loss. Low severity is the accurate rating.

code.title: Explorer rate-limiter map never evicts stale per-IP keys (slow unbounded memory growth)
code.description: allowRequest trims expired timestamps WITHIN each key's slice (lines 515-520) but never deletes the key itself from h.stamps. Once a source IP has made one authenticated request, h.stamps[key] persists forever even after all its timestamps age out (the trimmed slice is written back as an empty-but-present entry at line 522/526). The map accumulates one entry per distinct authenticated client IP for the lifetime of the process. Auth (handlers.go:56) precedes allowRequest (line 60), so only valid-operator-token requests populate the map.
code.impact: Memory grows proportionally to distinct source IPs that successfully authenticate. Pre-auth traffic cannot grow the map. Not internet-exploitable pre-auth DoS; bounded to a leaked/shared operator token or an operator behind many rotating IPs.
code.recommendation: After trimming, delete keys whose slice is empty: if len(stamps) == 0 { delete(h.stamps, key) } else { h.stamps[key] = stamps }. Optionally add a periodic idle-key sweep. Add a test driving many distinct RemoteAddr values asserting no empty entries are retained.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED as described and severity is already correctly LOW. allowRequest (handlers.go:505-528): line 515 `stamps := h.stamps[key][:0]`, loop 516-520 keeps only timestamps After(cutoff), then line 522 (cap-exceeded path) and line 526 (normal path) both write `h.stamps[key] = stamps` — there is no `delete(h.stamps, key)` anywhere, so a key with an empty trimmed slice remains present. The auth-before-ratelimit ordering is real: ServeHTTP checks h.authorized(r) at line 56 (returns 401 on failure) BEFORE h.allowRequest at line 60, and authorized() (line 501-503) requires the exact operator bearer token, so unauthenticated callers cannot seed the map. The map is keyed by clientAddrKey(r.RemoteAddr) = host (lines 530-536). Confirmed leak, but the auth gate plus 'process restart resets the map' bound the practical impact, and the reviewer already rated it low — verdict confirmed, severity unchanged.

code.title: Dead code: countReady is never referenced
code.description: func countReady(providers []pool.Provider) int is defined but has zero call sites across the entire module. poolOverview (handlers.go:584-596) computes ready_providers inline instead of using it.
code.impact: No runtime impact; minor maintenance noise and latent risk that future edits diverge the two ready-count code paths. go vet does not flag unused package-level functions.
code.recommendation: Remove countReady, or wire poolOverview to use it so there is a single source of truth for the ready-provider count.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED. grep -rn 'countReady' over internal/ returns exactly ONE line: store.go:545, the definition itself — zero call sites anywhere in the module. The function body (store.go:545-553) counts pool.StateReady providers; poolOverview (handlers.go:571-610) independently computes ready_providers inline via `case pool.StateReady: out["ready_providers"] = ...+1` (line 586-588). So the dead code is real and the duplicate-logic risk is accurate. Correctly rated info — purely cosmetic, no behavioral impact. Verdict confirmed, severity unchanged.

code.title: Operator token compared with non-constant-time string equality
code.description: authorized() compares the bearer token with plain ==: r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+h.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey. Go string == short-circuits on the first differing byte, leaking a timing signal proportional to the matching prefix length. This guards the explorer, which is mounted on the public-internet WS mux and fronts the money authority's session/ledger/settlement data. subtle.ConstantTimeCompare is available and used elsewhere (internal/buyer/server.go:2613, internal/tier2/pillar_c.go:270); the WS admin handler at internal/ws/server.go:1481 uses the same non-constant-time pattern.
code.impact: A remote attacker issuing many requests could in principle mount a timing attack to recover the operator token byte-by-byte. Practical network exploitability is limited by jitter and the high-entropy token, but a money-authority admin API warrants constant-time comparison.
code.recommendation: Replace == with subtle.ConstantTimeCompare over the full Authorization header, e.g. expected := "Bearer "+h.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey; return h.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey != "" && subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(got), []byte(expected)) == 1. Apply the same fix to the ws/server.go admin gate for consistency.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED factually, severity correctly LOW. authorized() (handlers.go:501-503) is exactly `return h.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey != "" && r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+h.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey` — plain == on a secret. subtle.ConstantTimeCompare is indeed used elsewhere: grep confirms buyer/server.go:2613 and tier2/pillar_c.go:270 both use it. The ws sibling gate authorizedOperator (ws/server.go:1480-1482) uses the same `== "Bearer "+OperatorKey` pattern (reviewer cited line 1481; actual func at 1480). The public-mux claim is CONFIRMED: ws/server.go Handler() (line 153-156) mounts the explorer on the SAME mux as /ws/provider (line 158), and main.go:113 serves wsServer.Handler() on providerAddr via ListenAndServe (line 137) — so the explorer is reachable on the provider-facing listener. I keep LOW (not downgrading to info) because the surface is a money-authority admin API and the fix is trivial, but I also do NOT raise it: remote timing attacks against an HTTP string compare are heavily masked by network jitter, Go scheduler noise, and TLS, and the token is high-entropy random — practical recovery over a network is near-infeasible. The reviewer's own 'medium confidence' and low severity are well-calibrated; verdict confirmed.

code.title: Token revocation by 6-char prefix can revoke unrelated tokens and kick the wrong provider (no prefix uniqueness)
code.description: token_prefix is the first 6 hex chars of the token (line 136: prefix := token[:6]) = 24 bits of entropy. The schema (lines 73-82) puts UNIQUE only on token_hash, NOT on token_prefix, and there is no per-prefix dedup at issuance. RevokeToken (line 192) runs `UPDATE provider_tokens SET revoked_at=? WHERE token_prefix=? AND revoked_at IS NULL`, which matches and revokes EVERY active token sharing that prefix. The code only checks `affected == 0` (line 200); it never detects `affected > 1`. It then calls tokenByPrefix (line 225) which returns a single row via `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1`, so the returned TokenRecord can describe a different token than the one(s) actually revoked. With a 24-bit prefix space, birthday collisions become likely in the low thousands of issued tokens.
code.impact: An operator revoking provider A's token can silently revoke provider B's still-valid token (availability/DoS for the colliding provider, real money impact since revocation kicks a paid provider off the pool). Worse, cmd/coordinator-cli revoke-and-kick consumes record.ProviderID from the LIMIT-1 row (cmd/coordinator-cli/main.go:137) and POSTs /admin/blacklist for whichever provider that row happens to be — so a prefix collision can blacklist the wrong provider entirely.
code.recommendation: Resolve revocation by the full token_hash (require the operator to paste the full token, or store and select the token by id/hash) instead of a truncated prefix; OR add a UNIQUE constraint on token_prefix and reject issuance on collision; OR at minimum treat affected>1 as an error in RevokeToken and refuse to act when more than one row matches. The CLI should print the exact provider_id(s) actually affected rather than a LIMIT-1 best guess.
code.evidence: Every code claim is verified. tokens.go:136 `prefix := token[:6]` over a 64-char hex token = 24 bits. Schema tokens.go:75-76 declares `token_hash TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE` and `token_prefix TEXT NOT NULL` (no UNIQUE on prefix). RevokeToken tokens.go:190 re-truncates `prefix := tokenPrefix[:6]` then tokens.go:192 UPDATEs by `token_prefix = ?` (matches ALL active rows), and tokens.go:196-202 only branches on `affected == 0` — there is no `affected > 1` check. tokenByPrefix tokens.go:225 selects `... WHERE token_prefix = ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1`, so the returned record is whichever row sorts last, not necessarily the revoked one. CLI consumes it at cmd/coordinator-cli/main.go:137 `targetProviderID := record.ProviderID` and POSTs /admin/blacklist via kickProvider (main.go:147,154-177). The defect is real. Downgraded from medium to low because: (1) likelihood at this deployment's scale is negligible — project memory and specs describe a handful of providers (M1/M4 etc.), and a 24-bit birthday collision requires ~thousands of concurrently-active prefixes to become probable; (2) the CLI provides a mitigation: revokeAndKick (main.go:138-143) accepts `--provider-id` and refuses with `token belongs to provider_id %s, refusing to kick %s` on mismatch (covered by TestRevokeAndKickRejectsMismatchedProviderOverride, main_test.go:50-62), so a careful operator can pin the target; (3) revoke/blacklist are privileged operator-only actions, not attacker-reachable. It is a latent correctness/robustness bug (the affected>1 gap is the cheapest real fix), not a medium-impact production hazard.

code.title: mockprovider double-closes stopHB channel -> deterministic panic on drain/shutdown
code.description: stopHB (created line 303) is closed from three unsynchronized sites: the signal-handler goroutine (line 367), the read-loop on ws read error (line 375), and the handleInbound 'drain' shutdown callback (line 382). close() on an already-closed channel panics. On the coordinator-initiated drain path this is deterministic: handleInbound for a `drain` message invokes the shutdown closure (line 381-384 / 436-439) which closes stopHB at 382 and calls conn.Close(); control returns to the for-loop, the next wsutil.ReadServerData fails because the conn is closed, and line 375 closes stopHB a SECOND time -> panic. The SIGINT path has the same race: the signal goroutine closes stopHB at 367 and conn at 368, then the read loop errors and closes again at 375.
code.impact: The mock provider panics during normal drain/shutdown, which is exactly the sequence the AC drain/failover stress tests exercise. This produces flaky, hard-to-diagnose test failures and crash output that can mask the behavior under test. No production impact (test tool only), but it undermines the reliability of the drain test harness.
code.recommendation: Guard the close with a sync.Once (or an atomic CAS / a dedicated done context), e.g. `var stopOnce sync.Once; stop := func(){ stopOnce.Do(func(){ close(stopHB) }) }` and call stop() from all three sites. Same treatment for the conn.Close() races.
code.evidence: Confirmed exactly as described. stopHB created at main.go:303 `stopHB := make(chan struct{})`. Three unsynchronized close sites: signal goroutine main.go:367 `close(stopHB)` (then conn.Close() at 368); read-loop error path main.go:375 `close(stopHB)` then `return`; and the drain shutdown closure passed to handleInbound at main.go:381-384 `func() { close(stopHB); _ = conn.Close() }`. The drain case main.go:434-439 invokes that closure inside a goroutine. Trace of the deterministic drain path: shutdown() closes stopHB (382) and conn (383); the outer `for` read loop at 372-373 then gets an error from wsutil.ReadServerData on the now-closed conn and executes `close(stopHB)` again at 375 -> close of a closed channel panics. grep for `recover` and `sync.Once` across the file returns NO matches, so nothing catches the panic. `go build` and `go vet ./tools/mockprovider/` both succeed (the bug is runtime, not compile-time). Severity kept at medium: real and deterministic on the drain path, but the impact is confined to the test/mock tool (no production reachability), matching the original medium rating.

code.title: Dead AuthorizedBearer helper uses non-constant-time comparison for a bearer secret (inconsistent with buyer path)
code.description: AuthorizedBearer compares the Authorization header to "Bearer "+expected with Go's `==` string comparison (line 34), which is not constant-time and short-circuits on first byte mismatch. The function has ZERO callers anywhere in the repo (grep across all .go files finds only its definition) — it is dead code. The same non-constant-time pattern is used for the live operator-key (the highest-value admin/money-authority secret) in internal/ws/server.go:1481 (authorizedOperator) and internal/explorer/handlers.go:502, whereas internal/buyer/server.go:2613 correctly uses subtle.ConstantTimeCompare with a length guard. So the codebase is internally inconsistent and the safe pattern exists but was not applied to the operator-key checks.
code.impact: As written, AuthorizedBearer is dead and harmless, but it is an attractive, easy-to-reuse helper that would introduce a timing-oracle if adopted; the same anti-pattern is already live for the operator key. Practical exploitability of HTTPS header timing is low (network jitter dominates), hence low severity, but the operator key gates blacklist/drain/ledger admin endpoints.
code.recommendation: Either delete the unused AuthorizedBearer, or rewrite it (and authorizedOperator at ws/server.go:1481 and the explorer check at handlers.go:502) to extract the bearer token and use subtle.ConstantTimeCompare with a length-equality guard, matching buyer/server.go:2613. Standardize on one helper to avoid drift.
code.evidence: Confirmed. tokens.go:33-34 `AuthorizedBearer` returns `expected == "" || r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+expected` — plain `==`, non-constant-time. Repo-wide grep for `AuthorizedBearer` returns a single hit: the definition at tokens.go:33, so it is genuinely dead code. The live operator-key checks use the same plain-`==` pattern: ws/server.go authorizedOperator `s.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey == "" || r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey` and explorer/handlers.go `h.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey != "" && r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+h.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey`. By contrast buyer/server.go:2613 does it correctly: `if len(token) != len(expected) { return false }` then `subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(token), []byte(expected)) == 1`. The inconsistency and dead-code claims are accurate. Severity kept at low: practical timing-oracle exploitation over HTTPS is dominated by network jitter, and the worst offender named (AuthorizedBearer itself) is unreachable; the live operator-key sites are the real (still low) consistency gap.

code.title: providerhttp.Client is an unsynchronized mutable package global
code.description: Client is a package-level *http.Client variable that Init() reassigns (line 16) and that tests overwrite directly (internal/buyer/server_test.go:1158). It is read concurrently by request handlers via providerhttp.Client.Do (internal/buyer/server.go:1194,1619 and internal/ws/server.go:901). There is no mutex or atomic.Pointer guarding the swap. Today this is safe only by convention: cmd/coordinator/main.go calls Init() at line 37 before any server goroutine starts, and the SIGHUP reload path does not re-Init. There is no comment or guard enforcing that invariant.
code.impact: No current data race (Init runs strictly before serving). But if a future change calls Init() during a config reload or adds any runtime re-tuning of the HTTP timeout, it becomes a data race on the global pointer read by in-flight forwarders, with undefined behavior under -race and potentially torn reads. Latent reliability risk.
code.recommendation: Make the timeout a field of an injected client/struct passed into the buyer and ws servers at construction, or store the client in an atomic.Pointer[http.Client] if it must stay package-global and ever be swapped at runtime. At minimum, document the 'Init must be called once before serving, never after' invariant on the variable.
code.evidence: Confirmed as a latent (not active) risk, consistent with the low rating. client.go:8-12 declares `var Client = &http.Client{...}` (package global); Init at client.go:15-22 reassigns it `Client = &http.Client{Timeout: ...}` with no mutex/atomic. Concurrent readers verified: buyer/server.go:1194 and :1619 `providerhttp.Client.Do(...)`, ws/server.go:901 `providerhttp.Client.Do(req)`; test overwrites at buyer/server_test.go:1157-1158 and restores at :1166. The single production write is cmd/coordinator/main.go:37 `providerhttp.Init(cfg.ProviderHTTP.TimeoutS)`, which runs before any server is constructed/started. I checked the SIGHUP path: cmd/coordinator/main.go:145-150 notifies SIGHUP and calls reloadTier2Config, whose body (main.go:191-226) reloads tier2/billing config and calls SetTier2Config/SetBillingConfig — it does NOT call providerhttp.Init. So there is no current data race; the finding's own framing (latent, would only become a race if Init is later called during reload) is accurate. Low severity is appropriate.

code.title: SSE stream scanner error (ErrTooLong / read error) is never checked; truncated stream settled as successful 'ok'
code.description: forwardStreamingChat reads the upstream SSE body with a bufio.Scanner whose buffer is capped at 1 MiB: scanner.Buffer(make([]byte, 0, 64*1024), 1024*1024) (line 1476). After the `for scanner.Scan()` loop exits (lines 1492-1517), the code never calls scanner.Err(). The post-loop logic only distinguishes client cancellation (r.Context().Err() == context.Canceled, lines 1518-1525) from the success path (lines 1526-1530). If Scan() returns false because a single SSE data line exceeds 1 MiB (bufio.ErrTooLong) or because of any other mid-stream read error, and the client did NOT cancel, control falls through to lines 1526-1530 and the request is settled as outcome="ok".
code.impact: Buyers are billed for and shown truncated/failed inference responses as if they completed normally; the failure is invisible in logs (logged status=200, outcome=ok). A provider emitting an oversized SSE line can deterministically trigger silent truncation. On a service that moves real USDC, mis-settling a failed stream as 'ok' is a money-correctness and reliability defect.
code.recommendation: After the scan loop, check `if err := scanner.Err(); err != nil` before the success branch. On a non-nil scanner error that is not a client cancellation, settle with outcome="upstream_error" (or a dedicated "stream_truncated" outcome) rather than "ok", and emit an error log line. Consider raising the per-line buffer cap or switching to a bufio.Reader with ReadBytes('\n') if legitimately large SSE lines must be supported.
code.evidence: Read server.go:1475-1531 verbatim. Line 1476: scanner.Buffer(make([]byte, 0, 64*1024), 1024*1024) caps the line buffer at exactly 1 MiB, so a single SSE line >1 MiB makes Scan() return false with scanner.Err()==bufio.ErrTooLong. The for-loop at line 1492 (`for scanner.Scan()`) is followed ONLY by: (a) line 1518 `if errors.Is(r.Context().Err(), context.Canceled)` -> cancel branch, then (b) line 1526 `if reported != nil` -> settleRequest(..., "ok") and (c) line 1530 settleRequest(..., int64(math.Ceil(float64(emitted)/4.0)), "gateway_estimated", "ok"). There is NO scanner.Err() call between the loop and these branches (grep for 'scanner.Err' in the file returned no hits). settleRequest (server.go:1599-1610) builds a storage.ReservationSettlement with the given Outcome and calls s.store.SettleReservation/SettleDemoReservation, i.e. it finalizes billing — so a read-error stream is billed with Outcome="ok". Handler documented for G3 observability (comment line 1208), which the silent mislabel defeats. Note one partial mitigation that does not change the verdict: a clean EOF close yields scanner.Err()==nil and already settles 'ok' by design (arguably acceptable); the real exposure is ErrTooLong and non-EOF read errors (connection reset, ErrUnexpectedEOF), which are mis-settled. Severity high upheld for an operator-triggerable money-correctness defect. Confirmed.

code.title: Operator/admin bearer token compared with non-constant-time string equality (timing side-channel)
code.description: operatorAuthorized (line 1933) authorizes every admin/operator endpoint with `r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey`, and shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit (line 1942) repeats the same `==` comparison. Go's string `==` is not constant-time; it short-circuits on the first differing byte, leaking how many leading bytes of the supplied token matched the secret. This guards the kill-switch, capacity-tier, feedback-summary, and explorer endpoints. The codebase already uses crypto/hmac.Equal for demo tokens, and crypto/hmac is already imported in server.go.
code.impact: An attacker who can issue many requests and measure response latency could attempt a byte-by-byte timing attack to recover the operator key, granting full operator control (toggle kill switch, change capacity tiers, read explorer buyer PII). Practical exploitability over a network is limited by jitter, but the fix is trivial and the asset is high-value.
code.recommendation: Compare with a constant-time primitive, e.g. `hmac.Equal([]byte(r.Header.Get("Authorization")), []byte("Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey))` (or subtle.ConstantTimeCompare), in both operatorAuthorized and shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit. Hashing both sides to a fixed length first also avoids leaking length.
code.evidence: Read server.go:1932-1945 verbatim. Line 1933: `if r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey` — plain Go string == on the secret, returns early on first byte mismatch (true side-channel). Line 1942 in shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit repeats the identical comparison. Confirmed operatorAuthorized guards real admin endpoints: callers at server.go:632 (handleFeedbackSummary, read 627-634), 657, 702, 740, plus explorer.go:247 via explorerAllowed (read 246-256) gating all six explorer handlers (explorer.go:27,46,72,94,113,137). The constant-time primitive IS available and used elsewhere: read internal/auth/demo.go:53 `if err != nil || !hmac.Equal(expected, got)`; crypto/hmac imported in server.go (import line 7, used at deriveConversationKey line 1588). NOTE: finding cited 'demo.go:53' — correct line number but the file is internal/auth/demo.go, not internal/router/demo.go (which does not exist); this path imprecision does not affect substance. Medium upheld: real leak on a high-value secret, but network jitter makes remote recovery of a high-entropy key impractical, so not high. Confirmed.

code.title: Proxy copies hop-by-hop response headers (Connection, Transfer-Encoding, Keep-Alive) verbatim to the client
code.description: copyCleanHeaders copies every upstream response header to the downstream response except those matching x-macprovider-* and Content-Length. It does not strip RFC 7230 hop-by-hop headers (Connection, Keep-Alive, Proxy-Connection, TE, Trailer, Transfer-Encoding, Upgrade). It is used on the proxied non-streaming chat response, the streaming response (line 1469), /v1/models, and the no-provider passthrough (line 1535). The upstream is the coordinator (trusted), so this is hygiene rather than an active exploit, but copying an upstream Transfer-Encoding or Connection header to a response that Go's net/http server frames itself is technically incorrect proxy behavior.
