code.impact: Potential response-framing inconsistencies with downstream intermediaries (CDN/load balancer) and, if the coordinator ever forwarded an upstream Connection: <token> header, unintended dropping of named headers. No direct attacker capability given the trusted coordinator boundary; primarily a standards-conformance and robustness gap.
code.recommendation: In copyCleanHeaders, also skip the standard hop-by-hop header set (Connection, Keep-Alive, Proxy-Authenticate, Proxy-Authorization, TE, Trailer, Transfer-Encoding, Upgrade) and any header named in the upstream Connection header, mirroring net/http/httputil.ReverseProxy behavior.
code.evidence: Read server.go:2218-2227 verbatim: copyCleanHeaders loops over src headers and `continue`s only when isMacProviderHeader(key) (prefix 'x-macprovider-', confirmed isMacProviderHeader server.go:2241-2243) or strings.EqualFold(key,"Content-Length"). No hop-by-hop header set is excluded — claim accurate. Confirmed invoked on proxied responses: line 1469 (streaming, before WriteHeader(StatusOK)) and line 1535 (passThroughNoProviderCoordinatorError). Verdict agrees with the finding's own low/hygiene self-rating: per CLAUDE.md the upstream is the trusted coordinator, and Go's net/http server overrides framing headers it manages, so practical impact is minimal. Low severity upheld. Confirmed as a real standards gap, correctly rated low.

code.title: Streaming token-too-long / scanner-error path has no test coverage
code.description: Grep of the router test files for scanner.Err, ErrTooLong, the 1024*1024 buffer cap, and operator-auth timing returns no matches. The 1 MiB SSE-line cap and the post-loop settlement classification are exercised only on the happy/cancellation path; there is no test asserting that a truncated or oversized upstream stream is settled as an error rather than 'ok'. Likewise no test pins constant-time operator-token comparison.
code.impact: The silent-truncation settlement bug could regress (or be 'fixed' incorrectly) without any test failing. Money-settlement branches on the streaming path are undertested.
code.recommendation: Add a streaming test with a fake coordinator client that emits a >1 MiB SSE data line (forcing bufio.ErrTooLong) and another that closes the body mid-stream with a non-EOF error, asserting the settlement outcome is an error classification and not 'ok'. This test will also drive the fix for the high-severity finding.
code.evidence: grep across phase5-gateway/internal/router/*_test.go (server_test.go, integration_test.go, cors_test.go, explorer_test.go, pages_test.go, security_headers_test.go) for 'scanner.Err', 'ErrTooLong', 'ConstantTime', 'operatorAuthorized timing' returned NO matches. The only streaming-related test hits are server_test.go:1478 and 1519 (Content-Type 'text/event-stream' assertions). I read that test (server_test.go:1470-1531): it emits a single 120-char line via fmt.Fprintf(pw, "data: %s\n\n", strings.Repeat("x",120)) — far under the 1 MiB cap — then exercises CLIENT CANCELLATION (cancel() at line 1505, asserts cancelSeen, then asserts billing). So existing coverage is happy/cancel path only; no test forces bufio.ErrTooLong (>1 MiB line) or a mid-stream non-EOF read error, none asserts outcome != 'ok' on truncation, and none pins constant-time operator comparison. Coverage-gap claim accurate. Low severity upheld (missing test, not itself a runtime defect). Confirmed.

code.title: LEFT JOIN fan-out inflates per-buyer token usage/reserved totals in ExplorerListBuyers
code.description: ExplorerListBuyers builds per-buyer aggregates with SUM(ue.total_tokens) AS used_tokens (line 34) and SUM(CASE WHEN qr.status='active' THEN qr.reserved_tokens ELSE 0 END) AS reserved_tokens (line 35), but the FROM clause LEFT JOINs four tables: account_identities (line 42), api_keys (line 43), usage_events (line 44), and quota_reservations (line 45), then GROUP BYs the account. Because account_identities and api_keys are independent one-to-many relations to the same account, every usage_events row and every quota_reservations row is duplicated (identities x api_keys) times in the joined rowset before SUM runs, so both SUMs are multiplied by that cross-product factor. The feedback_count and average_rating columns on lines 39-40 correctly avoid this by using correlated subqueries; the two token SUMs do not. The clean DailyUsage/dailyUsageTx path used for actual quota enforcement is unaffected, so this is a reporting/operator-visibility bug, not a billing-enforcement bug.
code.impact: The operator explorer buyer list shows wildly inflated daily-tokens-used and daily-tokens-reserved for any account with multiple identities or multiple API keys (the common case after key rotation, which leaves multiple key rows). Operators making capacity, abuse, or kill-switch decisions off these numbers will see e.g. 4x or higher phantom consumption, potentially throttling or blocking legitimate buyers on the basis of fabricated usage.
code.recommendation: Compute used_tokens and reserved_tokens with correlated subqueries scoped to the window (mirroring the feedback_count/average_rating pattern on lines 39-40), and drop the usage_events and quota_reservations LEFT JOINs. Keep the account_identities/api_keys LEFT JOINs only for the email/key-status filters. Add a regression test seeding 2 identities + 2 keys + 1 usage row and asserting the SUM equals the single row's value.
code.evidence: Confirmed by reading explorer.go directly. Line 34: COALESCE(SUM(ue.total_tokens), 0) AS used_tokens and line 35: COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN qr.status = 'active' THEN qr.reserved_tokens ELSE 0 END), 0) AS reserved_tokens are plain aggregates. Line 42 LEFT JOIN account_identities ai ON ai.account_id = a.account_id and line 43 LEFT JOIN api_keys ak ON ak.account_id = a.account_id are two independent one-to-many joins to the same account_id. Lines 44-45 LEFT JOIN usage_events ue and LEFT JOIN quota_reservations qr feed the SUMs. Line 54 GROUP BY a.account_id collapses the cross-product. This is a textbook SQL JOIN fan-out: with N identities and M api_keys, each usage/reservation row appears N*M times pre-aggregation, so both SUMs scale by N*M. The inconsistency is self-evident in the same SELECT: feedback_count (line 39) and average_rating (line 40) use COALESCE((SELECT ... FROM feedback_events f WHERE f.account_id = a.account_id ...)) correlated subqueries that are immune to the fan-out, while last_request_id (line 37) and active_concurrency (line 38) also use subqueries — only the two token SUMs were left on the join path. The enforcement path is genuinely unaffected: dailyUsageTx (store.go:794-810) runs two separate single-table queries (SELECT SUM(total_tokens) FROM usage_events WHERE account_id=? AND window_date=? and SELECT SUM(reserved_tokens) FROM quota_reservations WHERE account_id=? AND window_date=? AND status='active') with no joins, so quota enforcement reads correct totals. Severity high is justified: it is a real correctness defect on an operator-facing money-adjacent dashboard, but it does not affect billing/enforcement, so not critical.

code.title: ReserveQuota leaks raw SQLite UNIQUE-constraint error on duplicate request_id instead of a sentinel
code.description: The quota_reservations table has PRIMARY KEY (account_id, request_id) (migrate.go:93). When ReserveQuota is called twice with the same (account_id, request_id), the INSERT at lines 382-385 fails with the driver UNIQUE-constraint error, which is returned verbatim at line 387. errors.Is against ErrQuotaExceeded and ErrNotFound both report false. The storage package already defines storage.ErrReservationExists (errors.go:9) for exactly this case, but it is never used. The caller (router/server.go) maps the unrecognized error to HTTP 500 'quota_reservation_failed'. Because Admitted is false and no new row was written, the defensive RefundReservation is a harmless no-op, so there is no quota leak.
code.impact: Replayed or retried requests reusing a request_id produce confusing HTTP 500s and leak SQLite driver internals (constraint names, error code 1555) into gateway logs. No money or quota is mis-accounted, but it degrades observability and idempotency semantics on the hottest money path.
code.recommendation: After the INSERT at store.go:387, detect the unique-constraint violation and return storage.ErrReservationExists (or treat it idempotently by re-reading the existing reservation). Then map ErrReservationExists in router/server.go to a deterministic response (e.g. 409 or idempotent replay) rather than a generic 500.
code.evidence: Confirmed by reading store.go and the caller. migrate.go:93 has PRIMARY KEY (account_id, request_id) on quota_reservations, so a duplicate (account_id, request_id) INSERT violates the PK. store.go:382-388: the INSERT INTO quota_reservations(...) VALUES(...,'active',...) returns its error directly via `return storage.QuotaDecision{}, err` at line 387 with no constraint-classification — the raw driver error propagates. errors.go confirms ErrReservationExists = errors.New("quota reservation exists") is defined (line 9) but grep shows it is never referenced in store.go. The caller path is confirmed: server.go:1281 calls ReserveQuota; the duplicate-PK error is not ErrQuotaExceeded so it skips the 429 branch at 1286; decision.Admitted is false (the function returns the zero QuotaDecision on INSERT error) so the belt-and-suspenders 429 at 1296 is skipped (decision.LimitTokens==0); it falls through to line 1314 writeError(w, http.StatusInternalServerError, "server_error", "quota_reservation_failed", ...). The defensive RefundReservation at 1307 is indeed a no-op since no row was written and !decision.Admitted. Severity low is correct: no money/quota mis-accounting, observability/idempotency degradation only. NOTE on exploitability: this requires a buyer to replay the SAME request_id within the same window before the reservation expires or settles; requestID(r) is per-request, so collisions only occur on genuine client replay/retry, narrowing real-world impact — but the finding already scopes it as such, so low stands, not downgraded further.

code.title: decodeTime silently swallows parse errors, producing zero-time that mis-sorts corrupt rows
code.description: decodeTime does `t, _ := time.Parse(time.RFC3339Nano, s)` and discards the error, returning the zero time (0001-01-01) on any unparseable input. All timestamps are written via encodeTime (RFC3339Nano), so in normal operation this never triggers. The one security-relevant consumer, ConsumeOAuthState (store.go:308), fails safe: a corrupt expires_at decodes to zero time and `!now.Before(zero)` evaluates true, so the state is treated as expired and rejected. However, every other consumer silently coerces an unparseable timestamp to the epoch, mis-sorting that row in cursor-ordered results and rendering as 0001-01-01 in operator JSON, with no error surfaced.
code.impact: On any DB corruption or out-of-band write that puts a non-RFC3339 string into a timestamp column, affected rows silently render with epoch timestamps and sort incorrectly in explorer cursors/activity feeds, with no log or error to flag the corruption. Security-sensitive expiry checks fail safe, so there is no auth bypass; impact is silent data-quality degradation and harder debugging.
code.recommendation: Have decodeTime log (or surface) parse failures rather than swallowing them, or return (time.Time, error) and let callers decide. At minimum, add a sentinel/metric when a stored timestamp fails to parse so corruption is observable.
code.evidence: Confirmed by reading store.go. Lines 868-871: func decodeTime(s string) time.Time { t, _ := time.Parse(time.RFC3339Nano, s); return t } — the error is explicitly discarded with the blank identifier, returning Go's zero time on failure. encodeTime (lines 864-866) writes time.RFC3339Nano, so well-formed rows always round-trip. The fail-safe claim for ConsumeOAuthState is verified: store.go:308 reads `if consumedAt != "" || !now.Before(decodeTime(expiresAt))` — if expiresAt is corrupt, decodeTime returns the zero time, now.Before(zero) is false for any real `now`, so !false = true, returning ErrNotFound (treated as expired) — fails closed, no auth bypass. Other consumers confirmed to coerce silently: scanUsage (explorer.go:643), explorerQuotaReservations expires_at/created_at (546-547), the activity-feed created_at (explorer.go:318) all call decodeTime and use the result for sorting/display with no error path. Severity info is correct: requires out-of-band corruption to trigger (normal writes always use encodeTime), security path fails safe, impact is observability/data-quality only. Confidence in the description's 'medium' is appropriate; verdict confirmed at info.

code.title: ExplorerListBuyers indexes out.Items[q.Limit-1]; panics if a caller passes Limit<=0
code.description: After fetching Limit+1 rows, the pagination logic does `if len(out.Items) > q.Limit { next := encodeListID(out.Items[q.Limit-1].AccountID) ... }`. If q.Limit is 0 and more than zero rows are returned, out.Items[q.Limit-1] is out.Items[-1], which panics. The same pattern appears in ExplorerListSessions (lines 214-218) and ExplorerActivity (lines 348-352). The only HTTP entrypoint, parseExplorerLimit (router/explorer.go:233-244), always returns >=1, and the internal caller explorerBuyerByID passes Limit:1. So no current call path can hit this — it is a latent landmine guarded only by caller discipline.
code.impact: No impact today; all current callers pass Limit>=1. A future caller that passes Limit=0 with a non-empty result set would panic the request goroutine. For a money-handling edge service, an unguarded slice-index panic is a denial-of-service footgun.
code.recommendation: Defensively clamp Limit at the top of each Explorer* method (e.g. `if q.Limit <= 0 { q.Limit = 1 }` or return an empty page), so the store is robust regardless of caller.
code.evidence: The mechanism is real but UNREACHABLE by any current path, so the practical severity is info, not low. Confirmed at explorer.go:99-103: `if len(out.Items) > q.Limit { next := encodeListID(out.Items[q.Limit-1].AccountID) ...}` — with q.Limit==0 and a non-empty result, q.Limit-1 == -1 panics. Same pattern at ExplorerListSessions explorer.go:214-215 (out.Items[q.Limit-1]) and ExplorerActivity explorer.go:348-349. BUT every caller is guarded: parseExplorerLimit (router/explorer.go:233-244) initializes limit := explorerDefaultLimit (=50, confirmed explorer.go:15) and only overrides via `if parsed, err := strconv.Atoi(raw); err == nil && parsed > 0 { limit = parsed }` — the `parsed > 0` guard makes 0/negative impossible — then caps at explorerMaxLimit (=200). The internal caller explorerBuyerByID (explorer.go:423-424) hardcodes Limit:1. Note the query also runs `LIMIT q.Limit+1` (=1 when Limit==0), so even constructing a direct Limit==0 call requires >1 row from a LIMIT 1 query, which cannot return 2 rows — the panic guard `len(out.Items) > q.Limit` (1 > 0) could trip only if exactly 1 row returns, and out.Items[-1] would then panic. Still, no live path constructs Limit==0. Downgraded to info: real latent footgun, zero current reachability, no exploit path exists today. The fix recommendation remains valid as hardening.

code.title: Connection-scoped PRAGMAs depend on the single-connection pool; raising MaxOpenConns would silently drop WAL/foreign_keys/busy_timeout on new conns
code.description: Open sets SetMaxOpenConns(1)/SetMaxIdleConns(1) (lines 37-38) and then runs PRAGMA busy_timeout/foreign_keys/journal_mode/synchronous once via a single ExecContext (line 39). In SQLite (modernc.org/sqlite) busy_timeout and foreign_keys are per-connection settings. They persist here only because the pool holds exactly one connection reused for everything, including the beginImmediate path that draws from the same pool via s.db.Conn (line 849). The correctness of foreign-key enforcement and the 5s busy_timeout therefore silently hinges on MaxOpenConns staying at 1; if anyone raises it for throughput, freshly-opened connections would default to foreign_keys=OFF and busy_timeout=0.
code.impact: No current bug (pool is pinned to 1). It is a fragile coupling: a plausible future performance change (raising the connection cap) would silently disable foreign-key integrity and the busy-timeout backoff on all but the first connection, with no test catching it.
code.recommendation: Set the PRAGMAs via a connector hook so every connection inherits them regardless of pool size, or append them to the DSN (?_pragma=busy_timeout(5000)&_pragma=foreign_keys(on)). Add a comment at lines 37-39 documenting that the single-conn pool is load-bearing for PRAGMA durability.
code.evidence: Confirmed by reading store.go:37-42. Line 37 db.SetMaxOpenConns(1) and line 38 db.SetMaxIdleConns(1) pin the pool to one connection. Line 39 runs `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000; PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL; PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;` exactly once via a single db.ExecContext. journal_mode=WAL and synchronous=NORMAL are durable database-file/persistent settings, but busy_timeout and foreign_keys are per-connection in SQLite — this is accurate for modernc.org/sqlite. The dependency on the pinned connection is real: beginImmediate (store.go:848-858) calls s.db.Conn(ctx) to draw a connection from the same pool, and because MaxOpenConns==1 it always gets the one PRAGMA-configured connection. If MaxOpenConns were raised, sql.DB would open additional raw connections that never executed the PRAGMA block, defaulting foreign_keys OFF (disabling the REFERENCES accounts(account_id) constraints at migrate.go:20 and migrate.go:44) and busy_timeout 0. Note schemaSQL also contains `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;` at migrate.go:4, but that runs inside Migrate's single ExecContext on the pooled connection — it does not help new connections either. Severity info is correct: latent coupling, no runtime defect while the pool stays at 1, no test guards it. Verdict confirmed; the per-connection PRAGMA claim is technically sound.

code.title: Single-version migration model has no incremental-migration path
code.description: Migrate executes the entire schemaSQL blob (all CREATE TABLE/INDEX/TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS) and then does INSERT OR IGNORE INTO schema_migrations VALUES(1, ...). There is no logic that reads the current max version and applies forward steps; the schema_migrations table is written but never read. No ALTER TABLE statements and no migration runner exist. This is fine for the current locked v1 schema, but means any future schema change to an existing column/table cannot be expressed as a migration — IF NOT EXISTS skips an already-created table, so a column addition or constraint change would require a hand-rolled ALTER outside this framework, and schema_migrations would remain stuck at version 1.
code.impact: No runtime defect today. It is a forward-maintenance gap: the schema_migrations table gives a false impression of a versioned migration system that does not actually apply versions >1. A future schema evolution risks being applied inconsistently across environments.
code.recommendation: Either (a) document explicitly that the schema is single-version and additive-only via the schemaSQL blob, or (b) implement a real migration runner that reads MAX(version) from schema_migrations and applies an ordered list of versioned migration steps (including ALTERs) within a transaction.
code.evidence: Confirmed by reading store.go:59-65 and migrate.go. Migrate (store.go:59-65) runs s.db.ExecContext(ctx, schemaSQL) (the full IF-NOT-EXISTS blob) then `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO schema_migrations(version, applied_at) VALUES(1, ?)` — hardcoded version 1, INSERT OR IGNORE so re-runs no-op. There is no SELECT MAX(version) anywhere: I read the entire store.go and the only references to schema_migrations are the CREATE in migrate.go:6-9 and this single INSERT — the table is written once and never read. The full schemaSQL (migrate.go:3-251) contains exclusively CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS, and CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS statements; grep-level inspection of the blob confirms zero ALTER TABLE statements. The consequence described is correct: on an existing DB, CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS no-ops, so a changed column definition in schemaSQL would silently NOT apply to existing databases while fresh DBs get the new definition — divergence with no enforcement since version stays pinned at 1. Severity info is correct: no current defect (schema is locked v1 per project notes), purely a forward-maintenance/design gap. Verdict confirmed.

code.title: IPv6 demo-client IP normalization misuses net.IP, emitting a malformed string for every IPv6 client
code.description: normalizeDemoIP for IPv6 does `return net.IP(ip[:8]).String() + "::/64"`. `ip[:8]` is an 8-byte slice; net.IP.String() only formats 4-byte or 16-byte slices. For any other length it falls through to the hex-with-leading-'?' debug fallback in the stdlib. Verified empirically: input `2001:db8:1:2:3:4:5:6` yields the literal string `"?20010db800010002::/64"`, `::1` yields `"?0000000000000000::/64"`, `fe80::1` yields `"?fe80000000000000::/64"`. The intended value was presumably a real /64 prefix like `2001:db8:1:2::/64`. This normalized value is embedded in the signed demo token (DemoPayload.IP), re-derived on every Validate, and used as the account identifier `accountID = "demo:" + payload.IP` (server.go:607), so it is persisted into feedback/audit/quota rows as `demo:?20010db8...::/64`.
code.impact: Every IPv6 demo user gets a garbage, non-RFC IP identifier stored across token payloads, quota keys, feedback events, and audit logs. Because String() returns a deterministic (if malformed) value, the demo token still round-trips and IP-binding still 'works', so it is not a hard auth break — but it corrupts operator-facing data, makes audit/abuse correlation by IP unreliable for IPv6, and signals the /64 grouping logic does not actually do what the code comments imply.
code.recommendation: Build the /64 prefix correctly: zero the low 8 bytes of a full 16-byte address and emit a real CIDR, e.g. `m := ip.To16(); copy(m[8:], make([]byte, 8)); return (&net.IPNet{IP: m, Mask: net.CIDRMask(64,128)}).String()` (yields `2001:db8:1:2::/64`). Add table-driven tests for IPv4, IPv6, mapped-v4, and loopback inputs.
code.evidence: Reproduced empirically. Compiled and ran the exact normalizeDemoIP function from demo.go:79-92. Output: `2001:db8:1:2:3:4:5:6` => "?20010db800010002::/64"; `::1` => "?0000000000000000::/64"; `fe80::1` => "?fe80000000000000::/64" — exactly the malformed strings claimed. The leading '?' is the stdlib net.IP.String() fallback for non-4/16-byte slices (ip[:8] is 8 bytes). IPv4 paths are unaffected: `192.168.1.5` => "192.168.1.5" and `::ffff:192.168.1.5` => "192.168.1.5" because demo.go:84 returns v4.String() first. Confirmed the value flows to the account identifier: server.go:607 sets `accountID = "demo:" + payload.IP`, and demo.go:36 stores normalizeDemoIP(clientIP) into the signed DemoPayload.IP. The IP is re-derived and compared on every Validate (demo.go:67), so the malformed value is stable and round-trips, matching the 'not a hard auth break but corrupts data' characterization. Severity kept at medium: data-quality/auditability defect on the dominant IPv6 address family, no auth bypass.

code.title: Operator admin token compared with non-constant-time string equality
code.description: operatorAuthorized gates the money-authority admin endpoints (/admin/kill-switch, /admin/capacity-signal, /admin/capacity-tier/evaluate, /admin/feedback-summary) with `if r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey`. The same plain `==` compare is repeated at line 1942 (shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit). Go string `==` short-circuits at the first differing byte and is not constant-time. Every other secret comparison in this codebase is constant-time (demo.go:53 uses hmac.Equal; API keys validate via a SHA/HMAC DB hash lookup), so this is the lone timing-vulnerable secret check.
code.impact: An attacker who can reach the admin endpoints and measure response timing could attempt a byte-at-a-time timing recovery of the operator key. The operator key toggles the global kill switch and drives capacity-tier signals that influence the money path. Network jitter makes remote exploitation hard, but the endpoints are on the internet edge and the fix is trivial.
code.recommendation: Compare with crypto/subtle: `subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(r.Header.Get("Authorization")), []byte("Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey)) == 1`. Apply to both call sites (1933 and 1942). Consider hashing both sides first so length is not leaked.
code.evidence: Confirmed the code is exactly as described. server.go:1933 in operatorAuthorized uses `r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey` and server.go:1942 repeats the same `==` in shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit. Verified operatorAuthorized gates four admin handlers — call sites at server.go:632, 657, 702, 740 — and route registrations at server.go:150-153 map those to /admin/feedback-summary, /admin/kill-switch, /admin/capacity-signal, /admin/capacity-tier/evaluate, exactly the money-authority endpoints named. Confirmed the 'lone timing-vulnerable check' claim: grep for subtle/ConstantTimeCompare/hmac.Equal across internal/router and internal/auth returns ONLY demo.go:53 (hmac.Equal for demo tokens); the operator path has no constant-time helper. The real-world exploitability is what drives the downgrade. Go strings carry their length, so `==` compares lengths first and only iterates bytes when lengths match — this leaks key length but not a clean per-byte oracle for the secret bytes, and HTTP handler dispatch (header parsing, mux routing, map lookups, response writing) adds far more timing variance than a 32-byte memcmp short-circuit. Remote byte-at-a-time recovery of a high-entropy key over the network against this noise is not practically demonstrated. Real defense-in-depth gap with a trivial fix, but the medium rating overstates exploitability; adjusted to low.

code.title: internal/auth package has zero test coverage on all critical auth primitives
code.description: `go test ./internal/auth/...` reports `[no test files]`. There are no unit tests for GitHubProvider.Exchange (token+user HTTP flow, scope rejection), ScopesAllowed/splitScopes, KeyManager.Generate/Validate/Hash (prefix gating, hmac vs sha256 modes), DemoManager.Issue/Validate (signature, expiry, IP binding, version check), or normalizeDemoIP. The router integration tests exercise some happy paths through fakeOAuth, but the auth package's own logic — including the IPv6 normalization that is demonstrably broken — is untested.
code.impact: Regressions in token signing, scope enforcement, key hashing-mode selection, or IP normalization can ship undetected. For a service moving real USDC where these primitives gate billing identity and demo abuse limits, lack of coverage on the auth core is a reliability/correctness risk, not just a hygiene gap.
code.recommendation: Add table-driven unit tests for demo.go (round-trip Issue→Validate, tampered signature, expired token, wrong-IP rejection, IPv4/IPv6/mapped normalization), keys.go (prefix mismatch returns ErrNotFound, hmac_sha256 vs sha256 produce different hashes, Hash determinism), and oauth.go (ScopesAllowed allow/deny matrix, splitScopes on space- and comma-delimited input, Exchange against an httptest server covering forbidden-scope and missing-user-id branches).
code.evidence: Verified `go test ./internal/auth/...` prints `?   github.com/augstar/macprovider-gateway/internal/auth   [no test files]`. `find internal/auth -name '*_test.go'` returns nothing — the package contains only demo.go, keys.go, oauth.go (confirmed via directory listing) and no test files. The untested primitives exist as described: oauth.go has GitHubProvider.Exchange (line 50), ScopesAllowed (108), splitScopes (121); keys.go has Generate (38), Validate (56), Hash (63) with the hmac_sha256-vs-sha256 branch at 64-70; demo.go has Issue (31), Validate (46), normalizeDemoIP (79). The 'direct reason the IPv6 defect shipped' link is sound — a round-trip/normalization table test would have caught the malformed output reproduced in finding 1. Severity low is appropriate (a test-debt/process gap, not an exploitable defect itself); kept at low.

code.title: Demo token TTL parameter is dead — Issue ignores caller-supplied ttl in practice
code.description: DemoManager.Issue takes a `ttl time.Duration` parameter but clamps any value <=0 or >24h to exactly 24h, and the sole production caller (server.go:348) always passes `24*time.Hour`. So the parameter can never produce a value other than 24h in the current wiring; it is effectively vestigial. Not a correctness bug, but it gives a false impression that demo session length is configurable when it is hardcoded.
code.impact: Operators reading the signature may believe demo TTL is tunable per-call or via config; it is not. Minor maintainability/clarity concern only.
code.recommendation: Either drive the TTL from config (e.g. a quotas/limits field) and pass it through, or drop the parameter and document the fixed 24h demo session lifetime. If kept, add a comment noting the 24h hard cap.
code.evidence: Confirmed at demo.go:31-35: Issue's signature accepts `ttl time.Duration`, then `if ttl <= 0 || ttl > 24*time.Hour { ttl = 24 * time.Hour }`. The clamp leaves any value in (0, 24h] intact, so the parameter is not strictly dead — a caller passing e.g. 1h would get a 1h TTL. However, grep for the production caller confirms the only non-test invocation is server.go:348 `s.demoMgr.Issue(ip, s.now(), 24*time.Hour)`, which always passes exactly 24h; the only other caller is in tests (server_test.go uses keyMgr.Issue, unrelated). So in current wiring the parameter is vestigial as claimed and 24h is effectively hardcoded. Accurate as an info-level maintainability note; severity info kept. Minor precision caveat: the parameter is dead only because of the call sites, not because the function ignores it — the recommendation to config-drive or document is the correct framing.

code.title: launchd agent booted out before binary replacement — replace failure leaves provider permanently stopped
code.description: applyValidatedUpdate() runs drain first (drainLaunchdIfInstalled, line 179/193-201), which executes `launchctl bootout gui/<uid> live.streamvc.macprovider` to STOP the running agent, THEN calls replaceCurrentBinary (line 184), THEN restartLaunchdIfInstalled (line 189). replaceCurrentBinary (lines 159-173) can throw at copyItem (line 166), setAttributes (line 167), or rename (line 168 -> renameFailed). If any of those throw, the error propagates up out of applyValidatedUpdate and restartLaunchdIfInstalled (which performs the `launchctl bootstrap` re-start at line 211) is NEVER reached. The agent has already been booted out, so the provider process is now stopped and will not be relaunched. There is also no rollback: the old binary may already be unlinked by a partially-completed rename.
code.impact: A transient filesystem error (disk full, permission change, SIP/quarantine on the staged file, ENOENT on the parent dir) during the replace step turns a routine self-update into a hard outage: the provider is drained, the launchd agent is unloaded, and nothing restarts it. The contributor Mac silently drops off the marketplace until a human re-runs the installer or `launchctl bootstrap` manually. Because drain already told the coordinator the provider is going away, no automatic recovery occurs.
code.recommendation: Re-order so replacement is staged and validated before the agent is stopped, or wrap drain+replace+restart so that any failure after bootout always attempts restartLaunchdIfInstalled in a defer/cleanup block. Concretely: do the copy+chmod of the staged file BEFORE drain, and on any error path after bootout, call the restart (bootstrap) to bring the existing binary back. Consider keeping the rename atomic-or-nothing and only booting out immediately before the rename.
code.evidence: Verified applyValidatedUpdate (lines 175-191): grep confirms it has NO defer/cleanup block (the only `defer` in the file is line 64, an unrelated temp-dir removeItem in run()). The drain(179) -> replace(184, throwing) -> restart(189) ordering is real, and a throw at replace does skip restart. So the core 'no restart on replace-failure' defect is CONFIRMED. BUT two material claims in the description are false, which lowers severity: (1) 'the old binary may already be unlinked by a partially-completed rename' is FALSE — replaceCurrentBinary copies to a sidecar staged path (line 164) and only swaps via POSIX rename(staged, current) at line 168, which is atomic; the original binary is never unlinked until rename succeeds, and on rename!=0 the staged file is removed (line 170). There is no partial/torn binary state. (2) 'permanently stopped' overstates it: drainLaunchdIfInstalled/restart guard on the plist still existing on disk (lines 194-198, 204-208); the plist is NOT removed, so the agent re-loads on next login/reboot (RunAtLoad) — the outage is until next login, not literally permanent without manual intervention. Real bug (missing restart-on-failure), but bounded blast radius and self-healing on reboot, so low rather than medium.

code.title: No timeout on new-binary self-test or tar/openssl subprocesses — a hung self-test stalls the update indefinitely while drained
code.description: runProcess (lines 214-223) and processOutput (lines 265-278) both call process.waitUntilExit() with no timeout/deadline. Line 92 executes the freshly downloaded binary as `runProcess(newBinary.path, ["self-test"])`; SelfTestCommand (MacProviderCLI.swift:133-148) loads the configured model via ModelRuntime and runs a startup inference. If model load or inference hangs (GPU/Metal stall, model file lock, network fetch of a HuggingFace model inside ModelRuntime), waitUntilExit() blocks forever. The same applies to the `tar -xzf` (line 89) and `openssl dgst -verify` (line 250) calls. There is no cancellation path.
code.impact: The `update` command hangs with no progress and no error. Note that self-test (line 92) runs AFTER drainBeforeReplace only in the test-injected path; in the production run() flow self-test runs before applyValidatedUpdate (so the agent is not yet drained at line 92) — but a hung tar/openssl earlier, or a hung self-test, still leaves the operator with a wedged `update` process and a half-downloaded temp dir. If the operator kills it mid-applyValidatedUpdate the provider can be left in the stopped state from finding #1.
code.recommendation: Add a wall-clock timeout to runProcess/processOutput (e.g. a Task that calls process.terminate()/process.interrupt() after N seconds, or DispatchSource timer), and fail the update with a clear error on timeout. The self-test in particular should have a bounded deadline since it loads a model.
code.evidence: Confirmed by reading runProcess (lines 214-223: try process.run(); process.waitUntilExit(); no deadline) and processOutput (lines 265-278: same pattern). grep for timeout|deadline|terminate|interrupt|DispatchSource|asyncAfter in SelfUpdate.swift returns only the bare waitUntilExit() calls — no cancellation path exists. The self-test invocation (line 92) and SelfTestCommand (MacProviderCLI.swift:133-148, which builds a ModelRuntime and calls measureStartupThroughput) are as described. However, severity is overstated as medium: (1) the finding itself concedes that in the production run() path self-test runs at line 92 BEFORE applyValidatedUpdate at line 93, so a hang occurs while the agent is still LIVE and serving — no outage, just a wedged foreground `update` CLI the operator can Ctrl-C. (2) This is an operator-facing, interactively-run command (UpdateCommand, MacProviderCLI.swift:152-169), not an unattended daemon path, so an indefinite wait is a UX/robustness gap, not a service-availability failure. The only path to a real outage is the compound 'operator kills mid-applyValidatedUpdate' scenario, which is the already-downgraded finding #1. Real missing-timeout robustness gap → low.

code.title: Redirect target not re-validated after validateDownloadURL — host allowlist only checks the pre-redirect URL
code.description: validateDownloadURL (225-232) is applied to the GitHub `browser_download_url` (lines 68-70), which is a `github.com/.../releases/download/...` URL. GitHub 302-redirects release-asset downloads to `objects.githubusercontent.com` (and historically to S3/Azure blob hosts). download() (151-157) uses the default URLSession which follows redirects automatically with no URLSessionTaskDelegate / willPerformHTTPRedirection hook, so the actual host the bytes come from is never re-checked against the allowlist. The allowlist does include objects.githubusercontent.com, but only the initial URL is validated; the realized redirect chain is unconstrained.
code.impact: Defense-in-depth gap only: the downloaded checksums.txt is ECDSA-signature-verified against a pinned public key (lines 245-263) and the tarball is SHA-256-matched against that signed manifest (lines 81-84), so a hijacked redirect cannot substitute content without breaking the signature. The practical risk is limited to a malicious redirect serving a different-but-still-failing artifact (DoS), not code execution.
code.recommendation: Install a URLSessionTaskDelegate that re-runs validateDownloadURL on each redirect target (willPerformHTTPRedirection), or set the session to not follow redirects and validate+follow manually. Low priority given the signature gate, but it tightens the trust boundary.
code.evidence: Confirmed accurate as written, including the self-assessed low severity. download() (lines 151-157) calls session.download(from: url) with no delegate and no redirect handling; validateDownloadURL is only invoked on the asset URLs at lines 68-70 against the static allowlist (lines 225-232: https + host in {github.com, *.github.com, objects.githubusercontent.com}). No willPerformHTTPRedirection hook exists. The finding's own impact analysis is correct and verified in-code: checksums.txt is openssl ECDSA-verified against the pinned checksumPublicKeyPEM (verifyChecksumSignature, lines 245-263; key embedded lines 7-12), and the tarball SHA-256 is matched against that signed manifest (lines 81-84 guard actualSHA == expectedSHA), so a hijacked redirect cannot substitute trusted content — it can only cause a checksum/signature failure (DoS), not code execution. Genuine defense-in-depth gap; low is the correct rating.

code.title: Checksum manifest parser rejects sha256sum binary-mode (`*filename`) and BSD formats
code.description: expectedSHA256 splits each line on spaces/tabs and requires parts[1] == filename exactly (line 295). Standard `sha256sum` output is `<hash><space><space><filename>` (text mode) which yields parts == [hash, filename] and works. But `sha256sum --binary` emits `<hash><space>*<filename>`, making parts[1] == "*macprovider-..." which will not equal the asset name, and BSD `shasum`/`openssl dgst` style is `SHA256(filename)= <hash>` which has no matching line at all. In those cases the function throws checksumMissing even though the manifest is valid and signed.
code.impact: If the release pipeline ever generates checksums.txt in binary or BSD mode (a one-character difference in a Makefile or CI step), every contributor's `update` breaks with a confusing 'checksums.txt does not contain <file>' error despite a perfectly valid signed manifest. Brittle coupling between the release tooling's exact output format and the client parser.
code.recommendation: Strip a leading `*` from the filename token before comparison, and/or also support the `SHA256(<name>)= <hash>` form. At minimum, document and pin the exact `sha256sum` invocation the release pipeline must use so the format cannot drift.
code.evidence: The parser fragility is real as code: expectedSHA256 (lines 292-300) tokenizes on space/tab and requires parts[1] == filename exactly (line 295), with a hex-64 regex on parts[0]. A leading `*` (binary mode) or the BSD `SHA256(name)= hash` shape would indeed not match and throw checksumMissing. BUT the actual release pipeline was inspected and produces the compatible format today: .github/workflows/release.yml line 95 runs `shasum -a 256 "$asset" > checksums.txt` (text mode, no -b/--binary), which emits `<hash>  <filename>` — exactly what the parser handles. The 'objects.githubusercontent.com'-style BSD form is not used. So this is not a current bug; it is latent brittleness contingent on a hypothetical future pipeline change ('if the release pipeline ever generates...'). With the producing pipeline pinned to the matching format and signed, there is no defect today. Downgraded to info (a hardening/maintainability note, not a live correctness bug).

code.title: findBinary requires exactly one file named macprovider-cli — extra copies (dSYM, nested dirs) break the update
code.description: findBinary enumerates the extracted tree for entries named exactly `macprovider-cli` that are regular, executable, non-symlink files, collects them into `matches`, and throws missingExtractedBinary unless `matches.count == 1` (line 319). If a future release tarball legitimately contains more than one such file (e.g. an arm64 + x86_64 layout, a debug copy, or a nested directory) the update fails hard.
code.impact: A benign change to the release archive layout (adding a second executable named macprovider-cli, or a universal-binary staging dir) silently breaks self-update for all clients on the new release, with the generic 'archive does not contain macprovider-cli' error. The strict ==1 guard is good for rejecting decoys but couples the client to an exact archive shape.
code.recommendation: Either anchor the expected path (e.g. require the binary at a known relative path like `./macprovider-cli` or `bin/macprovider-cli`) so additional copies elsewhere are ignored, or keep the strict check but make the error message enumerate the matches found to aid diagnosis. Add a unit test for the multi-match case.
code.evidence: The strict `matches.count == 1` guard is real (findBinary lines 308-323; line 319 throws missingExtractedBinary unless exactly one match), and matches are filtered to regular, non-symlink, executable files named exactly `macprovider-cli` (lines 313-317). But the cited 'benign triggers' do not apply to the actual archive: package.sh (lines 52-60) builds the tarball with only `macprovider-cli` plus `mlx-swift_Cmlx.bundle` and `swift-nio_NIOPosix.bundle`; `find` inside those two shipped bundles returns ZERO files named macprovider-cli. The dSYM (the description's headline example) is (a) NOT included in the tarball, and (b) even if it were, the DWARF copy at macprovider-cli.dSYM/.../DWARF/macprovider-cli is mode `-rw-r--r--` (verified via ls -la: non-executable, 644), so it is excluded by the isExecutable==true filter at line 315. There is also no x86_64/universal layout — the asset is darwin-arm64 single-arch (release.yml line 88). So with the current build the function deterministically yields exactly one match; the multi-match break is purely hypothetical-future. Downgraded to info (couples client to archive shape — a maintainability/robustness note, not a present defect).

code.title: Attestation envelope falls back to the challenge as the `token` when the MDA artifact omits a token
code.description: When a managed-device-attestation artifact is present but contains no `token` field, makeAttestationToken builds the envelope with `tokenBase64URL: artifact.tokenBase64URL ?? challengeBase64URL` (line 62). baseTokenEnvelope then sets envelope["token"] = that value (line 159). So the `token` claim becomes the verifier-supplied challenge echoed back, not a real attestation token. The artifact still must carry a valid certificate_chain and CSR (parse() enforces those, lines 326-339), and a binding signature is added (lines 73-78) only if a signing key path is configured — otherwise envelope["signature"] stays whatever the artifact provided (possibly nil).
code.impact: The provider can emit a structurally-complete attestation_token whose `token` field carries no genuine device-attestation assertion (just the echoed challenge) and, absent MACPROVIDER_TIER2_MDA_SIGNING_KEY_PATH, no binding signature. Whether this is exploitable depends entirely on coordinator-side validation: if the coordinator treats presence of attestation_token + cert chain as sufficient and does not require a non-echo token and a valid binding signature, a contributor could present a weak/forged attestation. This is a contract concern that must be confirmed against the coordinator's attestation verifier.
code.recommendation: Do not fall back to echoing the challenge as the token; if the artifact has no real token, return nil (attestation unsupported) rather than a token that aliases the challenge. Cross-check the coordinator audit: confirm it rejects envelopes where token == challenge and requires a verified ES256 binding signature over the canonical payload (lines 205-244). Confidence is low because exploitability lives in the coordinator, not this file.
code.evidence: The code behavior is confirmed exactly as described, and the finding's own low rating and low-confidence caveat are appropriate. makeAttestationToken line 62 passes `tokenBase64URL: artifact.tokenBase64URL ?? challengeBase64URL`; baseTokenEnvelope line 159 sets `"token": tokenBase64URL`, so when the artifact omits a token the `token` claim is the echoed challenge. parse() enforces a non-empty certificate_chain (lines 325-328) and CSR (lines 334-339) but token is optional (line 340 `nonEmptyString(dict["token"])`). The binding signature is only added when MACPROVIDER_TIER2_MDA_SIGNING_KEY_PATH is set and envelope["signature"] is nil (lines 73-78); otherwise envelope["signature"] carries whatever artifact.signature was, possibly nil (lines 71, 114-116, 348). Crucially, exploitability is entirely coordinator-side: the coordinator's attestation verifier is NOT in this repo's reviewable Swift (this is provider-binary code only), so whether token==challenge with no binding signature is accepted cannot be disproven or confirmed here. Kept as confirmed-low: the echo-fallback is a genuine smell worth removing, but it only becomes a real vuln if the coordinator under-validates — which is out of scope for this component and correctly flagged for the coordinator audit.

code.title: Dead code: fetchText(from:) is defined but never called
code.description: fetchText(from:) performs an HTTP GET and returns the body as a string, but no call site references it (the checksums/signature/tarball are all fetched via download(from:to:) instead). Confirmed by grep: the only occurrence of `fetchText` is its own definition.
code.impact: None functionally; it is unreachable code that adds maintenance noise and a slightly larger attack-surface review burden in a supply-chain-critical file. A future reader may assume it is used in the verification flow.
code.recommendation: Remove fetchText, or if it is intended for an upcoming path, add a call site and a test. Keeping unused network helpers in the self-update module is best avoided.
code.evidence: Confirmed by grep across Sources/ and Tests/: the only occurrence of `fetchText` is its definition at SelfUpdate.swift line 143 (`private func fetchText(from url: URL) async throws -> String`). No call site anywhere. It is genuinely dead/unreachable code. The data-fetching in run() is done exclusively via download(from:to:) (lines 75, 76, 80) and latestRelease() via session.data(for:). Accurately rated info; severity unchanged.

code.title: Local HTTP inference path leaks tasks and head-of-line-blocks on client disconnect (no channelInactive/cancellation)
code.description: RouterHandler implements only channelRead; it has no channelInactive or errorCaught override. handleChatCompletions (line 196) and handleStreamingChatCompletions (line 238) each launch a fire-and-forget `Task.detached` that calls `modelRuntime.complete`/`modelRuntime.stream`. The task handle is never retained, and ResponseWriter (line 464, @unchecked Sendable capturing ChannelHandlerContext) writes back via `context.eventLoop.execute`. If the local HTTP client disconnects mid-inference, nothing cancels the detached task: the inference runs to completion, holding the single `inferenceGate` permit (AsyncSemaphore value=1) the whole time, then writes to a dead channel. There is no per-request timeout and no shouldCancel hook on the HTTP path (HTTP calls the no-arg `complete`/`stream` overloads that pass `shouldCancel: { false }`, ModelRuntime.swift:13-22).
code.impact: A single slow/abandoned local request blocks every other local inference request (head-of-line blocking through the value=1 semaphore) until the abandoned generation finishes on its own. Repeated connect-then-disconnect requests pin the permit and stall the node. Wasted compute and, in aggregate, reduced provider availability that the operator cannot see (the work keeps running invisibly).
code.recommendation: Track the per-request detached Task in the RouterHandler and implement channelInactive/errorCaught to cancel it; or thread a `shouldCancel` closure into the HTTP `complete`/`stream` calls that flips when the channel goes inactive. Add a server-side max-inference-duration timeout so an abandoned generation cannot pin the permit indefinitely.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED structurally, DOWNGRADED on severity. (1) RouterHandler (HTTPServer.swift:41) overrides ONLY channelRead — `grep -n 'channelInactive|errorCaught|func channel'` returns a single hit at line 62 (channelRead). No channelInactive/errorCaught exist. (2) The detached tasks at lines 196 and 238 are fire-and-forget: their return value is discarded into no stored property, so nothing holds a handle to cancel them. (3) Both call the no-arg overloads `modelRuntime.complete(request)` (line 199) / `modelRuntime.stream(request){...}` (line 266), which the protocol extension (ModelRuntime.swift:13-22) routes through `shouldCancel: { false }` — so the in-loop cancel check at ModelRuntime.swift:109 and 167 can only fire via `Task.isCancelled`, which never becomes true because the Task is never cancelled. (4) `inferenceGate = AsyncSemaphore(value: 1)` (ModelRuntime.swift:31) is held for the whole `container.perform` body (withPermit wraps it at ModelRuntime.swift:96/150), so an abandoned generation blocks the single permit. The mechanism is real. DOWNGRADE rationale: (a) the server binds 127.0.0.1 only (HTTPServer.swift:35), so this is reachable only by local processes — not an external attack surface; (b) MLX `generate` is bounded by `request.maxTokens` (passed at ModelRuntime.swift:104), and max_tokens is validated > 0 at parse time (ChatCompletionRequest.swift:37) — so an abandoned generation self-terminates in bounded time rather than pinning the permit indefinitely (no unbounded loop exists); (c) the revenue-bearing WS relay path is NOT affected — InferenceRelay threads a real `shouldCancel: { state.isCancelled }` (InferenceRelay.swift:253, 319) and handles cancel/disconnect. Real bug on a loopback dev/diagnostic path with self-terminating worst case = low.

code.title: Validated request parameters seed/presence_penalty/frequency_penalty/response_format are silently ignored by the runtime
code.description: ChatCompletionRequest.parse fully validates `seed`, `presence_penalty`, `frequency_penalty`, and `response_format` (ChatCompletionRequest.swift:63-78, 249-257), but ModelRuntime only ever constructs GenerateParameters with maxTokens/temperature/topP (verified: grep for seed/frequencyPenalty/presencePenalty/responseFormat in ModelRuntime.swift returns nothing). So `seed` does not make generation deterministic, the penalties have no effect, and `response_format: json_object` is accepted (HTTP 200) yet the model output is never constrained to or post-validated as JSON.
code.impact: Buyers paying real USDC get responses that contradict the accepted request: non-deterministic output despite a fixed seed, ignored penalties, and free-form text returned for a json_object request. This is a silent contract violation on a paid inference endpoint and can break clients that depend on JSON-mode or reproducibility.
code.recommendation: Either wire these parameters into GenerateParameters / a JSON-mode post-validation step where MLX supports them, or reject unsupported parameters at parse time with a clear 400 (e.g., reject non-default seed/penalties and response_format=json_object) instead of validating-then-ignoring. At minimum, enforce/validate json_object output before returning it.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED. (1) Parse-time validation of all four params exists: presence_penalty range-checked (ChatCompletionRequest.swift:63-66), frequency_penalty range-checked (68-71), seed parsed (73), response_format parsed into a ResponseFormat enum with .text/.jsonObject cases (78, 168-171, 249-257). All four are stored fields on the struct (ChatCompletionRequest.swift:11-14). (2) ModelRuntime never reads them: `grep -c 'seed'` in ModelRuntime.swift returns 0; `grep -c 'esponseFormat'` returns 0. (3) Both GenerateParameters constructions pass only maxTokens/temperature/topP — non-streaming at lines 103-107, streaming at lines 157-161 — and the startup-probe one at line 233. There is no JSON-mode post-validation anywhere in `complete`/`stream` (the only post-processing is applyOutputFilters at 116/191, which strips stop tokens, not JSON enforcement). This is a genuine validate-then-ignore contract gap on the paid endpoint. Severity medium upheld: it is silent and affects paid output correctness for JSON-mode/seed-dependent clients, but causes no crash, money-accounting error, or security breach, so medium (not high) is correct.

code.title: Health/status `requests_queued` is hardwired to 0 (dead telemetry)
code.description: `requestsQueued` is declared (line 79) and stored (private var, line 110, initialized 0) but never incremented or decremented anywhere in ProviderStatus (verified by grep). It is surfaced in the /v1/health response (HTTPServer.swift:356 -> snapshot.requestsQueued) and the snapshot. Because requests actually queue on the inferenceGate semaphore, the real queue depth can be > 0 while the reported value is always 0.
code.impact: Operators and any coordinator-side autoscaling/health logic that reads requests_queued get a constant 0, masking real backpressure on the single-slot inference gate. Misleading rather than corrupting, but it hides the exact overload condition the field exists to expose.
code.recommendation: Either compute requestsQueued from the inference-gate waiter count / (requestsInFlight - maxConcurrency clamp), or remove the field from the public health/status payload so it does not imply a measurement that is not taken.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED exactly as described. `grep -n 'requestsQueued'` across Sources returns precisely three sites and no others: declaration on the snapshot struct (ProviderStatus.swift:79 `let requestsQueued: Int`), private var initialized to 0 (line 110 `private var requestsQueued = 0`), and the read in snapshot() (line 191 `requestsQueued: requestsQueued`). There is NO `requestsQueued += 1` / `-= 1` anywhere — beginRequest (lines 130-137) increments only requestsInFlight, finishRequest (139-157) decrements only requestsInFlight; the queueing actually happens invisibly inside AsyncSemaphore.waiters (AsyncSemaphore.swift:5, 10) which ProviderStatus has no visibility into. It is surfaced to clients at HTTPServer.swift:355 (`"requests_queued": snapshot.requestsQueued`). Constant-0 dead telemetry confirmed; low severity (misleading observability, no correctness/money impact) is correct.

code.title: Throughput estimate divides completion tokens by total request latency (includes queue wait and prompt processing)
code.description: finishRequest computes `elapsed = max(Date().timeIntervalSince(startedAt), 0.001)` where startedAt is captured in beginRequest BEFORE the request waits on the inferenceGate semaphore and before prompt processing. It then does `windowGenerationSeconds += elapsed` (line 154) and snapshot() reports throughput as `windowCompletionTokens / windowGenerationSeconds` (line 182). So generation seconds actually include semaphore queue-wait and prompt-encode time, not just token generation.
code.impact: Under any concurrency the reported throughput_tps_since_last systematically understates real generation speed (the more queueing, the worse the underestimate). If the coordinator uses this TPS for routing/pricing/capacity decisions, providers are mis-ranked. Not a correctness bug for inference output, but feeds wrong numbers into scheduling.
code.recommendation: Measure generation time from the actual generate() call (or derive from MLX result timings) rather than from beginRequest-to-finishRequest wall clock, and exclude semaphore wait. Keep latency-since-last (which legitimately includes queue wait) separate from a true tokens/second figure.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED. The `startedAt` timestamp is created and returned by beginRequest (ProviderStatus.swift:136 `return Date()`), and beginRequest is called by callers BEFORE inference: in the HTTP path at HTTPServer.swift:197 (`let startedAt = await providerStatus.beginRequest()`) the detached task awaits beginRequest, then calls modelRuntime.complete which internally waits on inferenceGate (ModelRuntime.swift:96) and does prompt prepare (line 101) before any token is generated; the relay path is identical (InferenceRelay.swift:182 beginRequest precedes modelRuntime.complete/stream at 253/319). finishRequest then does `let elapsed = max(Date().timeIntervalSince(startedAt), 0.001)` (line 149) and `windowGenerationSeconds += elapsed` (line 154). snapshot() reports `throughput = windowGenerationSeconds > 0 ? Double(windowCompletionTokens) / windowGenerationSeconds : nil` (line 182). So the divisor is full wall-clock (queue wait + prompt encode + generation), not pure generation time — TPS is systematically understated under queueing. Note there IS a separate, accurate generation-only measurement (measureStartupThroughput, ModelRuntime.swift:222-244, which times only the generate call) used for the capacity estimate, but the per-window throughput_tps_since_last does conflate. Low severity upheld: scheduling/metrics inaccuracy, no inference-output or money correctness impact.

code.title: Streaming delta reconciliation can silently drop or fail to retract output when filtered text is not a growing prefix
code.description: stream() maintains `emittedText` and emits `delta(from: emitted, to: candidate.text)`, where delta returns "" whenever `current` is not prefixed by `emitted` (line 402). candidate.text comes from streamingSafePrefix, which both strips stop tokens (stopTokenFilter.stripping replaces occurrences anywhere, StopTokenFilter.swift:16-22) and applies a suffix holdback (line 364-384). If stripping removes characters that occur in already-emitted text, or if the final applyOutputFilters at lines 191-195 yields `final.text` shorter than what was already streamed, the per-chunk and final delta both compute to "" and the already-streamed bytes cannot be retracted. The non-streaming path applies the same filter once at the end and is unaffected; the divergence is streaming-only.
code.impact: In the edge case where a stop sequence or special token appears partway through already-emitted text, the SSE stream can emit content that the final filtered result would have removed (cannot un-send) or drop a legitimate delta. The buyer's streamed transcript can differ from the canonical final content. Bounded and model/stop-token dependent, so impact is occasional output inconsistency, not crash or money error.
code.recommendation: Make streaming emission monotonic against the same filter used for the final result: only emit when final-filtered text strictly extends previously emitted text, and treat a shrink as a stop/cancel rather than a no-op. Add a unit test feeding a chunk sequence where an interior stop token forces the filtered text to shrink.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED as a real, bounded edge case. delta() returns "" whenever current is not prefixed by emitted: `guard current.hasPrefix(emitted) else { return "" }` (ModelRuntime.swift:402). Per-chunk emission only advances emittedText when delta is non-empty (lines 177-181); a shrink yields delta="" and is silently a no-op rather than a retraction. StopTokenFilter.stripping does `replacingOccurrences(of: token, with: "")` for every token (StopTokenFilter.swift:18-19) — it removes ALL occurrences anywhere in the text, not just a trailing stop, so if a special/stop token appears interior to already-emitted text on a later decode, the freshly-filtered candidate.text can be SHORTER than emittedText and no longer prefix it. The final reconciliation at lines 191-198 uses the same delta() against final.text, so a final that shrinks below emittedText also produces finalDelta="" (cannot un-send). The streamingSafePrefix holdback logic (lines 364-384) reduces but does not eliminate this — holdback only guards trailing partial-token suffixes, not interior occurrences. The non-streaming complete() path applies applyOutputFilters once (line 116) so it is unaffected — divergence is streaming-only as claimed. SSE chunks are already flushed to the buyer (HTTPServer.swift:267 / InferenceRelay.swift:319-327) so they genuinely cannot be retracted. Real but low: requires a stop/special token to appear mid-stream after being emitted, model/tokenizer dependent, bounded to transcript-vs-final inconsistency, no crash or accounting error. Low upheld.

code.title: Local HTTP chat-completions path has no per-connection concurrency limit; all requests pile onto the value=1 inference gate
code.description: Unlike the WS relay (InferenceRelay enforces `active.count < maxActiveRequests`, InferenceRelay.swift:70-79, with maxActiveRequests=1), handleChatCompletions performs no admission check: every POST spawns a Task.detached (line 196) that blocks on inferenceGate inside ModelRuntime. There is no cap on the number of queued detached tasks, no 429/queue_full on the HTTP path, and no request timeout. The server binds 127.0.0.1 only (line 35), so this is reachable only by local processes.
code.impact: A local client can open many concurrent chat requests; each accumulates a detached task and buffered request body waiting on the single permit, growing memory and task count without bound and with no queue-full signal. Mitigated by the loopback-only bind (not remotely exploitable), so this is a robustness/self-DoS concern rather than an external attack surface.
code.recommendation: Apply the same bounded-admission policy as the relay on the HTTP path: reject with 429/queue_full once an in-flight+queued cap is reached, and add a request timeout. This also composes with the channelInactive cancellation fix above.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED. handleChatCompletions (HTTPServer.swift:180-227) performs zero admission/concurrency check before spawning the detached inference task at line 196 — the only guards earlier are body-size (line 93 bodyTooLarge) and request parsing (line 187). There is no analogue of the relay's `guard active.count < maxActiveRequests` gate (InferenceRelay.swift:70-79) which returns an `error_queue_full` end-frame; the HTTP path has no 429/queue_full and no timeout. Each POST allocates a detached task that then blocks on inferenceGate.withPermit (ModelRuntime.swift:96) so excess requests stack as suspended tasks + buffered bodies. The AsyncSemaphore queues all waiters in an unbounded `waiters` array (AsyncSemaphore.swift:5,10) so there is no backpressure ceiling. CORRECTLY scoped: bind is `bootstrap.bind(host: "127.0.0.1", port: config.port)` (HTTPServer.swift:35) — loopback only, not remotely reachable, so this is self-DoS/robustness, not an external attack surface. Low severity upheld.

code.title: NAK in_reply_to uses the literal type string instead of request_id for invalid/duplicate inference requests
code.description: On the missing-fields and duplicate-request-id paths, sendNAK is called with `inReplyTo: "inference_request"` (lines 43, 61, 66), the frame type literal, whereas the tier2 decrypt-failure path correctly uses `inReplyTo: requestID` (line 49, 55). For the duplicate-id case the actual requestID is known (line 66 even interpolates it into the message) yet in_reply_to is still the generic type. The existing test asserts the literal value (InferenceRelayTests.swift:126), so this is intentional/locked behavior, but it is inconsistent and makes coordinator-side correlation harder for these NAKs.
code.impact: Coordinator cannot correlate the duplicate-id / invalid-message NAK back to the specific request via in_reply_to (it must parse the message string), unlike the tier2 path. No correctness or money impact; purely diagnostic friction.
code.recommendation: When request_id is known (duplicate-id branch at line 66, and arguably the missing-stream/body branch), set in_reply_to to the request_id for consistency with the tier2 path, updating the corresponding test expectation.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED. sendNAK is invoked with the type literal `inReplyTo: "inference_request"` on three paths: the missing request_id/stream guard (InferenceRelay.swift:43), the cleartext missing-body branch (line 61), and the duplicate-request-id branch (line 66) — and at line 66 the real requestID IS already known (it is interpolated into the message: `"Duplicate active request_id: \(requestID)"`), yet in_reply_to is still the generic literal. By contrast the tier2 paths correctly pass the actual requestID: line 49 (`inReplyTo: requestID`, tier2_encrypted_frame_required) and line 55 (`inReplyTo: requestID`, tier2_aead_decrypt_failed). sendNAK writes in_reply_to verbatim (lines 160-168). The behavior is locked by InferenceRelayTests.swift:126 (`XCTAssertEqual(frames[0]["in_reply_to"] as? String, "inference_request")`) for the missing-fields case, confirming it is intentional/asserted, not accidental. info severity upheld: pure diagnostic-correlation friction, no correctness or money impact; for the missing-request_id branch (line 43) the requestID genuinely is not yet known so the literal is defensible there, but the duplicate-id branch (66) is a real inconsistency.

code.title: Console dashboard interpolates server-controlled /v1/status into innerHTML under unsafe-inline CSP
code.description: renderDashboard sets row.innerHTML from a template literal interpolating val; the Status row val is ps.status, raw unsanitized JSON from fetch of /v1/status (fetchStatus 781-786). Other dynamic values use textContent; this is the lone HTML sink. CSP is script-src unsafe-inline, so an injected img onerror executes.
code.impact: If /v1/status is ever attacker-influenced, JS runs in-origin, reads the demo_token (805-818) and exfiltrates localStorage chat history. Needs a malicious upstream.
code.recommendation: Render Status via textContent/className, html-escape val, drop unsafe-inline from script-src.
code.evidence: Confirmed at index.html:1093 — `row.innerHTML = `${key}${val}`` with no escaping. The Status row's `val` is `ps.status` (line 1086: `{ key: 'Status', val: ps ? ps.status : 'checking', ... }`), where `ps = poolStatus` (line 1083). poolStatus is assigned raw at line 783 `poolStatus = j` from `j = await r.json()` of `fetch(API + '/v1/status')` (lines 781-782). So server JSON reaches innerHTML unescaped. The two numeric rows are safe — `String((ps.pool && ps.pool.ready) || 0)` (lines 1087-1088) coerces to a number, and the model-tag loop uses `tag.textContent = m` (line 1109). The `cls` token for Status is derived from constrained comparisons (line 1086: `ps.status === 'up' ? 'ok' : ...`), not raw input, so only `val` is the injection vector — exactly as the finding states. CSP confirmed at nginx-console.streamvc.live.conf:27: `script-src 'unsafe-inline'`, so an injected `` inline handler would execute. The finding correctly scopes this to medium given the precondition that the demo's own /v1/status API must be attacker-controlled/compromised (not a direct external input path); fetchStatus also re-fires every 30s (line 1158 setInterval), keeping the sink live. Real defense-in-depth XSS sink; medium is justified.

code.title: companion.py 1-second timestamp PRIMARY KEY + INSERT OR REPLACE silently overwrites sub-second samples
code.description: ts_utc TEXT PRIMARY KEY, INSERT OR REPLACE (85), 1-second timestamp (82). Loop blocks 1s in cpu_percent then sleeps interval-1 (92); with --interval 1 sleep is 0, so two iterations share a second and the second write overwrites the first silently.
code.impact: Silent telemetry gaps; real data loss under --interval 1.
code.recommendation: Use AUTOINCREMENT or microsecond timestamps with a plain INSERT.
code.evidence: All cited mechanics verified. companion.py:33 `ts_utc TEXT PRIMARY KEY`; line 82 `ts = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="seconds")` truncates to whole seconds; line 85 `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO host_metrics`. Line 92 `remaining = args.interval - 1` so with `--interval 1` remaining is 0 and the inner `while remaining > 0` sleep loop (lines 93-96) never executes. The per-iteration timing is only the ~1s of `psutil.cpu_percent(interval=1)` (line 79) plus body work, so two consecutive iterations can stamp the same whole second; INSERT OR REPLACE then silently overwrites the earlier row. Bug is real and exactly as described. Severity correctly LOW: argparse default is 60 (line 64), documented usage in the module docstring (lines 10-12) is 60s/10s, and `--interval 1` is not a documented/expected mode; at any interval >= 2 the collision cannot occur because successive timestamps differ by >= 1s. Confirmed at low.

code.title: harness.py rotate model-select reads/writes index file unlocked; concurrent runs skip/repeat a model
code.description: resolve_model rotate reads model_index, writes next index (150-151), selects current index mod len (159). Non-atomic read-modify-write: a manual --once overlapping the hourly cron reads the same index and advances identically, so rotation skips/repeats.
code.impact: Biases which model is benchmarked; no corruption.
code.recommendation: Guard with fcntl.flock or temp-file+os.replace.
code.evidence: Read-modify-write confirmed non-atomic at harness.py:145-151: `idx = int(index_file.read_text().strip())` (146), then `next_idx = (idx + 1) % len(models_list)` (150), then `index_file.write_text(str(next_idx))` (151) — no flock, no temp-file+rename, no lock of any kind around the read and the write. Two processes entering this block concurrently both read the same idx and both write the same next_idx, so one rotation step is lost (skip/repeat) and both runs benchmark the same model — exactly as described. Severity correctly LOW: (a) no data corruption, only selection bias; (b) the bug is latent under the CURRENTLY INSTALLED schedule — CRON_TEMPLATE.txt shows the only active lanes are coord-cooperative.sh (line 31) and coord-adversarial.sh (line 40) with no overlapping rotate-mode crons, and `model_select: "rotate"` is commented out in every live config (config.yaml:19, config-coord.yaml are commented; config-m1/m4.yaml use a single `model:` string with no `models:` list at all, so resolve_model returns early at harness.py:135 and never reaches the rotate branch). Triggering requires enabling rotate AND running two harness invocations that overlap inside this ~microsecond window. Real but conditional; low is appropriate.

code.title: install.sh readiness substring grep false-positives a superstring model id
code.description: grep -Fq of the model string is a substring match; a served id containing the requested one (e.g. ...-4bit vs ...-4bit-DWQ) passes despite a different loaded model.
code.impact: Reports Ready for a mismatched model.
code.recommendation: Match the exact JSON id value.
code.evidence: The mechanism is real: install.sh:683 uses `grep -Fq "$model"` which is an unanchored fixed-string substring match against the /v1/models JSON body. But the concrete collision the finding cites does NOT exist for this installer's model set. The only model ids install.sh can select are the three at lines 270/272/274 (and the menu 300-302): `mlx-community/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-4bit`, `mlx-community/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-4bit`, `mlx-community/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-4bit`. None is a substring of another — notably `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-4bit` is NOT a substring of `Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-4bit` (7B vs 14B diverge before the shared suffix). The hypothetical `-4bit` vs `-4bit-DWQ` superstring pair the finding invents has no corresponding entry anywhere in the installer or the beta configs (grep for DWQ/6bit/8bit returns nothing). MACPROVIDER_MODEL (line 280-281) can inject an arbitrary string, but a false Ready still requires the *served* id to be a strict superstring of the requested one, which the local macprovider-cli (loading exactly the requested `--model`, line 595/644) will not produce. The grep is also paired with an `owned_by macprovider` check (line 682). So the bug is a latent fragility with no triggering input in the current product — downgraded from low to info.

security.title: Provider payout is billed on the provider's own self-reported token counts with no attestation/verification
security.description: ComputeCredits treats usage_source='provider_reported' prompt/completion token counts as ground truth and converts them directly into provider_credits. Those counts originate from the UNTRUSTED provider: in internal/buyer/server.go:1539 `attempt.PromptTokens, attempt.CompletionTokens = tokenPointersFromUsageObject(end.Usage)` parses the provider's own WebSocket `end` frame `usage` object. The only sanity gate is invalidBillableTokenCount(), which merely rejects v<0 or v>maxBillableTokens (10,000,000). There is no cross-check of reported tokens against bytes actually streamed (byte estimation is used only as a fallback when the provider reports nothing), and the attestation_class column declared in store.go:65 is never written by any billing or buyer code (grep returns no INSERT setting it), so no attestation gate exists. A provider therefore controls the multiplicand of its own payout up to 10M prompt + 10M completion tokens per request.
security.impact: A malicious or compromised provider can over-report completion_tokens (up to 10M) on real or trivial requests to inflate provider_credits and thus its real-USDC payout at settlement, draining operator funds / over-billing buyers. This is the core money-integrity boundary of the marketplace.
security.recommendation: Do not pay providers purely on self-reported usage. Bind billing to an independently observable quantity: cap/validate provider_reported completion_tokens against the byte-derived estimate (estimatedCompletionTokensFromBytes) with a tolerance band, quarantine rows whose reported tokens exceed the byte estimate by more than X%, and/or require a signed attestation (populate attestation_class) before treating usage as provider_reported. Lower maxBillableTokens to a realistic per-request ceiling.
security.evidence: Verified end-to-end. (1) server.go:1539 `attempt.PromptTokens, attempt.CompletionTokens = tokenPointersFromUsageObject(end.Usage)` and the parser at server.go:2766-2778 unmarshals `prompt_tokens`/`completion_tokens` straight from the provider's `end` frame with no bounds. (2) formula.go:124-134: in the default branch UsageSource is forced to 'provider_reported' and completion = *completionTokens verbatim; the only gate is invalidBillableTokenCount (formula.go:176-178: `v < 0 || v > 10000000`). (3) estimatedCompletionTokensFromBytes is invoked ONLY as a fallback: server.go:1548-1550 guards it with `if attempt.CompletionTokens == nil`, and the disconnect/timeout paths (1564,1570,1575,1582) — it never caps a value the provider DID report on the success path. (4) zeroTokenFault (server.go:2730-2741) only fires when completion_tokens==0 with abnormal finishReason — it detects UNDER-reporting, not inflation, so it does not mitigate over-reporting. (5) attestation_class is confirmed write-never: grep shows the only references are the schema decl (store.go:65) and two READ sites (endpoints.go:110 MAX(attestation_class), endpoints.go:143 nullStringAny(attestation)); the hot-path INSERT at hotpath.go:192-199 omits the column entirely. Severity kept high: this is the marketplace's core payout-integrity boundary and the inflation path is real. Note on exploitability for prioritization: the actor must be an onboarded/authenticated provider (not anonymous), which fits the threat model but is not fully unauthenticated.

security.title: Operator admin key compared with non-constant-time string equality
security.description: Admin authentication uses `r.Header.Get("Authorization") != "Bearer "+h.operatorKey`, a plain Go string comparison that short-circuits on the first differing byte. The same codebase already uses subtle.ConstantTimeCompare for secret comparison elsewhere (internal/buyer/server.go:2613 and internal/tier2/pillar_c.go:270), so this is an inconsistent, weaker check on the high-value operator credential that gates /admin/ledger/summary, /providers, and /reconcile.
security.impact: Theoretically allows a byte-by-byte timing recovery of the operator key, which grants full read access to the ledger (all provider earnings, totals, reconciliation) and the ability to trigger reconcile runs. Practically hard to exploit because the provider port defaults to a 127.0.0.1 bind behind the gateway and network jitter dominates, but it is a real deviation from the project's own secure pattern.
security.recommendation: Compare with crypto/subtle: `subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(r.Header.Get("Authorization")), []byte("Bearer "+h.operatorKey)) == 1`, matching buyer/server.go and tier2/pillar_c.go.
security.evidence: The non-constant-time compare is real: endpoints.go:61 is exactly `if h.operatorKey != "" && r.Header.Get("Authorization") != "Bearer "+h.operatorKey`, Go string `!=` which short-circuits per byte. The inconsistency claim is verified: subtle.ConstantTimeCompare exists at buyer/server.go:2613 (`return subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(token), []byte(expected)) == 1`) and tier2/pillar_c.go:270. Downgraded from medium to low for two reasons that the finding's own mitigation text gets partly wrong: (a) the admin endpoints are NOT purely localhost-only as one might assume — dist/coordinator.yaml:2-4 documents that nginx reverse-proxies `/admin/*` to provider_port, so they are reachable over the public internet; BUT (b) that same remote path means an attacker measures timing across TLS+nginx+internet jitter, which swamps the sub-microsecond per-byte signal, making practical recovery of the operator key infeasible; and (c) the key is a 256-bit openssl rand -hex 32 value (dist/coordinator.yaml:44-45), so even a noiseless oracle requires an impractical number of timed requests. Real hygiene deviation, very low practical exploitability — low is the justified severity.

security.title: Admin ledger auth fails open when operator key is empty
security.description: The admin guard is `if h.operatorKey != "" && r.Header.Get("Authorization") != "Bearer "+h.operatorKey`. When h.operatorKey is the empty string the entire condition is false, so the request is allowed with no authentication. The billing handler thus fails OPEN rather than closed.
