This is currently mitigated by config validation (internal/config/config.go:398-399 rejects an empty auth.operator_key, and 569-570 for explorer), but the handler itself provides no defense-in-depth if ever instantiated with an empty key (e.g., a future caller, test harness, or misconfigured embedding).
security.impact: If the operator key is ever empty/unset at the handler layer, /admin/ledger/summary, /admin/ledger/providers, and /admin/ledger/reconcile become fully unauthenticated, exposing all provider earnings and totals and allowing reconcile runs.
security.recommendation: Fail closed: if h.operatorKey == "" reject all admin requests (return 403) rather than allowing them, so the handler does not depend on an external validator to be safe.
security.evidence: The fail-open branch is exactly as described: endpoints.go:61 short-circuits the whole guard with `h.operatorKey != "" &&`, so an empty operatorKey skips the 403 at endpoints.go:62 and falls through to fn(w,r) at endpoints.go:65. The claimed mitigation is also verified real and load-bearing: config.go:397-400 `func (c Config) Validate()` returns an error `auth.operator_key must be set` when `c.Auth.OperatorKey == ""`, and validateExplorer at config.go:568-571 enforces it when explorer is enabled; main.go:115-116 passes cfg.Auth.OperatorKey into Handlers() only after config load. So in the shipped binary the key is non-empty and the handler authenticates. Confirmed at low: it is a genuine defense-in-depth gap (handler safety depends on an external validator), not an exploitable production bug today. Severity stays low.

security.title: Internal error strings echoed to HTTP clients
security.description: Multiple handlers return raw database/runtime error text to the caller via `writeError(w, http.StatusInternalServerError, "internal_error", err.Error())`. err.Error() from modernc.org/sqlite can leak SQL fragments, column names, or schema details. The /admin/* paths are behind operator auth, but the same writeError-with-err.Error() pattern is used on the admin reconcile path that is reachable once the operator key is known.
security.impact: Leaks internal schema/SQL details that aid an attacker who has (or is brute-forcing) the operator key. Low severity because it is behind operator auth and a localhost-bound port.
security.recommendation: Log the detailed error server-side and return a generic message (e.g. "internal error") to the client; do not include err.Error() in the response body.
security.evidence: All eight cited lines verified to pass raw err.Error() into the response body via writeError(...,"internal_error", err.Error()): endpoints.go:117 and 128 (providers() query/scan errors), 166/171/177/188/194 (reconcile() sumErr/buyerEquivalentCredits errors), and 210 (reconcile() INSERT error). writeError (endpoints.go:522-524) serializes the message into JSON `error.message` sent to the client. The leak is real. Severity correctly low: every one of these lines is inside handler funcs (providers, reconcile) reachable only through h.admin (endpoints.go:43-48, 56-66) which requires the operator bearer; the DB is modernc.org/sqlite so leaked text is SQL/schema fragments, not secrets. Note for accuracy: the bind is loopback (config.go:220) but nginx proxies /admin/* publicly (dist/coordinator.yaml:3), so 'localhost-bound' overstates the isolation slightly — still gated by operator auth, so low stands.

security.title: Per-provider N+1 subquery in admin providers listing enables amplified load
security.description: providers() runs the main grouped aggregate query, then for every returned provider issues an additional `SELECT SUM(provider_credits) FROM ledger_payout_ready WHERE provider_id=? AND status='ready'` (line 139). With limit clamped to 200, each admin call can fan out to ~200 extra point queries. The reconcile endpoint's buyerEquivalentCredits (endpoints.go:226-279) additionally runs per-row correlated subqueries over request_log inside a 5s context. These are admin-authenticated so not a remote-unauth DoS, but a holder of the operator key (or a future relaxation of auth) can drive amplified DB load.
security.impact: Amplified database load (CPU/IO) on the coordinator's SQLite from a single authenticated admin request; can contend with the hot-path billing writes that share the same DB. Not exploitable without the operator key.
security.recommendation: Replace the per-provider pending-payout subquery with a single LEFT JOIN aggregate over ledger_payout_ready grouped by provider_id; bound reconcile scans and consider a stricter time/row budget.
security.evidence: The N+1 is real and structural: endpoints.go:123 `for rows.Next()` loop body at 135-144 calls `h.sum(ctx, ...ledger_payout_ready WHERE provider_id=? AND status='ready', providerID)` at endpoints.go:139 once per returned provider; limit is clamped to 200 at endpoints.go:93-95, so up to ~200 extra point queries per call. The reconcile correlated-subquery claim is verified: buyerEquivalentCredits (endpoints.go:226-279) runs a per-row correlated subquery `COALESCE((SELECT COUNT(*)-1 FROM request_log prior WHERE prior.request_id=rl.request_id AND prior.id<=rl.id),0)` (endpoints.go:230-232) and inside the rows.Next() loop calls byteEstimatedLedgerGross (per-row query at endpoints.go:281-315) and snapshotAt (endpoints.go:271) — all under a context.WithTimeout(...,5*time.Second) (endpoints.go:162). Both paths sit behind h.admin operator auth (endpoints.go:45-48). Confirmed at info: correct severity given it requires the operator key and the 5s cap on reconcile bounds the worst case; it is a performance/amplification concern, not a security vulnerability.

security.title: Buyer-controlled X-Request-ID drives billing idempotency; reuse zero-credits served requests (under-billing / free inference)
security.description: handleChatCompletions takes the caller's X-Request-ID header (server.go:801), passes it through requestIDForBuyerRequest which simply echoes any valid UUIDv4 (server.go:2832-2839), and uses it verbatim as originalRequestID -> requestlog.Row.RequestID (server.go:832) -> billing HotPathInput.RequestID (server.go:869). The request_log table stores request_id as NOT NULL but with no UNIQUE constraint (requestlog/store.go:88-110, only a non-unique index). billing.WriteHotPath then derives the billing attempt number from SELECT COUNT(*) FROM request_log WHERE request_id = ? (hotpath.go:54-56) and, for any derived attempt_n>0 / >1, takes the 'ambiguous_attempt_n' branch that runs result = zeroCredits(result) before inserting the ledger row (hotpath.go:75, 107). Because the buyer fully controls X-Request-ID and only its UUIDv4 format is validated (not its uniqueness or prior use), a buyer can submit many genuinely-distinct, successfully-served paid requests all carrying one fixed valid UUIDv4. Every request after the first is treated as a later 'attempt' of the same logical request and is billed at zero gross/provider/operator credits.
security.recommendation: Do not let the client choose the billing identity. Generate the billing request_id server-side (uuid.NewString) and keep the client's X-Request-ID only as an opaque correlation/log field that never feeds attempt derivation. Alternatively, make request_log.request_id+attempt_n a UNIQUE/idempotency key whose first-write wins and reject (HTTP 409) or fully re-bill (not zero-credit) collisions from distinct payloads, and verify the request body hash matches before collapsing two request_ids into one logical request. Ensure the gateway also regenerates/overwrites X-Request-ID so it cannot be pinned by the end client.
security.evidence: Read every cited line and traced the full path including the upstream gateway. requestIDForBuyerRequest (server.go:2832-2838) returns parsed.String() verbatim when uuid.Parse succeeds and parsed.Version()==4, so any valid UUIDv4 the client sends is echoed as the billing request_id. handleChatCompletions sets originalRequestID = requestID (server.go:804) and feeds it into requestlog.Row.RequestID (server.go:832) and billing.HotPathInput.RequestID via row.RequestID (server.go:869). billingAttemptN starts at 0 each HTTP request (server.go:810). In WriteHotPath the request_log row is inserted FIRST (hotpath.go:46 InsertExec) THEN counted (hotpath.go:55 SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE request_id=?), so the count includes the just-inserted row. For the Nth distinct HTTP request reusing one UUIDv4: requestCount=N, derived=N-1; for N>=2 the condition derived>in.AttemptN (1>0) and in.AttemptN!=derived (0!=1) is true, entering the ambiguous branch at hotpath.go:56-86 which executes result=zeroCredits(result) (hotpath.go:75) and inserts a quarantined zero-credit ledger row (insertRequestCreditTx with quarantined=true, reason 'ambiguous_attempt_n', hotpath.go:77) and NO operator credit row. The request_log schema (store.go:87-110) has only a non-unique index idx_request_log_request_id_id, confirming no uniqueness guard. CRITICALLY, I verified the gateway does NOT regenerate a valid client UUID: gateway middleware (phase5-gateway/internal/router/server.go:168-171) keeps the client's X-Request-ID whenever isUUIDLike(requestID) is true, and isUUIDLike requires the v4 version nibble (v[14]=='4') and an 8/9/a/b variant -- i.e. exactly a valid UUIDv4 passes through unchanged. The gateway then forwards it verbatim to the coordinator (server.go:1349 upReq.Header.Set('X-Request-ID', requestID(r))). So the exploit is reachable end-to-end via the public chat path with no special privilege. Confirmed at high: trivial exploitation, direct USDC revenue loss, provider under-payout, normal-client reachability.

security.title: Unauthenticated /v1/pool/check: X-Forwarded-For-spoofable rate limit over an unbounded, never-evicted map (memory-exhaustion DoS)
security.description: handlePoolCheck is an unauthenticated GET on the public buyer router (server.go:335, 583). Its only protection is allowPoolCheck (server.go:617-627), which keys a 1-request/second limit on clientIP(r). clientIP (server.go:629-641) returns the first value of the attacker-supplied X-Forwarded-For header when present, before falling back to RemoteAddr. Because the buyer port is loopback-fronted by the gateway, RemoteAddr is effectively constant, so the rate-limit identity is whatever XFF the caller sends. The rate-limit state lives in s.poolCheckLast, a sync.Map that is only ever Load-ed and Store-d (server.go:620, 625) and never pruned, TTL-expired, or size-capped (grep confirms only those two call sites at lines 620/625).
security.recommendation: Do not trust X-Forwarded-For for rate-limiting unless it originates from a configured trusted proxy hop (parse the chain and take the right-most trusted entry, or use RemoteAddr only). Replace the unbounded sync.Map with a bounded, TTL/LRU-evicting limiter (or a token-bucket keyed on a capped set of buckets). Cap total tracked keys and evict the oldest.
security.evidence: The two low-level mechanics are real and confirmed: clientIP (server.go:629-641) returns the leftmost X-Forwarded-For entry before falling back to RemoteAddr, and grep over internal/buyer confirms poolCheckLast is declared at server.go:72 and only Load-ed (server.go:620) and Store-d (server.go:625) -- never pruned, TTL-expired, or size-capped, so it does grow unbounded. HOWEVER the finding's core severity driver -- 'reachable without authentication and at high request volume' from the public internet -- is false. The coordinator buyer port binds to 127.0.0.1 by default (config/config.go:220 BindAddress='127.0.0.1', consumed at cmd/coordinator/main.go:111 buyerAddr and :126 buyerHTTP), and the public gateway does NOT proxy /v1/pool/check at all: the complete gateway mux route set is /auth/demo-session, /v1/models, /v1/chat/completions, /v1/sticky, /v1/status (phase5-gateway/internal/router/server.go:138-147) -- pool/check is absent. The gateway also never sets or forwards X-Forwarded-For anywhere (grep for X-Forwarded-For in the gateway router returns nothing), and copyForwardHeaders forwards only Accept and X-MacProvider-Retry to the coordinator (server.go:2209+). Therefore /v1/pool/check is reachable ONLY from the coordinator host's loopback (same-host process or SSRF from a co-located service), not by an unauthenticated remote attacker. The map growth and XFF-spoof are genuine code defects, but exploitation requires the same loopback-access precondition that finding 5 already calls out as the amplifier; the realistic blast radius is local-only DoS of the coordinator by something already on its loopback. Downgraded high -> low accordingly.

security.title: X-MacProvider-Account is trusted unauthenticated for billing/sticky attribution and cross-account purge
security.description: The buyer server treats the X-MacProvider-Account header as an authenticated identity with no verification. stickyStore writes AccountID directly from headers.Get('X-MacProvider-Account') (server.go:2436), and the internal sticky-purge endpoint deletes all sticky entries whose stored AccountID matches an attacker-suppliable account_id query param (handleInternalStickyDelete server.go:512-529 -> purgeStickyAccount server.go:2439-2449). The account header is also part of hasInternalRoutingHeader (server.go:2584-2596) but is only gated on the internal port; on the public buyer port nothing binds the account header to a paying identity. Because the value is unauthenticated and self-asserted, account attribution carried into billing/log rows and sticky entries cannot be trusted as an authorization subject.
security.recommendation: Derive the account identity from an authenticated, signed token (set by the gateway after auth and verified by the coordinator, e.g. an HMAC/JWT the coordinator validates), not from a plain client-settable header. At minimum, document and enforce that the gateway strips any inbound X-MacProvider-Account from external clients and re-sets it only after authentication.
security.evidence: The in-component code is exactly as described: stickyStore writes AccountID: headers.Get('X-MacProvider-Account') with no verification (server.go:2436), and purgeStickyAccount deletes every sticky entry whose stored AccountID equals the caller-supplied account_id (server.go:2439-2449), invoked from handleInternalStickyDelete (server.go:512-529). But the realistic exploitability is much lower than 'medium' for three reasons I verified: (1) handleInternalStickyDelete is bearer-gated up front (server.go:513 internalBearerAuthorized) using subtle.ConstantTimeCompare against a configured non-empty key (function body read: returns false if expected key empty, requires 'Bearer ' prefix, length-checks then constant-time compares) -- so cross-account purge requires the operator key, which the finding itself concedes. (2) The public gateway does NOT forward a client-supplied X-MacProvider-Account to the coordinator: copyForwardHeaders forwards only Accept and X-MacProvider-Retry (phase5-gateway/internal/router/server.go:2209+), and the account header reaching the coordinator is set explicitly from the AUTHENTICATED subject.AccountID (gateway server.go:1359 upReq.Header.Set('X-MacProvider-Account', subject.AccountID)), only when sticky routing conditions hold. Note the gateway's stripInternalMacProviderHeaders only strips x-macprovider-internal-* (isInternalMacProviderHeader matches lower=='x-macprovider-internal-conv' or prefix 'x-macprovider-internal-'), so it does NOT strip a raw inbound X-MacProvider-Account -- but since copyForwardHeaders doesn't copy it anyway, the client value never reaches the coordinator through the real path. (3) The finding concedes billing money math keys on request/provider, not account, so forged account attribution does not move money. Net: the only forge-able effect via the documented coordinator component is sticky-affinity metadata mislabeling, and only if the loopback buyer port is reached directly (per finding 5). Downgraded medium -> low.

security.title: Provider-reported usage tokens pass through the buyer layer unclamped against actual request size (payout/over-billing inflation)
security.description: Token counts that drive billing are taken verbatim from the untrusted provider's response. tokenPointersFromUsageObject (server.go:2766-2778) and tokenPointersFromChatResponse (server.go:2756-2764) return the provider-supplied prompt_tokens/completion_tokens *int64 with no bound or sanity check, and these are handed straight to billing (e.g. server.go:1204 non-stream HTTP path, server.go:1400-1404 WS non-stream path). Note the explicit maxRequestLogUsageTokens (1e7) clamp exists ONLY on the byte-estimated path (estimatedCompletionTokensFromBytes server.go:2788-2789), not on the provider-reported path. The only ceiling is downstream in billing.invalidBillableTokenCount, which rejects values >10,000,000 (formula.go:16,176-177) and negatives; within [0,1e7] the provider's self-reported counts are billed as-is and are never reconciled against the actual prompt size or emitted bytes.
security.recommendation: Cross-check provider-reported usage at the buyer layer: clamp completion_tokens to the byte-estimate (estimatedCompletionTokensFromBytes already exists) plus a tolerance, clamp prompt_tokens to an estimate from the actual request body, and flag/zero-out or quarantine responses whose reported usage is implausibly larger than observed bytes. Lower the absolute per-field ceiling toward realistic context limits rather than 1e7.
security.evidence: Confirmed by reading the token-extraction and billing-formula code. tokenPointersFromUsageObject (server.go:2766-2778) unmarshals prompt_tokens/completion_tokens straight into *int64 and returns them with zero bounds/sanity checks; tokenPointersFromChatResponse (server.go:2756-2764) delegates to it. These pointers feed billing directly: non-stream HTTP path server.go:1204 (promptTok, completionTok := tokenPointersFromChatResponse(respBody); logProviderRow(...promptTok, completionTok...)) and WS non-stream path server.go:1400-1404 (tokenPointersFromUsageObject(end.Usage)). The 1e7 clamp truly exists only on the byte-estimate path: maxRequestLogUsageTokens=int64(10000000) (server.go:116) is applied only inside estimatedCompletionTokensFromBytes (server.go:2788-2789), with no equivalent on the provider-reported values. In ComputeCredits the provider path sets UsageProviderReported and uses the raw completionTokens/promptTokens (formula.go:119-134); the only guard is invalidBillableTokenCount(v) = v<0 || v>maxBillableTokens where maxBillableTokens=10000000 (formula.go:16,176-177), which zero-credits ONLY out-of-[0,1e7] values (formula.go:135-138). Thus any reported count in [0,1e7] is billed verbatim with no reconciliation against actual prompt bytes or emitted response bytes. Real over-bill/payout-inflation vector from an untrusted provider. Kept at medium: the abuse requires a malicious or buggy provider (not an anonymous remote attacker), is bounded by the 10M per-field cap and the configured rate card, and is per-request rather than unbounded.

security.title: No authentication on the public buyer API and no WriteTimeout; full reliance on loopback + gateway as the only trust boundary
security.description: Server.Handler() registers /v1/chat/completions, /v1/models, /v1/pool/check, /healthz with no auth middleware (server.go:331-338), and handleChatCompletions performs no API-key/identity check (server.go:800 onward). main.go mounts it raw via newHTTPServer (main.go:126) and the http.Server sets ReadHeaderTimeout/ReadTimeout/IdleTimeout but no WriteTimeout (main.go:181-189). Security depends entirely on the default 127.0.0.1 bind (config.go:220) plus the gateway sanitizing/authenticating requests; the component itself trusts every X-MacProvider-* header and the X-Request-ID it receives. If the buyer port is ever exposed (bind_address change, container networking, SSRF from a co-located service), there is zero in-process authn/authz, and the missing WriteTimeout means a slow buyer reading a stream can hold a connection (and its provider slot) indefinitely.
security.recommendation: Add an in-process authentication gate (shared secret or signed token from the gateway) on the buyer router even though it is loopback-bound, treat all X-MacProvider-*/X-Request-ID headers as untrusted unless authenticated, set a WriteTimeout (or per-stream deadline) on the buyer http.Server, and assert/log if bind_address is ever non-loopback without auth enabled.
security.evidence: Confirmed exactly as described. Server.Handler() (server.go:331-338) registers /healthz, /v1/models, /v1/pool/check, /v1/chat/completions with NO auth middleware wrapping the chi router. handleChatCompletions (server.go:800 onward) performs no API-key/identity check -- its first action is reading the X-Request-ID header. newHTTPServer (cmd/coordinator/main.go:181-189) sets ReadHeaderTimeout:10s, ReadTimeout:310s, IdleTimeout:120s and indeed NO WriteTimeout field. buyerHTTP := newHTTPServer(buyerAddr, buyerServer.Handler()) mounts it raw (main.go:126). The sole compensating control is the loopback default: config/config.go:220 BindAddress='127.0.0.1', used for buyerAddr (main.go:111). This is correctly characterized as low-severity-but-amplifier: it is the precondition that makes findings 2 and 3 reachable, and the missing WriteTimeout is a genuine slow-reader connection/slot-holding risk on streaming responses. Kept at low given the loopback bind default and gateway fronting.

security.title: No read/idle deadline or frame-size limit on hijacked provider WebSocket (pre-auth slowloris + unbounded-buffer DoS)
security.description: handleProvider calls gobwas.UpgradeHTTP (server.go:169) which hijacks the net.Conn. After hijack, the http.Server ReadTimeout/IdleTimeout/ReadHeaderTimeout configured in newHTTPServer (main.go:185-187) no longer apply to the raw connection. The WS code never calls conn.SetReadDeadline / SetWriteDeadline anywhere in the connection lifecycle. The first auth read wsutil.ReadClientData(conn) at server.go:221 blocks indefinitely with no deadline, and the per-session liveness monitor (monitorHeartbeat) only starts AFTER a session is registered post-auth (registerProviderSession, server.go:607). Additionally, ReadClientData in readProviderLoop (server.go:613) reads an entire WS text frame into memory with no max-frame-size cap (contrast io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20) at server.go:909). Impact: two unauthenticated DoS vectors against an internet-facing edge accepting untrusted contributor Macs — (1) slowloris/half-open goroutine+FD exhaustion via pre-auth connections that send nothing, (2) memory exhaustion / OOM-kill via a single multi-GB text frame buffered whole.
security.recommendation: Immediately after UpgradeHTTP, set an initial conn.SetReadDeadline for the handshake (e.g. 10s), and in readProviderLoop reset SetReadDeadline each iteration to (heartbeat interval * miss-threshold) so silent/half-open peers are reaped without depending on the post-auth monitor. Set SetWriteDeadline before each write. Enforce a maximum frame size via a wsutil.Reader configured with MaxFrameSize (or io.LimitedReader + reject oversize) rather than wsutil.ReadClientData. Cap in-flight unauthenticated upgrades.
security.evidence: Verified directly. server.go:169 `conn, _, _, err := gobwas.UpgradeHTTP(r, w)` hijacks the net.Conn; per Go semantics a hijacked conn is no longer managed by http.Server, so ReadTimeout(310s)/IdleTimeout(120s)/ReadHeaderTimeout(10s) at main.go:185-187 stop applying — those are plain http.Server fields with no ConnState/BaseContext hook re-applying them (ListenAndServe at main.go:137). grep across internal/ws/ shows SetReadDeadline/SetWriteDeadline appear ONLY in *_test.go (e.g. server_test.go:1368), never in production server.go/relay.go. server.go:221 is the first auth read with no preceding deadline. The reaper monitorHeartbeat (server.go:1212, which calls conn.Close() at :1245) is started by registerProviderSession at server.go:607, reached only via handleV1Conn line 268 AFTER prepareProviderAdmission succeeds — strictly post-auth; a connection stuck on the :221 pre-auth read has no monitor. Frame-size: readProviderLoop (server.go:613) and the auth read (:221) use wsutil.ReadClientData with no MaxFrameSize (grep confirms none in internal/ws), versus server.go:909 io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20). Both vectors real; high is justified — unauthenticated, trivial, against the money-authority coordinator.

security.title: Non-constant-time comparison of operator bearer token guarding all admin/poolz endpoints
security.description: authorizedOperator compares the presented Authorization header against the configured operator key with plain string equality: r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey. This == short-circuits on the first differing byte and is not constant-time. It gates every privileged endpoint: /poolz (handlePoolz:1357), /admin/blacklist (handleBlacklist:1435), /admin/provisional, /admin/promote/ and /admin/reject/ (admin_endpoints.go). The project already knows the correct pattern — internal/buyer/server.go:2613 uses subtle.ConstantTimeCompare for an analogous bearer token — so this is an inconsistency, not a missing primitive. config.Validate at config.go:398 requires OperatorKey to be non-empty, so the empty-key total-bypass branch is unreachable in a validated production config. Impact: a remote attacker could in principle mount a network timing side-channel to recover the operator key byte-by-byte, then drain/blacklist/promote/reject providers and read the full pool; network exploitability is low (timing noise) but blast radius if recovered is full operator control.
security.recommendation: Compare using crypto/subtle: subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(r.Header.Get("Authorization")), []byte("Bearer "+s.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey)) == 1, mirroring internal/buyer/server.go:2613. Keep the existing empty-key guard or remove it now that Validate enforces a non-empty key.
security.evidence: Verified. server.go:1480-1481 reads `func (s *Server) authorizedOperator(r *http.Request) bool { return s.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey == "" || r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey }` — a non-constant-time == with a short-circuiting empty-key bypass disjunct. grep for subtle/ConstantTimeCompare in internal/ws/server.go and admin_endpoints.go returns nothing. The correct pattern exists at internal/buyer/server.go ~2613: `subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(token), []byte(expected)) == 1` with a length-equality pre-check, confirming the inconsistency. config.go:398 `if c.Auth.OperatorKey == ""` is part of Validate, so the empty-key branch is unreachable in production, as the finding notes. Low is appropriate: HTTP string-compare timing side-channels are extremely noisy and hard to exploit, while the finding keeps blast radius in view. Severity unchanged.

security.title: Session writer can block indefinitely on a single slow/stuck provider (no write deadline)
security.description: runWriter loops over writeCh and calls wsutil.WriteServerText(ps.conn, payload) with no write deadline set on the connection. If a malicious or wedged provider stops reading from its socket, the kernel send buffer fills and this write blocks, hanging the writer goroutine. send() (relay.go:118) is non-blocking (returns ErrRelayBackpressure when writeCh is full), so buffered messages queue up and are never flushed; the provider is only torn down later when a downstream monitor fires. Control messages routed through send() (e.g. cancel at relay.go:195) may never reach a stuck provider. Impact: a single misbehaving provider can pin a writer goroutine and starve delivery of control frames (drain, cancel, blacklist), degrading operator control and contributing to goroutine accumulation under attack; combined with the missing read deadline this widens the DoS surface.
security.recommendation: Call ps.conn.SetWriteDeadline(time.Now().Add(writeTimeout)) before each wsutil.WriteServerText in runWriter; on timeout, treat it as a write failure (failAll + conn.Close, as already done on error). This bounds how long a stuck peer can hold the writer.
security.evidence: Verified. relay.go:98-106 runWriter is `for payload := range ps.writeCh { if err := wsutil.WriteServerText(ps.conn, payload); err != nil { ps.failAll(...); ps.conn.Close(); return } }` with no SetWriteDeadline preceding the write (grep confirms no SetWriteDeadline / writeTimeout constant in production relay.go/server.go). On a full kernel send buffer this blocks. send() at relay.go:118-130 is a non-blocking `select { case ps.writeCh <- payload: ... default: return ErrRelayBackpressure }`. cancelActive at relay.go:195 routes a cancel through ps.send(), confirming control frames share this path and can be stranded. Mitigation already reflected in the medium rating: monitorHeartbeat (server.go:1245) independently calls conn.Close() once the provider is inactive past threshold, unblocking the wedged write via teardown — so the goroutine is held for up to the heartbeat-miss threshold rather than literally forever, and control-frame delivery is degraded in the interim. Medium justified and unchanged.

security.title: Attacker-controlled numeric provider fields are not validated/clamped; max_concurrency<=0 disables the per-session concurrency cap
security.description: requireInt accepts any JSON integer including zero and negatives, and neither ParseHello/ParseHeartbeat nor prepareProviderAdmission clamp or bound max_concurrency, slots_free, slots_total, ram_gb, model_params_b, etc. The hello-advertised MaxConcurrency is copied verbatim into SlotsFree/SlotsTotal (server.go:520-522) and into the per-session concurrency guard. In addActive (relay.go:141) the cap is only enforced when maxConcurrency > 0: `if maxConcurrency > 0 && len(ps.active) >= maxConcurrency`. A provider that advertises max_concurrency: 0 (or negative) bypasses the cap entirely, permitting unbounded concurrent active relay entries on that session (each allocating a 256-deep chunk channel). Inflated slots_free/slots_total also feed routing scoring. Impact: a malicious provisional provider can (a) bypass the in-session concurrency ceiling to force unbounded active-request allocations, and (b) advertise inflated free slots to attract disproportionate buyer traffic. Money/routing impact is bounded by the provisional per-hour quota (admission.go:133-152) and buyer-side dispatch, so this is a fairness/resource concern not direct theft, but the missing bounds are a latent footgun.
security.recommendation: In prepareProviderAdmission and ApplyHeartbeat, reject or clamp out-of-range values: require max_concurrency >= 1 and <= a sane ceiling, slots_free in [0, slots_total], ram_gb/model_params_b > 0. Treat max_concurrency<=0 as an admission failure rather than as 'unlimited' in addActive.
security.evidence: Verified. requireInt (messages.go:443-452) does `json.Unmarshal(v, out)` with no range/sign check, accepting 0 and negatives. ParseHello calls requireInt for max_concurrency at messages.go:258 with no subsequent bound. prepareProviderAdmission (server.go:512-536) copies hello.MaxConcurrency verbatim into MaxConcurrency, SlotsFree, SlotsTotal (lines 520-522) — no clamp. addActive (relay.go:132-153) guards with `if maxConcurrency > 0 && len(ps.active) >= maxConcurrency` (line 141), so max_concurrency<=0 skips the cap; addActive is invoked with provider.MaxConcurrency at relay.go:418, and each active allocates `chunks: make(chan InferenceResponseChunk, 256)` (line 147), confirming the unbounded-allocation-per-session vector. The bounding mitigation is real: admission.go TryReserveRequest (~133-152) returns false past ProvisionalQuotaPerHour for TierProvisional providers, capping request volume from an untrusted provisional provider. Low is justified — a fairness/resource footgun bounded by quota and buyer-side dispatch, not direct theft. Severity unchanged.

security.title: Provider-reported usage in inference_response_end is relayed verbatim and ultimately drives billing (trust boundary note)
security.description: openInferenceEnd / handleInferenceEnd parse the provider-supplied InferenceResponseEnd.Usage (messages.go:175-182) and forward it unchanged on active.done. The downstream buyer/billing layer (internal/billing/formula.go, internal/buyer/server.go) derives completion/prompt token counts — and therefore payout/charge — from this provider-reported usage. Within the WS relay this is transported faithfully and is correctly scoped; the relay does not itself mis-bill. Flagging only to make the trust boundary explicit: the WS layer treats the untrusted provider's self-reported token usage as authoritative input to the money path, while the actual integrity decision (estimate vs. provider-reported, capping) lives in the billing component, outside this audit's file set. Impact: if billing trusts provider-reported completion_tokens without an independent cap/estimate, a malicious provider could over-report tokens to inflate payout/charge — to be verified in the billing/buyer audit; no defect is asserted here for the WS relay itself.
security.recommendation: Confirm in the billing audit that provider-reported usage is bounded by a coordinator-side estimate or hard cap and cannot exceed plausible limits (the codebase has EstimatedCompTokens / UsageSource machinery in formula.go for exactly this). No change required in internal/ws.
security.evidence: Verified as an accurate, correctly-scoped info-level trust-boundary note (no defect asserted in WS). InferenceResponseEnd.Usage is `json.RawMessage` (messages.go:174-181), parsed in handleInferenceEnd (relay.go:526) and forwarded unchanged via `active.done <- end` at relay.go:576 — the relay performs no token arithmetic, so it cannot itself mis-bill, exactly as the finding states. The claim that the integrity decision lives in billing is corroborated: internal/billing/formula.go defines UsageSource, EstimatedCompTokens (*int64) and UsageProviderReported and switches on UsageSource (formula.go:23-210); internal/buyer/server.go derives completion tokens from end.Usage via tokenPointersFromUsageObject (server.go:1400,1539) with estimatedCompletionTokensFromBytes fallbacks (server.go:1345,1549). The recommendation correctly defers cap/estimate verification to the billing/buyer audit. info severity correct and unchanged.

security.title: MDA freshness OID is not bound to the coordinator's per-connection challenge; replay resistance rests entirely on the binding signature
security.description: verifyMDAFreshness only checks that the leaf certificate's Apple freshness extension equals SHA256(token.Token) (line 268: expectedMDAFreshnessDigest(token.Token)). token.Token is a provider-supplied field of the attestation JSON, not the coordinator's challengeBytes. The test TestVerifyAttestationTokenUsesDeviceTokenForMDAFreshness (pillar_c_test.go:438-453) confirms a token whose FreshnessToken/Token is the fixed string 'device-attestation-token' (unrelated to the challenge) is still AttestationStatusAttested. Therefore the Apple MDA cert + its committed device-attest token can be captured once and replayed across connections without the freshness OID ever rejecting it. The ONLY thing that ties an attestation to this connection's fresh nonce is verifyAttestationBindingSignature (line 228), a software ECDSA/Ed25519 signature by the leaf key over authAttemptID/challenge.
security.impact: A captured genuine MDA certificate chain + device-attest token blob can be replayed indefinitely as far as the cert/freshness/device-property checks are concerned; freshness across connections is enforced solely by the binding signature. Defense-in-depth is weaker than the layered checks suggest. No direct money/RCE impact given the SE-key assumption.
security.recommendation: Require the device-attest token (the MDA freshness nonce, token.Token) to incorporate the coordinator-issued challenge, and verify it: e.g. assert that the freshness extension equals SHA256 of a value derived from challengeBytes, or pass challengeBytes into verifyMDAFreshness and reject when token.Token does not commit to it. That makes Apple's own freshness mechanism a second, hardware-rooted anti-replay control independent of the software binding signature.
security.evidence: The narrow technical claim is TRUE: line 204 calls verifyMDAFreshness(certs[0], token.Token), and verifyMDAFreshness (lines 260-279) computes expectedMDAFreshnessDigest(deviceAttestToken)=sha256.Sum256([]byte(token.Token)) (line 277-279) with no reference to the coordinator challenge. The test at pillar_c_test.go:438-453 sets FreshnessToken/TokenValue='device-attestation-token' (decoupled from challenge='challenge-1') and asserts AttestationStatusAttested, so the freshness OID alone does not bind the connection nonce. HOWEVER the finding's IMPACT framing ('anti-replay is single-pillar', 'captured chain can be replayed indefinitely') is overstated: it omits a SECOND independent software challenge gate that runs BEFORE the production-MDA path. VerifyAttestationToken lines 119-123 compute wantChallenge=base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(challenge) and, if token.Challenge != wantChallenge, return AttestationStatusStale (logged 'challenge_mismatch'/'attestation_replay'). token.Challenge is also folded into the binding-signature payload at attestationBindingPayload line 414 (Challenge: token.Challenge) which is verified at line 228. So a chain captured on connection A and replayed on connection B (fresh challenge) is rejected at line 120 unless the attacker forges both a matching token.Challenge AND a fresh leaf-key binding signature over it. Two controls (plaintext challenge-equality at 120 + binding signature at 228) gate cross-connection replay, not one. The freshness-OID gap is a real defense-in-depth weakness, so this is not a false positive, but 'medium' overstates it given the redundant challenge binding already present; low is justified.

security.title: Attestation accepts self-asserted claimed/binary_version fields with no certificate-level corroboration
security.description: attestationHardwareFamilyAllowed (line 256) reads token.Claimed['hardware_family'] directly from provider-controlled JSON and only checks the string equals 'apple_silicon'; nothing in the MDA certificate is consulted to corroborate it. Similarly attestationBindingPayload (line 392) signs token.BinaryVersion and the full token.Claimed map with the leaf key, but a signature by the genuine leaf key only proves the device asserted these values, not that they are true. A dishonest provider running on genuine Apple Silicon (hence holding a valid MDA leaf + SE key) can therefore set arbitrary binary_version / claimed model metadata and still reach AttestationStatusAttested. Attestation here proves 'genuine Apple hardware + live possession of the SE leaf key', not 'running the expected binary/model'.
security.impact: Attestation cannot be relied on to prove software/binary integrity; a provider can attest as Apple Silicon while self-reporting a false binary_version or claimed metadata. Mitigated in practice because RAMTierAttested is hardcoded false (ws/server.go:420) and model integrity is handled separately by Pillar-A model-hash verification, so this does not by itself produce billing/payout manipulation.
security.recommendation: Document explicitly (and enforce in callers) that claimed/binary_version are self-asserted and must not gate trust or payout decisions; derive hardware_family from a certificate-rooted property (e.g. a device-property OID) rather than from token.Claimed, and continue to depend on Pillar-A hash verification for model integrity.
security.evidence: Confirmed as described at low severity. attestationHardwareFamilyAllowed (lines 255-258) reads hardwareFamily, _ := token.Claimed['hardware_family'].(string) and returns ok && hardwareFamily=='apple_silicon' — purely string-equality against provider JSON, no x509 extension consulted. attestationBindingPayload (lines 392-422) marshals token.Claimed (line 393) into ClaimedSHA256 and sets BinaryVersion: token.BinaryVersion (line 413) into the signed struct; the binding signature (verifyAttestationBindingSignature, lines 312-348) only proves the leaf key signed these self-asserted values, exactly as the finding states. The cited mitigations both hold: ws/server.go:420 literally sets RAMTierAttested: false with no other assignment (grep across non-test code shows only this one write plus the struct-field decl in messages.go:114), and ModelHash status is reported separately (server.go:422). The vuln is a genuine but correctly-bounded trust-boundary documentation/hardening gap; severity is appropriately low.

security.title: Production MDA chain verification uses ExtKeyUsageAny and does not constrain the leaf to a non-CA end-entity
security.description: verifyAttestationCertificateChain calls certs[0].Verify with KeyUsages:[]x509.ExtKeyUsage{x509.ExtKeyUsageAny} (line 675), accepting any extended key usage, and the leaf checks (verifyMDALeafPublicKey, lines 236-253) only validate the public-key type/curve (P-256/P-384 ECDSA). There is no assertion that certs[0] is an end-entity (e.g. IsCA == false / BasicConstraints) or that it carries an MDA-specific EKU/OID. Intermediates are taken from attacker-supplied certs[1:] (line 668). Because the chain must still terminate at a configured Apple root, this is not directly exploitable, but the permissive EKU and absence of a leaf/end-entity constraint widen the set of certs that the configured root could be coerced into endorsing as a valid 'leaf' relative to a tightly-pinned policy.
security.impact: Reduced robustness of the leaf-cert policy: any certificate that chains to a configured root and has a P-256/P-384 ECDSA key qualifies as an MDA leaf regardless of its intended EKU or CA status. Low impact given roots are operator-pinned Apple MDA roots, but it is looser than the Apple MDA profile warrants.
security.recommendation: After chain verification, pin the leaf to the Apple MDA end-entity profile: require IsCA == false, and assert the presence of the expected MDA leaf EKU/marker OID; replace ExtKeyUsageAny with the specific EKU(s) Apple uses for MDA attestation certificates.
security.evidence: Confirmed at low severity. Line 675 passes KeyUsages: []x509.ExtKeyUsage{x509.ExtKeyUsageAny}, accepting any EKU. verifyMDALeafPublicKey (lines 236-253) only validates *ecdsa.PublicKey type and curve name in {P-256,P-384}; a full grep of pillar_c.go and server.go for IsCA/BasicConstraints returns no hits, confirming no end-entity assertion on certs[0]. extractAttestationCertificateChain (lines 538-568) builds the cert slice from token.CertificateChain, token.X5C, and the JWS x5c header — all provider/attacker-controlled — and verifyAttestationCertificateChain (lines 659-678) feeds certs[1:] into the intermediates pool (line 668). The finding correctly self-limits exploitability: the chain must still terminate at an operator-pinned Apple root (rootPool from cfg.AttestationRoots), and Go's x509.Verify independently enforces BasicConstraints/path-length/name-constraints on intermediates, so a non-CA cert cannot act as a signing intermediate. The residual gap (leaf could itself be a CA cert, or carry a non-MDA EKU) is a real but low-impact policy-tightening item. Severity low is correct.

security.title: OpenPillarBFrame accepts a legacy JSON-form AAD path that diverges from the canonical binary AAD
security.description: OpenPillarBFrame compares the provider-supplied aadRaw against the canonical binary expectedAADRaw and, on mismatch, still accepts the frame when aadRaw lacks the binary prefix and decodedAAD == expectedAAD (lines 311-315). The AAD actually authenticated by GCM is aadRaw (line 329), so integrity is preserved (the provider sealed the ciphertext over exactly that aadRaw and the struct fields are compared field-by-field via the comparable AEADFrameAAD). This is a legacy/JSON-compat acceptance path rather than a vulnerability, but it permits two distinct on-wire AAD encodings to satisfy the same logical frame, increasing parser surface (DecodeAEADAAD JSON path) and the risk of future canonicalization drift.
security.impact: No confidentiality/integrity break (GCM still binds aadRaw to the ciphertext). Maintenance/robustness only: dual AAD encodings complicate reasoning about replay/uniqueness and invite drift if the struct gains fields not covered by the equality check.
security.recommendation: Once all providers emit the binary AAD, drop the JSON fallback in DecodeAEADAAD and require bytes.Equal(aadRaw, expectedAADRaw); until then, ensure every field added to AEADFrameAAD remains part of the comparable struct so the decodedAAD == expectedAAD check stays exhaustive.
security.evidence: Confirmed as info/robustness-only, exactly as described. OpenPillarBFrame lines 311-315: after computing expectedAADRaw (canonical binary form via MarshalAEADAAD, line 303) and decoding the wire AAD (DecodeAEADAAD, line 307), the mismatch branch returns an error only if bytes.HasPrefix(aadRaw, pillarBAADPrefix) OR decodedAAD != expectedAAD — i.e. it ACCEPTS a non-prefixed (legacy JSON) aadRaw whose decoded struct equals expectedAAD. DecodeAEADAAD (lines 155-172) explicitly supports both the binary-prefixed path (parseBinaryAEADAAD) and a json.Unmarshal fallback. Crucially the GCM Open at line 329 authenticates the actual on-wire aadRaw (sealed = ciphertext||tag, gcm.Open(nil, nonce, sealed, aadRaw)), so integrity is preserved over whatever bytes the provider sealed; AEADFrameAAD is a flat comparable struct so '==' is an exhaustive field compare. No confidentiality/integrity break exists. This is a maintenance/canonicalization-drift concern, correctly rated info.

security.title: Operator token verified with non-constant-time string comparison (timing side channel)
security.description: authorized() gates the entire operator explorer with a plain Go string equality: `return h.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey != "" && r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+h.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey`. Go's `==` on strings short-circuits at the first differing byte, so comparison time correlates with the length of the matching prefix. This is the SAME secret (cfg.Auth.OperatorKey) that the coordinator's internal/buyer auth path compares with crypto/subtle.ConstantTimeCompare after a length-equalize check (internal/buyer/server.go:2610-2613) and that is passed as both the internal auth key and gateway bearer (cmd/coordinator/main.go:97 and :116). The explorer is the inconsistent path.
security.impact: An attacker able to send many requests and measure response latency could mount a byte-by-byte timing attack to recover the operator key. That key is the master operator credential: it unlocks the full explorer read model (all buyers' request history, buyer IPs, prompts/prefs, ledger, payouts) AND is reused as the gateway Bearer and internal auth key, so recovery is a full operator-plane compromise. Exploitability is reduced by network jitter and the 60 req/min cap, but the blast radius (money/PII authority) is high.
security.recommendation: Compare with constant-time primitives, mirroring the buyer path: extract the Bearer token, reject on length mismatch, then `subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(token), []byte(h.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey)) == 1`. Better yet, factor the buyer-side comparator into a shared helper so there is one auth code path for the operator key.
security.evidence: CONFIRMED-REAL but DOWNGRADED medium->low. handlers.go:501-503 verified verbatim: authorized() returns `h.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey != "" && r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+h.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey` — a plain Go `==` string compare, no crypto/subtle. The inconsistency claim is verified: internal/buyer/server.go:2599-2613 (internalBearerAuthorized) does length-equalize `if len(token) != len(expected) { return false }` then `subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(token), []byte(expected)) == 1`. Key reuse verified: main.go:97 `buyer.WithInternalAuthKey(cfg.Auth.OperatorKey)` and main.go:116 `billingStore.Handlers(cfg.Auth.OperatorKey, ...)` — same secret. The vulnerability exists. DOWNGRADE rationale: exploitability is far lower than 'medium' implies. The 60 req/min cap is not just a default — config.go:599-600 HARD-VALIDATES `RequestsPerMinuteCap` to be `< 1 || > 60 -> error`, so it can never exceed 60 and cannot be disabled (default 60 at config.go:340). It is enforced via allowRequest (handlers.go:60), which runs on every authorized-path request. Remotely measuring single-byte Go string-compare timing deltas (nanoseconds) over a network at a hard ceiling of 60 samples/min, against the jitter of an HTTP round trip, is not practically exploitable to recover a high-entropy key. The fix is cheap and the code path inconsistency is real, so this stays a confirmed defect — but severity is best classified low, not medium.

security.title: request_log (buyer IP + prompt-pref headers, PII) has no retention/pruning — unbounded growth and indefinite PII storage
security.description: The request_log schema stores buyer_ip (client IP, PII) and pref_header/provider_header per request (store.go:100,103-104), and OpenStore/migrate only ever CREATE/ALTER/INSERT — there is no DELETE, TTL, or VACUUM anywhere for this table (grep across internal+cmd finds no `DELETE FROM request_log` and no retention job; the only retention knob, provisional_retention_days in config, is unrelated). The explorer SessionDetail query selects and returns buyer_ip to operators (internal/explorer/store.go:61-68). Billing recovery also depends on these rows persisting (internal/billing/recovery.go), so naive deletion is not safe either.
security.impact: Personal data (buyer source IPs, linkable to USDC-spending accounts, plus request preference headers) is retained indefinitely with no expiry, increasing breach blast radius and creating GDPR/CCPA data-minimization and right-to-erasure exposure. Operationally the table grows without bound, eventually degrading SQLite performance and consuming disk on the trusted money coordinator, a slow availability risk.
security.recommendation: Introduce an explicit, configurable retention policy: a periodic job that deletes/anonymizes request_log rows older than the retention window (coordinating with billing.recovery so settled/reconciled rows are not needed before deletion), and consider not persisting raw buyer_ip beyond what billing/abuse needs (truncate/hash the IP). Document the retention period and add it to config validation.
security.evidence: CONFIRMED, severity held at medium. Schema verified at store.go:87-106: request_log persists `buyer_ip TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''` (line 100), `pref_header TEXT NULL` (line 103), `provider_header TEXT NULL` (line 104) — PII and request preference data. The store layer (store.go:1-275, read in full) exposes ONLY OpenStore/migrate/Insert/InsertTx/InsertExec/ensureColumns — every SQL statement is CREATE TABLE, CREATE INDEX, ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN, or INSERT; there is no DELETE, no TTL, no VACUUM, no expiry job. Repo-wide grep for `DELETE FROM request_log` returned ZERO matches across the entire phase4-coordinator tree. The grep for retention/TTL/prune surfaced only `provisional_retention_days` (config.go:268) and sticky/settlement TTLs — none touch request_log, confirming the 'unrelated knob' claim. PII egress to operators verified at explorer/store.go:61-68: SessionDetail SELECTs `buyer_ip` (line 65) and returns it. Billing dependency verified at billing/recovery.go:59,67,80,84,87 — recovery reads `FROM request_log` and flags `missing_request_log` (line 52), so blind deletion would break reconciliation, confirming the 'naive deletion is not safe' caveat. Every factual claim in the finding is accurate. Medium is appropriate: this is an indefinite-PII-retention + unbounded-growth issue on the money coordinator, not a directly remotely exploitable flaw, so it should not be raised, but it is a genuine compliance and slow-availability defect that should not be downgraded.

security.title: Explorer rate-limiter map grows unbounded (per-source-IP keys never evicted)
security.description: allowRequest keys h.stamps by client IP (clientAddrKey). On each request it prunes expired timestamps for that key, but when a key's slice prunes to empty it is still re-stored (`h.stamps[key] = stamps`) and never deleted from the map. There is no sweeper that removes keys with no live timestamps, so the map accumulates one entry per distinct source IP for the process lifetime. Mitigating factors: allowRequest runs only AFTER authorized() succeeds (handlers.go:56 before :60), so only authenticated operators can add keys, and RemoteAddr is the real TCP peer (not spoofable over TCP); behind a proxy all clients collapse to one key.
security.impact: Slow unbounded memory growth on the coordinator proportional to the number of distinct authenticated source IPs over uptime. Low real-world severity given the pre-auth gate and TCP peer addressing, but it is a genuine leak with no upper bound.
security.recommendation: Delete keys whose pruned slice is empty (`if len(stamps) == 0 { delete(h.stamps, key) } else { h.stamps[key] = stamps }`), or run a periodic sweep of stale keys. Optionally cap the number of tracked keys.
security.evidence: CONFIRMED at low. allowRequest verified at handlers.go:505-528. The leak mechanism is exactly as described: stamps is rebuilt by pruning expired entries (lines 515-520), and on BOTH the over-cap branch (line 522 `h.stamps[key] = stamps`) and the normal branch (line 526 `h.stamps[key] = stamps`) the key is unconditionally re-stored; there is NO `delete(h.stamps, key)` anywhere and no `if len(stamps) == 0` guard. The Handler struct initializes `stamps: map[string][]time.Time{}` (handlers.go:41) and no sweeper goroutine references h.stamps elsewhere. Pre-auth gate confirmed: ServeHTTP calls `if !h.authorized(r)` at line 56 (returns 401) BEFORE `if !h.allowRequest(r)` at line 60, so only requests bearing the valid operator bearer reach allowRequest and can add map keys. Key derivation confirmed via clientAddrKey (handlers.go:530-536) which uses `net.SplitHostPort(remoteAddr)` on r.RemoteAddr — the real TCP peer host, not a client-controlled header, so an attacker cannot inflate distinct keys without controlling distinct source IPs and a valid operator token. All factual claims, including the mitigating factors the finding itself raised, are accurate. Genuine unbounded-growth bug but correctly rated low given the post-auth gate and non-spoofable keying; severity held.

security.title: Operator-key admin/financial endpoints use non-constant-time bearer comparison (timing side channel)
security.description: Three LIVE operator-key authorization gates compare the incoming bearer token to the configured operator key with ordinary Go string comparison, which short-circuits on length and the first differing byte and is therefore not constant-time: billing/endpoints.go:61 `r.Header.Get("Authorization") != "Bearer "+h.operatorKey` (guards /admin/ledger/summary|providers|reconcile), ws/server.go:1481 `... == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey` (guards the operator admin surface incl. blacklist/drain), and explorer/handlers.go:502 (guards the operator explorer over buyer/ledger/settlement data). The same operator key is compared correctly in buyer/server.go:2613 via subtle.ConstantTimeCompare and in tier2/pillar_c.go:270, so this is an inconsistency, not a deliberate choice. All three handlers are wired from the in-scope cmd/coordinator/main.go (lines 82, 116-119, and the ws server). The dead helper auth.AuthorizedBearer (internal/auth/tokens.go:34) has the same non-constant-time pattern.
security.impact: A network attacker who can issue many requests and measure response-time differences can recover the operator key byte-by-byte. The operator key controls provider blacklist/drain (availability + money) and read access to the full revenue/payout ledger and per-buyer data. Recovery yields admin control over the money authority.
security.recommendation: Compare the bearer token using crypto/subtle.ConstantTimeCompare on equal-length byte slices, exactly as buyer/server.go:2599-2613 already does. Extract a single shared helper (e.g. auth.ConstantTimeBearer(header, expected)) and call it from billing, ws, and explorer; rewrite or delete the dead auth.AuthorizedBearer so the insecure pattern is not copied. Length-check first (len(token)!=len(expected) -> false) then ConstantTimeCompare.
security.evidence: All three gates confirmed by direct read. billing/endpoints.go:61 uses `r.Header.Get("Authorization") != "Bearer "+h.operatorKey` inside admin() which guards /admin/ledger/summary|providers|reconcile (endpoints.go:43-48,56-66). ws/server.go:1480-1482 authorizedOperator() uses `r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Auth.OperatorKey` and is called from admin_endpoints.go:18,51,88 and server.go:1357,1435 (blacklist/drain). explorer/handlers.go:501-503 authorized() uses the same `==` pattern, called at handlers.go:56. By contrast buyer/server.go:2599-2613 internalBearerAuthorized() does a length check then `subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(token),[]byte(expected))==1`, and tier2/pillar_c.go:270 uses ConstantTimeCompare. main.go confirms the SAME secret feeds all paths: billing gets cfg.Auth.OperatorKey (main.go:116), buyer gets WithInternalAuthKey(cfg.Auth.OperatorKey) (main.go:97), explorer handler wired at main.go:82 — so the constant-time path and the three vulnerable paths compare the identical operator key, confirming the inconsistency is real, not a deliberate distinction. The DEAD helper auth.AuthorizedBearer (tokens.go:33-35) indeed uses `==` (no caller found in non-test code). DOWNGRADED to low because: (1) network timing attacks against a high-entropy operator key over Go's `==` short-circuit are extremely difficult in practice (network jitter dwarfs the per-byte timing delta; Go compares length first then bytes, leaking at most coarse signal); (2) the explorer surface (handlers.go:505-524 allowRequest) is rate-limited to RequestsPerMinuteCap (config.go:599 caps it 1-60/min), throttling the request volume a timing attack needs. The ws blacklist/drain and billing gates are NOT rate-limited, so a residual real weakness remains and the fix (reuse the existing ConstantTimeCompare helper) is cheap — hence confirmed-but-low rather than false_positive.

security.title: Go standard-library CVEs in the build are call-path-confirmed (govulncheck)
security.lines: go.mod:3 (go 1.22 directive, built with go1.26.3); reachable via cmd/coordinator/main.go:141 and internal/tier2/pillar_c.go:671 / cmd/tier2-mda-artifact/main.go
security.description: govulncheck ./... reports two stdlib vulnerabilities whose symbols are actually reached by this code: GO-2026-5039 (net/textproto includes arbitrary inputs in errors without escaping) reachable from the HTTP servers started in cmd/coordinator/main.go:137-141 via http.Server.ListenAndServe -> textproto.Reader.ReadMIMEHeader; and GO-2026-5037 (inefficient/quadratic candidate-hostname parsing in crypto/x509) reachable from the attestation certificate-chain verifier (internal/tier2/pillar_c.go:671 x509.Certificate.Verify) and from cmd/tier2-mda-artifact. Both are fixed in go1.26.4. govulncheck also flagged GO-2026-5038 (mime) imported-but-not-called and GO-2026-5024 (golang.org/x/sys windows-only) not in the call path.
security.impact: x509 quadratic hostname parsing is reachable from untrusted provider-supplied attestation certificate chains, enabling CPU-amplification DoS against the trusted coordinator during provider admission. The textproto issue can surface attacker-controlled bytes unescaped in server error paths (log/response injection / information clarity). Both affect the trusted money authority.
security.recommendation: Rebuild and ship the coordinator with Go >= 1.26.4 (the version that fixes GO-2026-5037/5038/5039) and bump golang.org/x/sys to >= v0.44.0. Add `govulncheck ./...` to CI as a release gate so future stdlib/dependency CVEs in the call path block the build.
security.evidence: Reproduced govulncheck ./... in the module: it reports exactly GO-2026-5039 (net/textproto@go1.26.3, fixed go1.26.4) with trace `cmd/coordinator/main.go:141:35: coordinator.main calls http.Server.ListenAndServe, which eventually calls textproto.Reader.ReadMIMEHeader`, and GO-2026-5037 (crypto/x509@go1.26.3, fixed go1.26.4) with traces including `internal/tier2/pillar_c.go:671:27: tier2.verifyAttestationCertificateChain calls x509.Certificate.Verify` and `cmd/tier2-mda-artifact/main.go`. The tool also notes 1 imported-but-not-called and 1 required-but-not-called vuln, matching the finding's GO-2026-5038/GO-2026-5024 note. `go version` confirms go1.26.3; go.mod:3 has `go 1.22`; go.mod:23 pins golang.org/x/sys v0.22.0 (below recommended v0.44.0). x509.Verify reachability from untrusted input is corroborated by reading the call chain: ws/server.go:382 passes provider-supplied proof.AttestationToken into tier2.VerifyAttestationToken, which (pillar_c.go:83,176,196) extracts certs from the provider-controlled token and calls verifyAttestationCertificateChain -> certs[0].Verify (pillar_c.go:671). Severity kept MEDIUM: reachability and the call-path-confirmed nature are accurate, but the x509 DoS path requires tier2 production-MDA roots configured and the request must pass several prior guards (size caps MaxAttestationEnvelopeBytes/MaxAttestationTokenBytes at pillar_c.go:94,107; format/challenge/expiry checks at pillar_c.go:103-142) before reaching Verify, and the fix is a routine toolchain bump — consistent with medium, not higher.

security.title: 24-bit token_prefix lets token revocation collaterally revoke another provider's active token
security.description: Issued tokens are indexed for revocation by a 6-hex-character prefix (`prefix := token[:6]`, line 136) = 24 bits of namespace. RevokeToken (line 192) executes `UPDATE provider_tokens SET revoked_at=? WHERE token_prefix=? AND revoked_at IS NULL`, which revokes EVERY active token sharing that prefix, and then reports a single record via tokenByPrefix (line 225, `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1`). The affected-row count (res.RowsAffected, computed at line 196) is only used to detect zero matches; a >1 collateral revocation is silently ignored and the operator sees only one provider in the success line (coordinator-cli/main.go:81). By birthday bound a collision becomes likely well before the network grows large (~50% near 4,800 active tokens; non-trivial probability at a few hundred). The token secret itself is full 256-bit crypto/rand (line 130-134) and stored only as SHA-256, so this is not a brute-force/entropy weakness — it is a revoke-by-prefix integrity/availability defect.
security.impact: Revoking provider A by prefix can also revoke provider B's still-valid token if their prefixes collide, kicking an innocent earning provider offline (and, after revoke-and-kick, blacklisting only A while B's token is dead). Operator gets no warning of the collateral revocation. Availability/integrity for honest providers, with downstream earnings impact.
security.recommendation: Either revoke by a unique identifier (token id or full token_hash) instead of the 6-char prefix, or guard RevokeToken so that when RowsAffected>1 it errors out and asks the operator to disambiguate (e.g. require a longer prefix). Surface RowsAffected in the CLI output. Consider widening the stored prefix to 12+ hex chars to make collisions negligible.
security.evidence: Confirmed by direct read of tokens.go. IssueToken stores `prefix := token[:6]` (line 136, exactly 6 hex chars = 24 bits) into token_prefix. RevokeToken (lines 186-204) takes an operator prefix, but truncates it to `prefix := tokenPrefix[:6]` (line 190) REGARDLESS of how many chars the operator supplies, then runs `UPDATE provider_tokens SET revoked_at=? WHERE token_prefix=? AND revoked_at IS NULL` (line 192) — a non-unique WHERE that revokes every active token with that 6-char prefix. RowsAffected (line 196) is checked only for ==0 (line 200); any value >1 is silently accepted, and it returns a single record via tokenByPrefix (line 225, `... ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1`). CLI confirms the silent single-record output: coordinator-cli/main.go:81 prints only `record.TokenPrefix`/`record.ProviderName`, and revoke-and-kick (main.go:150) likewise reports one provider. Note token_prefix has no UNIQUE constraint (schema tokens.go:73-82; only token_hash is UNIQUE), so collisions are storable. Severity correctly LOW: tokens are full 256-bit crypto/rand (tokens.go:130-134), so this is an integrity/availability collision defect not an auth bypass; the birthday math is roughly right (50% near sqrt(2^24)~4,096 active tokens, finding says ~4,800) and the network is POC-scale, so real-world collision probability is currently small but non-zero and grows with the active-token count.

security.title: coordinator-cli transmits the operator key to an unauthenticated, scheme-unchecked admin URL
security.description: The revoke-and-kick subcommand takes --admin-url and --operator-key, then kickProvider (line 162-167) builds `<adminURL>/admin/blacklist` and sets `Authorization: Bearer <operatorKey>` using http.DefaultClient (line 169) with no validation that adminURL uses https and no verification of the server identity beyond default TLS. Unlike config.ValidateEndpointURL (config.go:636-646) and the explorer GatewayBaseURL check (config.go:602-613), which both reject non-loopback http, this operator path performs no scheme check. If the operator passes (or is tricked into passing) an http:// admin-url, the operator key is sent in cleartext; a malicious --admin-url value exfiltrates the key outright.
security.impact: Cleartext disclosure / exfiltration of the operator key, which controls provider blacklist/drain and full ledger read access. Requires operator misconfiguration or a malicious admin-url argument, so exploitability is limited to the operator's own environment.
security.recommendation: Validate --admin-url with the existing config.ValidateEndpointURL (or an https-only equivalent) before sending the key: reject any scheme other than https except explicit loopback. Optionally read the operator key from an env var / file instead of an argv flag (argv is visible in process listings).
security.evidence: Confirmed by direct read. revoke-and-kick parses --admin-url and --operator-key (coordinator-cli/main.go:118-119) and only checks they are non-empty (main.go:125-127) — no scheme validation. kickProvider (main.go:154-178) builds `url := strings.TrimRight(adminURL,"/") + "/admin/blacklist"` (line 162), sets `req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+operatorKey)` (line 167), and sends via `http.DefaultClient.Do(req)` (line 169) with zero scheme/host checks. The inconsistency is real: config.ValidateEndpointURL (config.go:636-646) rejects any scheme that is not https unless host is 127.0.0.1/localhost, and the explorer GatewayBaseURL validator (config.go:602-613) likewise requires https unless isLoopbackHost — neither guard is applied on the CLI operator path, so an http:// admin-url sends the operator key in cleartext and a hostile --admin-url exfiltrates it. Severity correctly LOW: exploitation requires the operator to supply a bad --admin-url (own-environment misconfiguration or a social-engineered/tampered argv), it is not remotely triggerable, and the operator key is additionally exposed via argv in process listings (a secondary issue the recommendation already notes).

security.title: Operator key compared with non-constant-time string equality (timing side-channel on the most privileged credential)
security.description: operatorAuthorized authenticates every privileged admin route with a plain Go string comparison: `if r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey`. The same plaintext == is repeated in shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit (line 1942). Go's string == short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading bytes of the supplied bearer token match the real operator key. This is the ONE credential check in the gateway that is not constant-time: API keys are validated via a hash lookup (auth/keys.go Validate/Hash) and demo tokens use crypto/hmac.Equal (auth/demo.go:53). The operator key is the highest-value secret in the system.
security.impact: An attacker who can make repeated requests and measure response-time differences could in principle recover the operator key byte-by-byte. Recovering the key yields full administrative control plus the gateway's coordinator bearer.
security.recommendation: Compare using a constant-time primitive. Pre-derive the expected header once and compare with crypto/subtle.ConstantTimeCompare, ideally after sha256-hashing both sides to a fixed length so length is not leaked. Apply the same fix to shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit (line 1942). Consider rotating the operator key.
security.evidence: VERIFIED at server.go:1933 the literal `if r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey` and the identical pattern at server.go:1942 — both plain Go `==`, which short-circuits per-byte. By contrast auth/demo.go:53 uses `hmac.Equal(expected, got)` (constant-time) and auth/keys.go Validate() routes through store.ValidateAPIKeyHash(m.Hash(fullKey)) (hash lookup, no plaintext compare) — confirming the finding's claim that the operator key is the only non-constant-time credential check. Blast radius confirmed: server.go:150-160 register /admin/feedback-summary, /admin/kill-switch, /admin/capacity-signal, /admin/capacity-tier/evaluate, and /admin/explorer/* ; explorer.go:246-256 explorerAllowed() calls operatorAuthorized(), and explorer.go:173-191 confirms the explorer accepts `email`, `email_prefix`, and `account_id` query params (real buyer PII). server.go:1359 confirms the same s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey is used as the gateway's Bearer to the coordinator. The vulnerability is real as described. Kept at medium (not downgraded) because the blast radius (global kill switch + capacity control + buyer-PII explorer + coordinator auth) is severe and the fix is trivial; however the practical remote exploitability is on the low side — recovering a high-entropy key byte-by-byte over the public internet through TLS, network jitter, Go scheduler noise, and SQLite I/O variance requires an enormous, possibly infeasible, sample count. Medium is the justified balance of real-leak + high blast radius vs. low remote exploitability.

security.title: HTTP server has no ReadTimeout / IdleTimeout / WriteTimeout — unauthenticated slow-body DoS
security.description: The internet-facing http.Server is constructed with only `ReadHeaderTimeout: 10 * time.Second` set. There is no ReadTimeout (whole request incl. body), no IdleTimeout, no WriteTimeout, and no MaxHeaderBytes. ReadHeaderTimeout stops a Slowloris that trickles headers, but it does NOT bound how long a client may take to send the request body after headers complete. handleFeedback decodes the JSON body BEFORE performing authentication for the non-playground scope, so /v1/feedback is reachable unauthenticated and will block in json.Decode waiting on a slow body. MaxBytesReader caps the byte count but not the time.
security.impact: An unauthenticated remote attacker can open many connections to /v1/feedback, send valid headers within 10s, then trickle the body, each connection pinning a server goroutine for an unbounded duration. With enough parallel connections this degrades or denies service.
security.recommendation: Set explicit bounds on the http.Server: ReadTimeout (e.g. 30s, above the largest legitimate upload time), IdleTimeout (e.g. 120s), and MaxHeaderBytes (e.g. 1<<16). Do NOT set WriteTimeout globally because SSE streams are long-lived; bound non-streaming handlers individually or rely on per-request context deadlines. Additionally, apply a request-scoped read deadline before the unauthenticated json.Decode in handleFeedback.
security.evidence: VERIFIED at main.go:64-68 the http.Server literal sets ONLY `Addr`, `Handler`, and `ReadHeaderTimeout: 10 * time.Second` — no ReadTimeout, IdleTimeout, WriteTimeout, or MaxHeaderBytes field is present in the struct. Nothing else mutates httpServer before ListenAndServe (main.go:69-75). The handleFeedback ordering claim is also confirmed: server.go:568 calls `json.NewDecoder(http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, ...)).Decode(&req)` and authentication for the non-playground path only happens later at server.go:609 (`s.requireBearer(w, r)`); the playground branch's demo-token check is at server.go:602. So an anonymous request that sets scope!=playground (or omits scope) reaches the body Decode before any credential check, and MaxBytesReader (server.go:568) bounds bytes, not wall-clock time. The slow-body goroutine-pinning DoS on an unauthenticated edge path is real. The coordinator http.Client has Timeout/ResponseHeaderTimeout (main.go:56-61) but that is the gateway's OUTBOUND client and does not bound INBOUND request bodies. Severity kept at medium: real and unauthenticated, but it is a resource-exhaustion DoS (no data/integrity impact) typically also mitigated by an upstream reverse proxy/LB at coordinator.streamvc.live; medium is appropriate.

security.title: Upstream coordinator response headers are passed through to buyers with minimal filtering (header-injection / response-splitting surface)
security.description: copyCleanHeaders copies EVERY header from the upstream (coordinator) response into the buyer-facing response, skipping only headers whose name starts with x-macprovider- and Content-Length. There is no allowlist: any header the upstream sets — Set-Cookie, Access-Control-*, Cache-Control, CSP, Location, etc. — is forwarded to the buyer. The coordinator is the trusted money authority, but it relays content originating on untrusted provider Macs, so a compromise that lets a provider influence a coordinator response header would be reflected to buyers. Go's net/http sanitizes CR/LF in header values, so classic response-splitting is blocked, but header injection is not.
security.impact: Defense-in-depth gap at the trust boundary: if a coordinator response ever carries unexpected headers, the gateway would relay Set-Cookie, CORS, or cache-control directives to buyers with no gateway-side guard. Low likelihood given the trusted coordinator.
security.recommendation: Replace the denylist with an explicit allowlist of headers safe to relay (e.g. Content-Type, X-Request-ID) and drop everything else — in particular always strip Set-Cookie, the Access-Control-* family, and Cache-Control/CSP from upstream responses. The gateway already sets Content-Type explicitly on these paths, so the allowlist can be very small.
security.evidence: VERIFIED at server.go:2218-2227 copyCleanHeaders iterates `src` and `continue`s only for isMacProviderHeader(key) (server.go:2241-2243, prefix 'x-macprovider-') or Content-Length, then `dst.Add(key, value)` for everything else — confirming the unbounded denylist passthrough. Callers confirmed at 444, 1428 (forwardNonStreamingChat), 1469 (forwardStreamingChat), 1535 (passThroughNoProviderCoordinatorError). Severity correctly LOW already, but the specific 'CORS bypass overriding the gateway's strict policy' impact is OVERSTATED and warrants the downgraded label: I read cors.go:9-29 — withCORS sets the gateway's CORS headers via setCORSHeaders (h.Set, cors.go:44-48) BEFORE calling next.ServeHTTP (cors.go:25-28), and the handler's copyCleanHeaders runs AFTER and uses dst.Add (server.go:2224). So an upstream Access-Control-Allow-Origin would be APPENDED as a duplicate header, not OVERRIDE the gateway's authoritative h.Set value — browsers reject responses with multiple Access-Control-Allow-Origin values, so this fails closed rather than enabling a CORS bypass. Additionally cors.go:46 hardcodes Access-Control-Allow-Credentials:false, so credentialed CORS abuse is not reachable. The Set-Cookie / cache-poisoning concerns remain valid defense-in-depth points and CR/LF splitting is correctly noted as blocked by net/http. Net: real but lower-impact than the description's CORS-override framing; remains LOW with verdict=downgraded to reflect the corrected (weaker) CORS impact.

security.title: Per-connection PRAGMAs (foreign_keys, busy_timeout, journal_mode, synchronous) can be silently lost on connection recreation
security.description: Open() sets the critical PRAGMAs via a one-time db.ExecContext after sql.Open: `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000; PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL; PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;` (line 39). busy_timeout and foreign_keys are CONNECTION-scoped settings in SQLite, but they are applied to whichever pooled connection database/sql happens to hand out at Open time, not encoded in the DSN ('sqlite', path at line 33) and not re-applied per connection. The pool is capped at SetMaxOpenConns(1)/SetMaxIdleConns(1) but ConnMaxLifetime and ConnMaxIdleTime are left at their zero (unlimited) defaults, so the single connection is normally reused — yet database/sql will discard and transparently re-open a fresh driver connection on certain driver errors (e.g. a connection-reset/SQLITE_BUSY classified as a bad conn). The replacement connection runs with SQLite defaults: foreign_keys OFF and busy_timeout 0. journal_mode=WAL is database-persistent so it survives, but FK enforcement and the 5s busy_timeout do not.
security.impact: If the pool ever rebuilds its connection, FK constraints stop being enforced (orphan api_keys/identities pointing at deleted accounts become insertable) and busy_timeout drops to 0 (immediate SQLITE_BUSY errors / failed writes instead of the intended 5s wait), degrading money-path writes under contention. Silent and intermittent, hard to detect in test where the conn is never recycled.
security.recommendation: Put the connection-scoped PRAGMAs in the DSN so every new connection gets them, e.g. open with `file:<path>?_pragma=busy_timeout(5000)&_pragma=foreign_keys(ON)&_pragma=journal_mode(WAL)&_pragma=synchronous(NORMAL)` (modernc.org/sqlite supports _pragma DSN params), OR register a connection hook / set them on every conn. Do not rely on a single post-Open ExecContext for per-connection PRAGMAs. Keeping SetMaxOpenConns(1) reduces but does not eliminate the recreate path.
security.evidence: Verified the architecture exactly as described. store.go:33 calls sql.Open("sqlite", path) with a plain path — grep for `_pragma`/`busy_timeout`/`foreign_keys` outside store.go returns nothing (only the single ExecContext at line 39 and migrate.go:4's one-time schema PRAGMA). store.go:37-38 set SetMaxOpenConns(1)/SetMaxIdleConns(1); grep for ConnMaxLifetime/ConnMaxIdleTime across internal/ and cmd/ returns zero hits, confirming both are at the unlimited zero default. Critically, every money-path tx goes through beginImmediate() at store.go:848-858, which calls s.db.Conn(ctx) to pull a connection from the pool and runs BEGIN IMMEDIATE on it — so a recreated bad-conn replacement would NOT have foreign_keys=ON or busy_timeout=5000 applied (those are connection-scoped and only set once at Open on the original conn). Schema confirms FK reliance: migrate.go:20 (account_identities REFERENCES accounts) and migrate.go:44 (api_keys REFERENCES accounts). journal_mode=WAL is DB-persistent and does survive. Driver is modernc.org/sqlite v1.33.0 (go.mod:7), which supports _pragma DSN params per the recommendation. Verdict confirmed: the latent-loss path is real.
