Severity kept at medium — it is a genuine integrity/availability latent condition on the money path, but exploitation requires the pool to actually classify a conn as bad and recreate it (probabilistic, not attacker-triggerable), and the SetMaxOpenConns(1) design makes recreation uncommon in steady state. Medium is the correct balance.

security.title: Settlement records uncapped provider-reported token counts into usage_events with no constraint relating settled usage to the reservation
security.description: SettleReservation looks up the active reservation, then writes settlement.TotalTokens straight into both quota_reservations.settled_tokens and a new usage_events row (lines 420-435). settlement.TotalTokens is computed from PromptTokens+CompletionTokens (line 417-419) which, per the router (settleRequest in router/server.go:1599-1609), can be 'provider_reported'. There is no check that settled_tokens <= reserved_tokens and no storage-level CHECK constraint tying the two (schema migrate.go:83-94 only enforces settled_tokens >= 0). Daily quota accounting in dailyUsageTx (store.go:794-810) sums usage_events.total_tokens for 'used' — so an inflated settle directly inflates consumed daily quota, and conversely a hostile/buggy upstream reporting fewer tokens than reserved under-bills. The reservation cap is only enforced at reserve time (RequestedTokens vs remaining, line 375), not at settle time.
security.impact: Over-billing or under-billing of a buyer's daily token quota driven by whatever token count the caller passes, with no storage-layer ceiling. In a system that moves real USDC, settled usage that exceeds the reserved amount means a buyer can be charged/quota-debited beyond what was admitted, or (if reported low) consume more real capacity than billed. Exploitability depends on how much the provider-reported count is trusted upstream; storage faithfully persists whatever it is told.
security.recommendation: Enforce the invariant in the storage layer: either cap settled tokens at reserved_tokens (clamp) or reject settlements where settlement.TotalTokens exceeds reserved_tokens, and/or add a CHECK/trigger so usage_events.total_tokens for a request cannot exceed the matching active reservation. At minimum, record both reserved and settled and have the billing layer reconcile against reserved, never trusting settled alone.
security.evidence: Verified at store.go:395-437. The SELECT at lines 403-405 fetches only window_date and status — reserved_tokens is never read, so there is no way for the function to compare settled vs reserved. The only gate is `if status != "active"` (line 411). settlement.TotalTokens defaults to PromptTokens+CompletionTokens (lines 417-419) and is written verbatim into quota_reservations.settled_tokens (UPDATE at 420-424) and usage_events.total_tokens (INSERT at 428-432). Schema confirms no relational CHECK: migrate.go:88 only enforces `settled_tokens >= 0`, migrate.go:74 only `total_tokens >= 0`. dailyUsageTx (store.go:794-809) sums usage_events.total_tokens for 'used' and reserved_tokens for active 'reserved', confirming an inflated settle inflates consumed quota. Provider-reported counts flow unvalidated from settleRequest: server.go:1496,1520,1527 pass reported.PromptTokens/reported.CompletionTokens (parsed from the upstream SSE stream via usageFromJSON) into settleRequest with source 'provider_reported', and settleRequest (server.go:1599-1609) applies no cap. Confirmed exactly as described. Severity kept low: real money-math gap but requires a hostile or buggy upstream provider (not the buyer directly) to report inflated counts, and reservations expire at +24h so the blast radius is bounded by daily quota; the over-/under-bill is a correctness defect rather than a direct drain.

security.title: Replayed client-controlled request_id surfaces a raw primary-key collision instead of an idempotent response
security.description: ReserveQuota inserts into quota_reservations whose PRIMARY KEY is (account_id, request_id) (migrate.go:93). The request_id originates from the client-supplied X-Request-ID header (router/server.go:168-171 accepts any UUID-like value), so a buyer fully controls it. If the same (account_id, request_id) already has a row (e.g. a retried/replayed request, or two in-flight requests sharing an id), the INSERT at line 382 fails with a UNIQUE/PK constraint error that ReserveQuota returns verbatim (line 386-387). The router then treats it as a generic store error and replies 500 (router/server.go:1301-1316). The transaction is BEGIN IMMEDIATE so there is no double-reservation (good), but there is no idempotency handling: the same logical request cannot be safely retried, and a caller can force 500s by reusing ids.
security.impact: No double-spend (PK + IMMEDIATE tx prevent a second reservation), but retries of a legitimately-failed request collide and return 500, and a malicious buyer can deliberately reuse request_ids to generate confusing internal errors. Correctness/availability gap rather than a fund-loss bug.
security.recommendation: Detect the duplicate-key case explicitly (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(account_id,request_id) DO NOTHING, or map the constraint error to storage.ErrReservationExists which already exists in errors.go) and return a defined idempotency outcome the router can translate to a stable response instead of a 500.
security.evidence: Verified. quota_reservations PRIMARY KEY is (account_id, request_id) at migrate.go:93. request_id is client-controlled: server.go:168-171 reads X-Request-ID and only regenerates it `if !isUUIDLike(requestID)`, so any UUID-like value the buyer supplies is honored. ReserveQuota's INSERT at store.go:382-385 has no ON CONFLICT clause; on PK collision the error is returned verbatim at 386-387 (`return storage.QuotaDecision{}, err`) without mapping to ErrReservationExists. The router quota-decision error handler at server.go:1301-1316 only special-cases the quota-exhausted 429 (line 1296) and context-cancel (1311); everything else falls through to writeError(...StatusInternalServerError... 'quota_reservation_failed') at 1314. ErrReservationExists is defined (errors.go:9) but grep confirms it is never returned by ReserveQuota — only ErrReservationNotFound is used (store.go:407,451,519). No double-spend confirmed: beginImmediate runs BEGIN IMMEDIATE (store.go:853) and the PK blocks a second active row. Verdict confirmed at low: availability/idempotency defect, attacker can force self-inflicted 500s by reusing their own request_ids, no fund loss or cross-account impact.

security.title: Capacity-tier runtime config serialized and parsed with fmt.Sprintf/Sscanf %q (brittle round-trip)
security.description: SetCapacityTier writes the runtime_config 'capacity_tier' value as `fmt.Sprintf('{"tier":%d,"signals":%q}', ...)` (line 710) and GetCapacityTier reads it back with `fmt.Sscanf(value, '{"tier":%d,"signals":%q}', ...)` (line 699). Unlike the kill_switch path which correctly uses encoding/json (lines 730,741), this hand-rolled format is fragile: Sscanf %q parsing is not a real JSON parser, and any future writer (migration, manual operator edit of runtime_config, or a Signals string with format-breaking content) that produces a value not matching the exact literal template makes GetCapacityTier return an error, which propagates into ExplorerHealth (explorer.go:366-370) and the capacity-tier read path, degrading health reporting.
security.impact: No injection (runtime_config is operator/internal-written, not attacker-reachable, and the value flows through a bound parameter), but a malformed or externally-edited capacity_tier row breaks tier reads and health output. Reliability/maintainability rather than security.
security.recommendation: Serialize and parse capacity_tier with encoding/json (a small struct) exactly as the kill_switch path already does, rather than fmt.Sprintf/Sscanf with %q.
security.evidence: Verified directly. SetCapacityTier at store.go:710 uses `value := fmt.Sprintf("{\"tier\":%d,\"signals\":%q}", tier.Tier, tier.Signals)` and GetCapacityTier at store.go:699 parses with `fmt.Sscanf(value, "{\"tier\":%d,\"signals\":%q}", &tier.Tier, &tier.Signals)` — a literal-template Sscanf, not a JSON parser. The kill_switch path is the contrasting correct pattern: GetKillSwitch uses json.Unmarshal (store.go:730) and SetKillSwitch uses json.Marshal (store.go:741). Both runtime_config writes use bound parameters (store.go:714-715, 751-752) so there is no SQL injection, confirming the 'no injection' framing. Value is operator/internal-written (SetCapacityTier is the only writer of key 'capacity_tier'). Verdict confirmed at info: this is a robustness/maintainability defect with no security impact; the worst case is GetCapacityTier returning an error that degrades health/tier reads if the row is ever malformed.

security.title: Operator-key comparison gating the PII-exposing explorer storage queries is non-constant-time (router, adjacent to this component)
security.description: The explorer storage methods (ExplorerListBuyers/BuyerDetail/Sessions/Activity in explorer.go) return account emails, client IPs, API-key prefixes and audit payloads (types.go:265-401). All explorer routes are gated by explorerAllowed -> operatorAuthorized (explorer.go:246-255), and operatorAuthorized compares the bearer token with a plain string `==` : `r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey` (lines 1933,1942). Go's == on strings is not constant-time, leaking timing information about the operator key. This is in the router, not the storage package itself, but it is the sole authorization barrier in front of every PII-returning storage query in this component, so it is in scope for the storage data's exposure.
security.impact: Theoretical timing side-channel on the operator key that protects all buyer PII / API-key-prefix / audit data exposed by the explorer storage queries. Exploitation requires high-resolution remote timing and is difficult in practice, but the fix is trivial and the data behind it is sensitive.
security.recommendation: Compare the operator bearer token with crypto/subtle.ConstantTimeCompare (or hmac.Equal, already imported elsewhere in this package per auth/demo.go:53) instead of ==, after a length-independent prefix check.
security.evidence: Verified. operatorAuthorized at server.go:1932-1938 uses `if r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey` — a plain Go string == (also repeated at server.go:1942 in shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit). Go's string == is byte-wise and short-circuits on first mismatch, so it is not constant-time. It is the sole auth barrier: explorerAllowed at explorer.go:246-247 returns false unless operatorAuthorized passes, and it gates the explorer routes. The data behind it is PII: storage types expose Email (types.go:268), KeyHashPrefix (types.go:274), ClientIP (types.go:54,63,70,76) and PayloadJSON (types.go:399). hmac.Equal is already used in the codebase (auth/demo.go:53), confirming a constant-time primitive is readily available. Verdict confirmed but kept at low: the side-channel is real yet remote timing extraction of a high-entropy bearer token over HTTP is extremely difficult in practice (network jitter dwarfs the per-byte comparison delta), and the protected surface is operator-only PII rather than fund movement. Low is the correct severity; the trivial fix justifies keeping it on the radar.

security.title: Operator/admin auth uses non-constant-time string comparison of the bearer token
security.description: operatorAuthorized gates every admin endpoint (handleKillSwitch, handleCapacitySignal, handleCapacityEvaluate, handleFeedbackSummary, and the /admin/explorer/* PII routes) by doing `if r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey`. Go's `==` on strings is a length-then-bytewise compare that short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the response/branch time leaks how many leading bytes of the supplied token are correct. The same plain `==` against the operator key is repeated at line 1942 in shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit. The OperatorKey is the single shared secret that authorizes the kill switch (can pause/unpause the entire public money API), capacity-tier changes, and read access to buyer/session PII via the explorer endpoints. Unlike the API-key path (which compares full-entropy SHA/HMAC hashes via a DB index, where timing is irrelevant) this compares the raw operator secret directly.
security.impact: An attacker who can make repeated requests and measure response latency can mount a byte-at-a-time timing attack to recover the operator key, then toggle the kill switch (denial of service against the live USDC inference API or, inversely, disable a protective pause), force capacity tier changes, and exfiltrate buyer/session PII from the explorer endpoints. These admin routes are explicitly exempted from the kill switch (publicPaused returns false for /admin/), so they remain reachable even when the rest of the API is paused.
security.recommendation: Compare with crypto/subtle.ConstantTimeCompare over fixed-length digests, e.g. hash both sides: `want := sha256.Sum256([]byte("Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey)); got := sha256.Sum256([]byte(r.Header.Get("Authorization"))); if subtle.ConstantTimeCompare(want[:], got[:]) == 1 { ... }`. Hashing first avoids leaking length and gives a constant-time compare. Apply the same fix at line 1942. Longer term, prefer a dedicated gateway-admin credential distinct from the coordinator OperatorKey so a leak of one does not compromise both surfaces.
security.evidence: CONFIRMED the code pattern: server.go:1933 `if r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey` and the duplicate at 1942 inside shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit. operatorAuthorized gates exactly the routes claimed: kill-switch (657), capacity-signal (702), capacity-evaluate (740), feedback-summary (632), and all explorer PII routes via explorerAllowed->operatorAuthorized (explorer.go:247). publicPaused at 1948 returns false for any /admin/ path, so admin routes stay reachable while paused — that part is accurate. The blast radius (kill switch, capacity, buyer/session PII) is real. HOWEVER the claimed severity is overstated for several concrete reasons that read as mitigations: (1) Go's string `==` for a hot comparison against a header is on the order of nanoseconds; the per-byte branch-time delta an attacker is trying to recover is a few CPU cycles, far below the timing noise floor of a remote HTTP request (network jitter, TLS, Go scheduler, GC). Remote byte-at-a-time recovery of a high-entropy secret over HTTP against an in-process `==` is not practically demonstrated and is widely considered infeasible without local co-residency and millions-to-billions of samples per byte — and the OperatorKey is a single opaque secret of unknown-but-presumably-high entropy, not a guessable short PIN. (2) The compare is length-then-bytewise: Go compares lengths first and only does the byte loop when lengths are equal, so an attacker must already know the exact length before any byte-position signal exists. (3) The explorer PII routes are gated behind Explorer.Enabled which defaults to false (config.go:186 `Explorer: ExplorerConfig{Enabled: false}`), so the highest-value target (PII) is off in the default build. (4) There is no per-request artificial delay or oracle that amplifies the signal. Constant-time comparison is still the correct hardening and the duplicate at 1942 should be fixed, so this is a real best-practice violation (LOW), but the 'recover the operator key remotely via latency' high-severity exploit narrative is not substantiated by the code or by realistic remote timing-attack feasibility. Downgraded high -> low.

security.title: Demo-token IP binding collapses IPv6 clients to a /64, allowing cross-user token replay
security.description: Demo tokens are HMAC-signed and bound to the client IP: Issue stores normalizeDemoIP(clientIP) in the payload and Validate rejects unless payload.IP == normalizeDemoIP(clientIP). For IPv4 the normalization keeps the full /32, but for IPv6 normalizeDemoIP returns `net.IP(ip[:8]).String() + "::/64"`, i.e. it discards the low 64 bits and binds only to the /64 prefix. A single residential or hosting IPv6 allocation is routinely a /64 (or larger) shared across every host/interface behind it. The demo IP is also used as the rate-limit / quota identity (`accountID = "demo:" + payload.IP` in handleFeedback line 607, and the demo path in authenticateAny line 1687) and demo sessions consume real provider inference (real USDC cost to the operator, gated only by DemoDailyTokensPerIP / DemoSessionsPerIPPerHour).
security.impact: Any client sharing the victim's IPv6 /64 (same ISP allocation, same cloud subnet, or an attacker who controls a /64) can replay a demo token minted for a different address within that /64 and pass Validate. This defeats the per-IP demo quota for IPv6 users (one issued token is reusable across many addresses in the prefix) and lets an attacker amplify demo inference consumption — directly increasing operator USDC spend — and pollute another user's demo feedback identity.
security.recommendation: Bind IPv6 demo tokens to the full /128 address (treat IPv6 like IPv4: return the canonical full-address string), or if /64 binding is intentional for NAT tolerance, also tie the token to an additional independent factor (a server-issued opaque session id stored server-side) so the IP prefix is not the sole anti-replay control. At minimum keep DemoDailyTokensPerIP low to bound blast radius.
security.evidence: CONFIRMED the normalization: demo.go:91 returns `net.IP(ip[:8]).String() + "::/64"` for IPv6, discarding the low 64 bits, while IPv4 keeps the full address (line 85 `v4.String()`). Validate rejects unless `payload.IP != normalizeDemoIP(clientIP)` (line 67). The IP is reused as quota/feedback identity at server.go:607 (`accountID = "demo:" + payload.IP`) and 1241. So the technical claim (IPv6 binding is /64-granular) is accurate. HOWEVER the impact is over-stated and this is closer to a design property than an authz break: (1) The /64 collapse is the SAME key used both for binding AND for the quota identity — i.e. all addresses in a /64 already share ONE quota bucket (`demo:...::/64`). So an attacker who 'replays' a token across the /64 is consuming the very same per-IP quota the legitimate /64 occupant would consume; there is no quota amplification beyond what a single /64 occupant already gets, because the quota itself is keyed on the /64. The 'defeats the per-IP demo quota / amplify consumption' claim is therefore largely self-cancelling: the binding and the budget collapse to the same /64 granularity by design. (2) To exploit cross-user replay you must already be on-path within the victim's /64 (same allocation) AND have captured the victim's token — at which point you are inside the same quota bucket and the same trust zone; this is not a privilege boundary that grants anything a co-located host did not already have. (3) Demo tokens are HMAC-signed (line 42, hmac.Equal at 53) and short-TTL (<=24h, line 32-35), and demo consumption is hard-capped by DemoDailyTokensPerIP / DemoSessionsPerIPPerHour (config.go:317-320 require these > 0). The real residual issue is purely the choice of /64 vs /128 granularity for the quota key, which slightly widens the shared bucket for IPv6 — a minor anti-abuse hardening, not a medium-severity authorization flaw. Downgraded medium -> low.

security.title: GitHub token exchange does not verify access_token is non-empty before using it
security.description: Exchange treats any 2xx response from GitHub's token endpoint as success. GitHub returns HTTP 200 with a body like {"error":"bad_verification_code",...} (and no access_token) for several failure modes; the code only decodes access_token/scope, never checks `tokenResp.AccessToken != ""`, and proceeds to call the user API at lines 81-86 with `Authorization: Bearer ` (empty token). The downstream guard is incidental: it relies on the unauthenticated /user call returning non-2xx (line 92) or user.ID==0 (line 102). It also does not parse or surface the GitHub error_description.
security.impact: Low: the empty-token user request will normally fail and the flow aborts with a generic 502, so this is robustness/defense-in-depth rather than an exploitable bypass. The risk is that the security of the exchange depends on an external API's error behavior rather than an explicit local check, and error diagnostics are lost (harder to detect a misconfigured or compromised OAuth app).
security.recommendation: After decoding the token response, explicitly fail when access_token is empty and when an `error` field is present, before issuing the user request: add an `Error string `json:"error"`` field and return an error if `tokenResp.Error != "" || tokenResp.AccessToken == ""`.
security.evidence: CONFIRMED the code: oauth.go:70-73 decodes only AccessToken/Scope, there is no `tokenResp.AccessToken != ""` check, and line 86 sets `Authorization: Bearer `+tokenResp.AccessToken (would be 'Bearer ' with an empty token) before the /user call. ALSO confirmed the two downstream guards the finding itself relies on: line 92 rejects any non-2xx from the user endpoint, and line 102 `if user.ID == 0 { return ... }` rejects a missing user id. An empty/invalid bearer to GitHub's /user endpoint returns 401, which is caught at line 92 and aborts with a 502 (server.go:266 oauth_exchange_failed). There is additionally a scope guard at oauth.go:78 (ScopesAllowed) and line 109 rejecting empty scopes, so a forged-but-2xx token response with no scopes is also rejected before any identity is minted. The finding's own description and impact already state this is 'robustness/defense-in-depth rather than an exploitable bypass' and 'Low'. Given that NO account is created and NO key is issued unless a valid GitHub user.ID is returned (server.go:269-280 only issues a key after a successful identity), there is no security boundary crossed by the missing check — it is purely a diagnostics/defense-in-depth nicety. This is an informational hardening item, not a vulnerability. Downgraded low -> info.

security.title: OAuth callback error path unhandled and Secure-cookie flag depends solely on https base_url (hardening note)
security.description: The mp_oauth_session cookie is set with Path=/auth/github, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Secure gated on base_url being https, MaxAge=600 — and the callback at /auth/github/callback is under that path, so the cookie is correctly sent and CSRF state binding works (ConsumeOAuthState requires both state_hash and session_id, single-use, time-bounded). Two minor observations, not vulnerabilities: (1) handleGitHubCallback does not inspect GitHub's `error`/`error_description` query parameters (e.g. user-denied), so a denial surfaces as a generic 'oauth_state_invalid' rather than a clean message; (2) secureCookies() returns true only when Public.BaseURL uses https, so a misconfigured http base_url would silently drop the Secure flag on the session and new-api-key cookies. Both are informational given the production base_url is https and the core CSRF/state machinery is sound.
security.impact: No direct security impact under the shipped production config. Recorded so the OAuth surface is documented as reviewed and the error-handling / secure-cookie dependency is explicit.
security.recommendation: Optionally handle the GitHub `error` query param in handleGitHubCallback for clearer UX, and consider validating in Config.Validate that Public.BaseURL is https when github_oauth_enabled or demo auth is enabled, so Secure cookies cannot be silently disabled. No change required for the current production config.
security.evidence: CONFIRMED all stated facts and the finding is correctly scoped as informational. Cookie set at server.go:228-231 with Path=/auth/github, HttpOnly:true, SameSite:Lax, Secure:s.secureCookies(), MaxAge:600 — and the callback route /auth/github/callback (registered line 137) is under that path, so the cookie is delivered. CSRF/state binding is sound: handleGitHubCallback requires the mp_oauth_session cookie (line 242), the state query param, and the code (line 243), then ConsumeOAuthState(StateHash(state), cookie.Value, now) at line 247 binds state-hash to session-id and is single-use/time-bounded (OAuthStateExpiry = now+10m, oauth.go:134-136). callbackAllowed re-validates the redirect URI (line 252). Observation (1) confirmed: handleGitHubCallback (235-286) never reads r.URL.Query().Get("error") / error_description, so a user-denied consent returns the generic oauth_state_invalid (line 244/249) — a UX issue, not a security flaw. Observation (2) confirmed: secureCookies() (1964-1967) returns true only when Public.BaseURL scheme == https, and Config.Validate (config.go:236, 303-316) only calls requireURL on base_url and does NOT assert https even when GitHubOAuthEnabled — so an http base_url would silently drop Secure on both mp_oauth_session and mp_new_api_key cookies. Production default is https (config.go:144 `BaseURL: "https://api.streamvc.live"`), so no impact in the shipped config. The finding self-classifies as info with no exploit; severity info is appropriate and the two hardening notes are accurate. Confirmed at info.

security.title: Pinned update-signing public key is overridable via environment variable, defeating the supply-chain signature root of trust
security.description: verifyChecksumSignature() reads the signature-verification public key from `ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["MACPROVIDER_CHECKSUM_PUBLIC_KEY_PEM"] ?? Self.checksumPublicKeyPEM` (line 247). The hardcoded `checksumPublicKeyPEM` (lines 7-12) is the single cryptographic root of trust that makes the whole self-update safe: the openssl `dgst -sha256 -verify` step (lines 250-259) is the only thing that authenticates checksums.txt, which in turn authenticates the tarball SHA-256 that gates execution at lines 82-93. Because the key can be replaced by an environment variable, an attacker who can set even one env var in the provider's process environment (a poisoned LaunchAgent plist, a compromised shell profile, a malicious wrapper, or a co-resident process that can influence the launch environment) can substitute their own public key. They then point MACPROVIDER_RELEASES_API_URL (line 31) at their own server, serve a checksums.txt + checksums.txt.sig signed with their matching private key plus a matching tarball, and every check passes.
security.impact: Full remote code execution / supply-chain compromise on the contributor Mac: the attacker-supplied binary is run via `runProcess(newBinary.path, ["self-test"])` (line 92) and then atomically installed over the live binary (lines 159-173, applyValidatedUpdate) and relaunched under launchd (lines 203-212). The replacement binary inherits the provider's coordinator session, ECDH/attestation private keys, and any money-bearing state, so this is a credential-theft and persistent-RCE primitive on every host an attacker can touch the environment of.
security.recommendation: Treat the signing public key as a non-overridable compile-time constant. Remove the MACPROVIDER_CHECKSUM_PUBLIC_KEY_PEM environment branch entirely (or gate it behind a build-time DEBUG flag that is never present in release builds). If a key-rotation mechanism is needed, ship multiple pinned keys in the binary and roll them via signed releases, never via env. Prefer verifying with CryptoKit's P256.Signing.PublicKey against the embedded PEM rather than shelling out to openssl with a key written to a temp file.
security.evidence: Read SelfUpdate.swift:247 verbatim: `let keyPEM = ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["MACPROVIDER_CHECKSUM_PUBLIC_KEY_PEM"] ?? Self.checksumPublicKeyPEM` — the env var unconditionally takes precedence over the embedded key. Confirmed NO `#if DEBUG`/`#if RELEASE` guard anywhere in the file (grep for `#if`/`DEBUG` in SelfUpdate.swift returned nothing) and Package.swift:65-67 only sets `.enableExperimentalFeature("StrictConcurrency")` with no DEBUG-define stripping — so this branch is live in release builds. The verification chain is exactly as claimed: line 248 writes keyPEM to a temp PEM, lines 250-259 invoke `openssl dgst -sha256 -verify` against it as the SOLE authenticator of checksums.txt; line 79 expectedSHA256 then trusts that text, lines 81-84 gate the tarball on its SHA, line 92 executes the extracted binary, lines 159-173 (replaceCurrentBinary copy+chmod 0755+rename) install it, lines 203-212 relaunch via launchctl bootstrap. The paired releases-URL override at line 31 exists and is unvalidated (see finding 2), so the attacker controls both key and metadata source. The env override is genuinely consumed in production code (also wired through scripts/test-tier2-provider-release.sh:131-178), confirming it is not dead code. Severity kept high rather than critical only because exploitation requires the attacker to already control the victim's process environment (write the LaunchAgent plist, shell profile, or launch wrapper), which on macOS already implies user-level code-exec or write to the user's Library — a meaningful precondition. Within that precondition the claim of persistent RCE and key/session theft is accurate. Real as described.

security.title: Release-API URL is environment/flag overridable and never validated for scheme or host
security.description: The release metadata endpoint comes from `releasesAPIURL ?? environment["MACPROVIDER_RELEASES_API_URL"] ?? defaultReleasesAPIURL` (lines 30-32) and is also settable via the `--releases-api-url` CLI flag (MacProviderCLI.swift:161-168). latestRelease() (lines 129-141) only checks `URL(string:)` parses — it does NOT enforce https or a github.com host, unlike the asset URLs which go through validateDownloadURL() (lines 225-232, which require https and a github.com / objects.githubusercontent.com host). So the metadata channel that supplies asset names, the tag/version used in the update-available gate, and the browser_download_url values can be plain http:// to an arbitrary host. The asset download URLs are still allowlisted, and the signature gate still authenticates the payload, so this alone is not code-exec; but it is an inconsistent trust boundary that enables a plaintext/downgraded metadata fetch and is the SSRF/downgrade half that pairs with the public-key-override finding above.
security.impact: On its own: information disclosure of the request (user-agent leaks current version) over cleartext, and forced-stale or forced-update version reporting. Combined with a substituted signing key, it completes an end-to-end attacker-controlled update channel.
security.recommendation: Run releasesAPIURL through the same validation as assets: require url.scheme == "https" and host == "api.github.com" (or the configured allowlist) before the fetch in latestRelease(). Reject the override unless it also satisfies the allowlist.
security.evidence: Confirmed the inconsistent trust boundary. SelfUpdate.swift:30-32 builds releasesAPIURL from flag, then MACPROVIDER_RELEASES_API_URL env, then default. latestRelease() at lines 130-131 does ONLY `guard let url = URL(string: releasesAPIURL)` with no scheme/host check, then fetches at line 136. validateDownloadURL() (225-232) enforces scheme==https and host in {github.com, *.github.com, objects.githubusercontent.com}, and is applied ONLY to asset URLs at lines 68-70 — grep confirmed validateDownloadURL is never called on releasesAPIURL. The CLI flag --releases-api-url is wired at MacProviderCLI.swift:161-168 with no validation. So the premise is fully real. Downgraded medium->low because: (1) the override is operator-supplied (CLI flag / the operator's own env), not attacker-injected over the network, so labeling it SSRF overstates it — there is no untrusted-request-forging surface, only a misconfigurable client endpoint; (2) it is explicitly NOT code-exec on its own because the actual payload is still gated by validateDownloadURL on assets (68-70) and the signature/SHA chain (77-84); (3) the only standalone impact is leaking the `macprovider-cli/<version>` user-agent (line 135) over cleartext and spoofing the version-available banner — genuinely low. The end-to-end-channel concern is already counted inside finding 1's precondition, so it is not independently medium here.

security.title: Extracted update binary is executed with the full attacker-influenceable inherited environment before validation completes
security.description: After checksum verification, the new binary is executed via `runProcess(newBinary.path, ["self-test"])` (line 92). runProcess() (lines 214-223) creates a Process with no environment scrubbing, so the child inherits every env var of the updater, including the MACPROVIDER_* overrides. This is post-checksum so the binary content is trusted, but it means the self-test (and the subsequently installed binary) runs under whatever environment the parent had, with no isolation. It is defense-in-depth context for the env-override findings rather than an independent vulnerability, but worth hardening since self-test runs untrusted-environment code paths during the update.
security.impact: Amplifies the blast radius of any environment-poisoning: the verified-but-environment-shaped binary executes immediately during update with full inherited env, before the operator has any chance to inspect it.
security.recommendation: Set an explicit minimal `process.environment` for the self-test invocation (drop MACPROVIDER_* and other non-essential vars), and run the self-test from the temp extraction directory rather than after-trust assumptions. This bounds what a shaped environment can do during the update step.
security.evidence: runProcess() at SelfUpdate.swift:214-223 constructs `let process = Process()`, sets only executableURL and arguments, and never assigns process.environment — so per Foundation semantics the child inherits the parent's full environment. Confirmed line 92 calls `runProcess(newBinary.path, arguments: ["self-test"])`. The finding correctly self-scopes this as defense-in-depth, not an independent vulnerability: it runs at line 92 AFTER the SHA-256 gate at lines 81-84 (binary CONTENT already authenticated), and the worst case is that the trusted binary observes an environment the operator already controlled. Low is the correct severity and the finding does not overclaim. Kept confirmed/low rather than info because env-scrubbing the self-test is a reasonable hardening that bounds the finding-1 precondition.

security.title: Staged binary is made executable before the atomic rename, briefly exposing a 0755 hidden file in the install directory
security.description: replaceCurrentBinary() copies the new binary to a hidden staged path in the install directory, calls setAttributes([.posixPermissions: 0o755]) (line 167), then rename()s it over the current binary (line 168). Between the copy/chmod and the rename there is a short window where a 0755-executable, fully-attacker-or-content-controlled file exists at a predictable-prefix path (`.<name>.update-<uuid>`) in the same directory as the live binary. Because the directory is owned by the same user, this is low impact (no privilege boundary is crossed), and the UUID suffix limits predictability, but the chmod-before-rename ordering is slightly riskier than necessary.
security.impact: Minor: a co-resident same-user process could observe/execute the staged binary during the window. No privilege escalation since it is already the user's own writable directory.
security.recommendation: chmod the staged file while it is still in the per-update temp directory (mode 0700 dir), then move it into place; or fchmod after rename. Keep the staged file mode 0700 until the rename so only the owner can execute it during the window.
security.evidence: Code reads exactly as described: SelfUpdate.swift:163-164 builds `staged` as `.<lastPathComponent>.update-<UUID().uuidString>` in the live binary's directory; line 166 copies; line 167 setAttributes([.posixPermissions: 0o755]); line 168 rename(staged.path, current.path) — so a 0755 file does exist between lines 167 and 168. However the finding itself concedes there is NO privilege boundary: the directory is the same user's writable install dir (staged is created via current.deletingLastPathComponent()), the suffix is a random UUID (un-pre-creatable by another process), and the only actor who could exploit the window is a same-user co-resident process that already holds the user's privileges and could read the binary anyway. There is no security gain to an attacker who is already same-uid. This is a best-practice ordering nit with effectively zero exploitable impact, so downgraded low->info. The technical description is accurate; the risk is negligible.

security.title: Coordinator-supplied recommended_binary_version is echoed into local status output and update prompts unsanitized
security.description: acceptCoordinatorSession() takes `payload["recommended_binary_version"]` straight from a coordinator (or, on the WS relay path, any party who can inject a hello_ack/auth_response frame) and stores it (line 385) and prints it (lines 390-393). LocalStatusFormatter renders coordinator-provided fields (recommended_binary_version, url, tier, session) into the terminal status block (SelfUpdate.swift:438, 433-438) via String(describing:) with no sanitization. A malicious/compromised coordinator can inject ANSI escape sequences or misleading text into the operator's terminal (e.g., to spoof a version string or hide output). It does NOT influence the actual update decision — the real update gate is GitHub + signature, and compareSemver only parses integer components (line 391) — so this is cosmetic/log-injection, not code-exec.
security.impact: Terminal/log injection and operator-display spoofing from a trusted-but-potentially-compromised coordinator; could mislead an operator about update status. No effect on the cryptographically gated update path.
security.recommendation: Sanitize coordinator-provided strings before printing (strip control/ANSI characters) in LocalStatusFormatter.string() and in the acceptCoordinatorSession print, and length-bound them.
security.evidence: Verified the full taint flow end to end. CoordinatorClient.swift:385 stores `payload["recommended_binary_version"] as? String` into providerStatus via setCoordinatorSession; lines 390-393 print it directly (`print("A newer version is available (v\(recommended))...")`) with no sanitization. ProviderStatus.swift:167/176/201 carries it into the snapshot, and HTTPServer.swift:392 emits it in the local /v1/status JSON as recommended_binary_version. StatusCommand (MacProviderCLI.swift:115) fetches that JSON via LocalStatusClient and passes it to LocalStatusFormatter.format (line 117). LocalStatusFormatter (SelfUpdate.swift:404-449) renders coordinator["recommended_binary_version"], url, session, tier at lines 434-438 via the string() helper, which at lines 446-448 does `String(describing: value)` with zero control-character stripping — so raw ANSI/escape bytes from the coordinator reach the operator's terminal. The mitigation claims are also accurate: this does NOT affect the update gate — compareSemver (SelfUpdate.swift:280-290) maps each component through `Int($0) ?? 0`, so non-numeric injected content cannot force a version bump, and the real update path (run()) authenticates via GitHub assets + openssl signature + SHA. So this is genuinely a cosmetic terminal/log-injection from a trusted-but-compromised coordinator, correctly rated low. Confirmed as described.

security.title: Local HTTP /v1/chat/completions has no concurrent-request limit — unbounded task and semaphore-waiter growth enables local memory/CPU DoS
security.description: handleChatCompletions parses the body and unconditionally spawns Task.detached per request (line 196) before any concurrency check. The only serialization is ModelRuntime.inferenceGate = AsyncSemaphore(value: 1) (ModelRuntime.swift:31), whose waiter array is unbounded (AsyncSemaphore.swift:10,36). The WS relay path enforces backpressure with `guard active.count < maxActiveRequests` and returns error_queue_full (InferenceRelay.swift:70-79), but the HTTP path has no equivalent gate — it never consults providerStatus capacity or any active-request count before enqueuing. Each queued request also retains its fully-parsed ChatCompletionRequest (messages can be up to maxRequestBodyBytes = 10 MB each; Config.swift:57) and its NIO channel/ByteBuffer. An attacker who opens N connections and POSTs valid completion requests causes N detached tasks plus N parsed-request closures plus N held channels to accumulate while exactly one runs, growing memory and FD usage without bound.
security.impact: Any unauthenticated local process or local user on the contributor's Mac (the endpoint requires no auth) can exhaust the provider's memory and file descriptors, degrading or crashing the inference service and denying revenue. Loopback-only bind limits this to same-host attackers (other apps, other users on a shared Mac, or a compromised local process), so it is local rather than remote.
security.recommendation: Mirror the WS relay's backpressure on the HTTP path: before spawning the detached task, check active in-flight count against providerStatus.capacity.maxConcurrency (or a dedicated AsyncSemaphore tryAcquire) and return HTTP 429/503 (e.g. APIError 503 code "queue_full") when full. Additionally cap the AsyncSemaphore waiter queue depth and reject new waiters past the cap instead of growing the array indefinitely.
security.evidence: Mechanics confirmed as described. HTTPServer.swift:196 spawns `Task.detached` inside handleChatCompletions with NO active-count guard — the only preceding checks are ChatCompletionRequest.parse (line 187) and validateModelMatches (line 188); there is no consultation of providerStatus capacity before enqueue. By contrast InferenceRelay.swift:70 has `guard active.count < maxActiveRequests else { ... error_queue_full ... }` — the HTTP path genuinely lacks this gate. The single point of serialization is ModelRuntime.swift:31 `inferenceGate = AsyncSemaphore(value: 1)`, used by complete()/stream() via withPermit (ModelRuntime.swift:96,150). AsyncSemaphore.wait() (AsyncSemaphore.swift:28-43) appends to `waiters` (line 36) with no cap check whatsoever — the array is genuinely unbounded, so queued requests (each holding a parsed ChatCompletionRequest) accumulate while exactly one runs. Body IS incrementally capped at maxBodyBytes (HTTPServer.swift:73-77), default 10MB (Config.swift:57), so a single request cannot exceed 10MB, but N concurrent requests still multiply. DOWNGRADED to low because: (1) the server binds 127.0.0.1 ONLY (HTTPServer.swift:35 `bind(host: "127.0.0.1"...)`) — there is no remote attack surface; (2) the deployment target is a contributor's own single-user Mac (per repo docs / M4 contributor context), so 'other local users / compromised local process' is a same-trust-domain attacker who already has code execution on the box; (3) per-request memory is bounded by the 10MB body cap and the small parsed request. The bug (unbounded waiter growth, no HTTP backpressure) is real, but blast radius is local-only on a single-trust-domain machine, which does not warrant medium.

security.title: NIO HTTP server sets no read/idle/header timeout — idle or slow connections accumulate (slow-loris style local DoS)
security.description: The ServerBootstrap pipeline (configureHTTPServerPipeline + RouterHandler) installs no IdleStateHandler and no read/header timeout. A client may open a connection and never send `.end`, or trickle bytes below maxBodyBytes slowly, holding the channel and its allocated bodyBuffer open indefinitely. channelRead only acts on `.end` (line 79-84); there is no deadline by which an incomplete request is aborted. Combined with backlog 256 (line 18) and no per-connection cap, many half-open connections can be held open.
security.impact: A local unauthenticated client can hold connections and buffers open indefinitely, contributing to FD/memory exhaustion and blocking legitimate local buyer traffic. Loopback-only bind keeps this local-host scoped.
security.recommendation: Add an IdleStateHandler (or NIO ByteToMessageHandler read timeout) to the childChannelInitializer to close connections that are idle or have not completed a request within a bounded window (e.g. 30-60s), and close connections whose request head has not arrived promptly.
security.evidence: Confirmed. The childChannelInitializer (HTTPServer.swift:20-32) only does `configureHTTPServerPipeline()` then adds RouterHandler — no IdleStateHandler, no read/header timeout handler. A repo-wide grep for IdleStateHandler|readTimeout|connectTimeout returned ZERO hits in phase3-binary/Sources (the recent ResponseHeaderTimeout commit is in the Go gateway, NOT this Swift binary). channelRead (HTTPServer.swift:62-85) only triggers handleRequest on `.end` (line 79-80); a connection that sends `.head` + partial `.body` but never `.end` holds requestHead and bodyBuffer with no deadline. backlog is 256 (line 18). Half-open/slow connections therefore accumulate. Severity low is correct and unchanged: bound to 127.0.0.1 only (HTTPServer.swift:35), bodyBuffer per connection is capped at maxBodyBytes/10MB (line 73), and the threat is a same-host local actor on a single-user Mac. The missing timeout is a genuine hardening gap but low-impact given loopback scope.

security.title: Provider self-reports prompt/completion token counts that the trusted coordinator must not trust for billing
security.description: The untrusted provider binary computes and returns prompt_tokens/completion_tokens (from MLX result.promptTokenCount/generationTokenCount in ModelRuntime.swift:132-133,215-216) and includes them in inference_response_end `usage` and in HTTP responses. These values are entirely under the provider's control. This is correct behavior for this component (it must report what it did), but it is a payment-integrity boundary: the provider is explicitly untrusted per the system threat model, so any billing or payout computation on the coordinator that derives amounts from these self-reported counts is manipulable (a malicious provider can over-report completion_tokens to over-bill, or under-report to evade limits).
security.impact: If the coordinator/gateway bills buyers or computes provider payouts from these provider-supplied token counts without independent measurement, a malicious provider can inflate or deflate usage to manipulate USDC settlement. No defect exists in this binary; the risk is realized only if the trusted side trusts these fields.
security.recommendation: Ensure the coordinator independently meters tokens (e.g. counts relayed chunks / measures on its own tokenizer) and treats provider-reported usage as advisory only. Document this trust boundary in the coordinator billing path. No change required in the provider binary.
security.evidence: Confirmed as an accurate (info-level) trust-boundary observation. The token counts originate from MLX in CompletionResult: ModelRuntime.swift:132-133 (`promptTokens: result.promptTokenCount, completionTokens: result.generationTokenCount`) and the identical pair at 215-216 for streaming. These flow verbatim into the wire `usage` object via InferenceRelay.swift:493-499 (the `usage(_:)` helper), and are emitted in inference_response_end frames at lines 277-280 (non-streaming complete) and 366-372 (streaming complete), plus RelayRequestState.setUsage (lines 557-565). The same self-reported values also appear in the local HTTP responses (HTTPServer.swift:296-298 and 340-342). All of these are computed entirely inside the provider binary with no coordinator-side cross-check in this component, so a malicious provider fully controls them. The finding explicitly and correctly states 'No defect exists in this binary' and scopes the risk to the coordinator's billing path — info severity is appropriate and unchanged. This is a real, correctly-characterized payment-integrity boundary, not a false positive.

security.title: DOM-XSS: coordinator-controlled /v1/status `status` string interpolated raw into innerHTML, with a CSP that permits inline execution
security.description: fetchStatus() (line 782) does `const j = await r.json()` from `GET https://api.streamvc.live/v1/status` and stores it as poolStatus. renderDashboard() then builds a pool row with a template literal written to innerHTML: line 1093 `row.innerHTML = ''+key+''+val+''`. For the Status row (line 1086) `val` is `ps.status` taken VERBATIM from the JSON response (the sibling rows for ready/total_providers are wrapped in String(...) and numeric, but `status` is an arbitrary server string and is NOT coerced or escaped). The other innerHTML template-literal sink (line 1047, stats grid) interpolates `value`/`label` that are derived from local numeric usage counters and hardcoded labels, so it is not attacker-reachable — but the `status` path is. Crucially the nginx CSP for console.streamvc.live (dist/nginx-console.streamvc.live.conf line 27) sets `script-src 'unsafe-inline'`, so an injected inline event handler such as `` WOULD execute; the CSP does not mitigate this sink.
security.impact: If the coordinator's /v1/status response is attacker-influenced (compromised/malicious coordinator response, a bug that reflects client input into status, or a successful TLS-stripping MITM despite HSTS), the returned `status` string is rendered as live HTML in the buyer's browser on the money-bearing console origin. An injected `onerror`/`onload` handler runs with access to localStorage (chat history) and can call ensureToken()/the demo-session + /v1/chat/completions flow or exfiltrate the minted X-Demo-Token. Exploitability is gated on controlling the API response (not a raw unauthenticated-internet vector); furthermore the gateway emits status from a fixed enum so in practice this is only reachable via first-party server compromise or MITM, which is why I downgrade to low.
security.recommendation: Do not build DOM with innerHTML from server data. Replace the line 1093 row construction (and any other innerHTML that includes ${val}/${cls}) with createElement + textContent, exactly as the model list at line 1106-1110 already does safely. Additionally tighten the CSP: drop `script-src 'unsafe-inline'` (move the inline <script> to an external file with a nonce/hash) so inline-handler injection cannot execute even if a sink is missed. Example: `const valEl=document.createElement('span'); valEl.className='pool-val '+cls; valEl.textContent=val; row.append(keyEl,valEl);`
security.evidence: SINK IS REAL: index.html:1093 literally does `row.innerHTML = `${key}${val}`` with no escaping; line 1086 sets `val: ps ? ps.status : 'checking'` where `ps = poolStatus` (line 1083) and poolStatus is the raw JSON assigned at line 783 (`poolStatus = j` after `const j = await r.json()` at 782). A grep of the whole file for escapeHtml/sanitize/DOMPurify returns ZERO matches, confirming no escaping helper exists; the sibling rows 1087/1088 use `String((ps.pool && ps.pool.ready) || 0)` (numeric) and the model list 1106-1110 uses `tag.textContent = m` (safe), so only the `status` string is the injectable point exactly as claimed. CSP CLAIM IS ACCURATE: nginx-console.streamvc.live.conf:27 sets `script-src 'unsafe-inline'`, which per CSP spec enables inline event handlers; `img-src 'self'` blocks the bogus image load, which is precisely what fires the onerror handler, so the CSP provides no defense for this sink. DOWNGRADE RATIONALE: phase5-gateway/internal/router/server.go:1751-1806 (aggregateStatus) sets `out.Status` only from a fixed enum — `"up"` (1755), `"idle"` (1802), `"degraded"` (1805) — and the error path at server.go:549 sets `"down"`; the value never reflects client input. So in all real operation `status` is a constant server-controlled enum, and exploitation requires controlling the first-party /v1/status response (gateway/coordinator compromise or TLS-strip-despite-HSTS MITM). The sink is a genuine defense-in-depth defect worth fixing, but practical exploitability is minimal because the data source is same-trust first-party infrastructure emitting a constant — hence low, not medium.

security.title: Legacy beta Vercel proxy is an open prompt-relay / SSRF-to-fixed-hosts (currently fenced behind a feature flag returning 410)
security.description: chat.js is an unauthenticated POST endpoint that forwards a caller-supplied prompt to p.tunnel_url + '/v1/chat/completions' (line 56). The destination is NOT user-controlled — `provider` only selects between two hardcoded https hosts in PROVIDERS (m1/m4.streamvc.live), so this is not arbitrary-URL SSRF, and max_tokens is capped to 512 (line 50). The real exposure is that, when enabled, it is an unauthenticated open relay anyone can use to burn the M1/M4 Macs' inference capacity (no auth, no rate limit, no origin check). Both chat.js (line 21) and providers.js (line 18) now hard-gate this behind `process.env.MACPROVIDER_ENABLE_LEGACY_BETA_PROXY !== '1'` and return HTTP 410 by default, so in the default Vercel deployment the endpoint is dead. Reported as info because the abuse path only exists if an operator explicitly sets the flag.
security.impact: If the env flag is ever set to '1', the endpoint becomes an anonymous, unmetered relay to the contributor Macs: capacity-exhaustion / cost DoS on the M1/M4 hosts, and the response includes X-Provider-Tunnel revealing the tunnel hostnames. No new-host SSRF and no auth bypass beyond that.
security.recommendation: Keep the flag off in production (current state is correct). If the proxy is ever re-enabled, add an Origin/Referer allowlist, a per-IP rate limit, and remove the X-Provider-Tunnel response header so hostnames are not disclosed. Consider deleting the legacy files entirely now that the front-door console talks directly to api.streamvc.live.
security.evidence: Every claim verified against the source. chat.js:21 `if (globalThis.process?.env?.MACPROVIDER_ENABLE_LEGACY_BETA_PROXY !== '1') { return new Response('legacy beta proxy disabled', { status: 410 }); }` — confirms the gate returns 410 by default before any other logic runs. chat.js:9-18 defines PROVIDERS with only two hardcoded https hosts (m1/m4.streamvc.live); chat.js:39-41 `const provider = body.provider; ... const p = PROVIDERS[provider]; if (!p || !prompt) return 400` — confirms destination is NOT user-controllable (key lookup into a fixed map), so this is fixed-host, not arbitrary-URL SSRF. chat.js:50 `max_tokens: Math.min(parseInt(body.max_tokens ?? 384, 10) || 384, 512)` — confirms the 512 clamp. chat.js:56 forwards to `p.tunnel_url + '/v1/chat/completions'` with no Authorization/Origin/rate-limit check anywhere in the handler — confirms unauthenticated open relay when enabled. chat.js:79 sets header `'X-Provider-Tunnel': p.tunnel_url` — confirms tunnel-hostname disclosure (mild, since these are public *.streamvc.live names). providers.js:18 has the identical gate returning 410. A secrets grep of both files found no api_key/password/bearer (only the comment text). The info severity and the 'only-if-flag-set' framing are accurate; verdict confirmed.

security.title: Localhost demo_server.py forwards an uncapped attacker-controlled max_tokens to the upstream model
security.description: do_POST builds the upstream payload with `"max_tokens": int(req.get("max_tokens", 512))` (line 90) and `"temperature": float(req.get("temperature", 0.7))` (line 91) with no upper bound, then POSTs to the tunnel_url with a per-request timeout of p['timeout_s'] (default 180s). Unlike the Vercel chat.js which clamps `Math.min(..., 512)` (chat.js line 50), the Python demo server passes whatever integer the client sends. The server binds 127.0.0.1:8765 (line 118), so this is reachable only by a local user / local browser page, which bounds the impact.
security.impact: A local caller (or a malicious web page making a same-machine fetch where the browser allows it) can request an enormous completion (e.g. max_tokens=100000000), tying up the contributor Mac's model for the full timeout window and wasting compute. Local-only, no remote exposure, no money path. A non-integer/garbage value raises ValueError which is uncaught and returns a 500 — minor robustness issue, not a security one.
security.recommendation: Clamp before forwarding, mirroring chat.js: `mt = min(int(req.get('max_tokens', 512) or 512), 512)` and wrap the int()/float() casts in try/except to return 400 on bad input. Since this is a dev-only demo on localhost it is low priority, but the one-line clamp removes the foot-gun.
security.evidence: All claims verified against beta/demo_server.py. Line 90 `"max_tokens": int(req.get("max_tokens", 512)),` — confirms NO upper clamp (contrast chat.js:50 which applies Math.min(...,512)). Line 91 `"temperature": float(req.get("temperature", 0.7)),` — confirms no bound. Line 95 `upstream = requests.post(url, json=payload, stream=True, timeout=p["timeout_s"])` and line 38 `"timeout_s": cfg.get("timeout_s", 180)` — confirm the 180s default timeout window the request can occupy. Line 118 `host, port = "127.0.0.1", 8765` — confirms localhost-only bind, bounding impact to local callers, no remote exposure. UNCAUGHT-VALUEERROR CLAIM ALSO CONFIRMED: the only try/except in do_POST is lines 70-75 wrapping `json.loads`/JSONDecodeError; the int()/float() casts at lines 90-91 are outside any try block, so a non-numeric max_tokens raises an uncaught ValueError → 500 (the BaseHTTPRequestHandler default). No auth/Authorization/X-Demo-Token check exists in this handler, consistent with a localhost dev demo. Low severity (local-only DoS foot-gun, no money path) is appropriate; verdict confirmed.

architecture.title: Coordinator restart is a single point of failure: all pool, session, and in-flight relay state is in-memory only
architecture.description: Every routing-critical structure is process memory with no rehydration: pool.Registry.providers/sessions/breakerFaults/recoveryHolds (provider.go:115-124), and ws.Server.sessions/pending/warmups/timers (server.go:50-55). On SIGTERM the shutdown path (main.go:158-169) drains and closes HTTP servers but persists none of this. After a restart the pool is empty; providers must re-establish WS, re-auth, and (if WarmupGateEnabled) pass a warm-up gate before StateReady, during which buyer requests get no_provider_available/503. Only auth tokens, the request_log, billing ledger, and admission counters are durable.
architecture.impact: A coordinator crash/restart/redeploy takes the entire marketplace offline for inference for the reconnect+warmup window. Buyers paying real USDC see a cliff of 503s.
architecture.recommendation: Treat the coordinator as a stateful singleton and minimize restart blast radius: graceful redeploys with a reconnect grace window, a lightweight provider-session hint to skip warmup for fast reconnects, and Retry-After on the gateway 503. Long term, the in-memory pool is the architectural SPOF that should be made HA before scaling provider count.
architecture.evidence: CONFIRMED. Registry holds providers/sessions/endpoints/seenModels/breakerFaults/recoveryHolds/lastBreakerRecoveries as plain Go maps guarded only by sync.RWMutex (provider.go:114-124); NewRegistry (provider.go:131-145) initializes empty maps with zero load-from-storage. ws.Server.timers/pending/warmups/sessions are sync.Map (server.go:50-55) with no persistence. A repo-wide grep for Rehydrate/LoadProviders/restoreProviders returned NOTHING — the only Registry read method is Snapshot() (provider.go:559), which strips conn and returns a copy; there is no inverse load path. main.go shutdown (158-169) calls stopBackground(), wsServer.DrainAll(), then buyerHTTP/providerHTTP.Shutdown — DrainAll (server.go:1042) closes connections but writes no state. WarmupGateEnabled sets initialState = pool.StateDegraded (not StateReady) at server.go:508-511, so a freshly reconnected provider is non-routable until warmup. The cited history is real: `git show c1cfc97` is titled 'fix(gateway): add ResponseHeaderTimeout to fast-fail buyers during coordinator restart' and its body states 'buyers to hang silently for up to 15s during coordinator restart + provider warmup ... returning 503 to buyers within 10s.' Severity high upheld: this is a confirmed total-inference-outage-on-restart SPOF; the only thing keeping it from critical is that money state (ledger/request_log) IS durable, so it is an availability cliff, not a money-loss event.

architecture.title: One SQLite money DB opened by two separate *sql.DB pools with no connection cap; PRAGMAs not pool-wide
architecture.lines: main.go:46-67 (auth.OpenStore + requestlog.OpenStore same DBPath; billing+admission reuse reqLogStore.DB()), requestlog/store.go:50-63, auth/tokens.go:46-71
architecture.description: cfg.Storage.DBPath is opened twice as independent connection pools: auth.OpenStore (main.go:46) and requestlog.OpenStore (main.go:52). Billing (main.go:63) and admission (main.go:58) reuse reqLogStore.DB(). None call SetMaxOpenConns(1)/SetMaxIdleConns. busy_timeout=5000 is issued as a single ExecContext (store.go:60, tokens.go:69) which under database/sql applies only to whichever pooled connection executed it; new pool connections created later via the driver's newConn do NOT inherit it. journal_mode=WAL is a persistent file attribute and survives.
architecture.impact: Under concurrent load two writers can collide; connections lacking the inherited busy_timeout return SQLITE_BUSY immediately instead of waiting, so the billing hot-path insert fails and falls back to WriteRequestLogWithIdentity, dropping the provider credit until nightly reconcile re-derives it.
architecture.recommendation: Open the money DB once and share one *sql.DB; set SetMaxOpenConns(1) for the writer DB OR apply busy_timeout/journal_mode via the driver DSN (_pragma=busy_timeout(5000)) / a RegisterConnectionHook so every pooled connection inherits them. Alarm the hot-path-fallback rate.
architecture.evidence: CORE TECHNICAL CLAIM CONFIRMED, SEVERITY OVERSTATED. Two independent sql.Open calls on the same path are real: auth/tokens.go:46 and requestlog/store.go:50. Repo-wide grep confirms SetMaxOpenConns/SetMaxIdleConns appear NOWHERE in production code. The busy_timeout-not-inherited claim is verified against the actual driver source (modernc.org/sqlite v1.33.0, go.mod:11): newConn (sqlite.go:818-862) only applies pragmas from DSN _pragma= query params via applyQueryParams (sqlite.go:881-893); the DSN here is the bare path with no query string, and the driver sets NO default busy_timeout. So `PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000` run once via s.db.ExecContext binds only to the single connection that executed it; connections the pool spawns later under contention have busy_timeout=0 and return SQLITE_BUSY immediately. WriteHotPath uses BEGIN IMMEDIATE (hotpath.go:37) which grabs the write lock eagerly, and buyer/server.go:887-896 has NO retry — first error falls straight through to WriteRequestLogWithIdentity. HOWEVER, three real mitigations lower this below 'high': (1) the driver opens with SQLITE_OPEN_FULLMUTEX (sqlite.go:843) and journal_mode=WAL is verified-enforced (billing/store.go:37-41 fails startup if mode != WAL), so readers never block writers and only writer-vs-writer collisions matter; (2) database/sql defaults MaxIdleConns=2, so the pragma-carrying connection is pooled and reused for the common serial-write case — the deficiency only bites the marginal extra connection opened under simultaneous writes; (3) all three money writers (billing hot-path, admission persist, request_log) share the SAME reqLogStore.DB() pool and SQLite serializes them on one file anyway, while the genuinely-separate auth pool is overwhelmingly read/token-validation traffic that rarely write-collides with the money path. The failure is real and worth fixing (a single capped pool or DSN pragma is a one-line fix) but the practical collision window is narrow and fails closed (under-credit recovered by reconcile, never double-credit), so medium.

architecture.title: TOCTOU race in provisional admission can exceed ProvisionalPoolMax
architecture.lines: server.go:467 + server.go:690-698 (connectedProvisional computed before lock), admission.go:78-95
architecture.description: prepareProviderAdmission calls s.connectedProvisional() (server.go:467) which snapshots the pool and counts provisional providers OUTSIDE the admission mutex (server.go:690-698), then passes that stale count into AdmissionManager.Admit, which only takes its lock at admission.go:82. Two providers connecting concurrently can both read connectedProvisional == max-1, both pass the >= ProvisionalPoolMax check (admission.go:93), and both are admitted. The count is derived from the pool registry, which is only updated later in registerProviderSession (server.go:599-608), widening the window.
architecture.impact: The provisional pool cap is a soft limit under concurrency; an attacker spraying provisional connections can overshoot ProvisionalPoolMax. Bounded overshoot, not unbounded, since rate-limit and per-provider records still apply.
architecture.recommendation: Make the pool-capacity check authoritative inside the admission critical section: track the live provisional count inside AdmissionManager under its mutex, or reserve a provisional slot atomically and release it on handleDisconnect.
architecture.evidence: RACE CONFIRMED, SEVERITY OVERSTATED. The lock-ordering flaw is exactly as described: connectedProvisional() (server.go:690-698) iterates s.pool.Snapshot() — Snapshot() takes pool.mu.RLock and RELEASES it before returning (provider.go:559-568), so the returned count is a point-in-time value with no lock held thereafter. That count is computed at the call site server.go:467 and only THEN passed by value into s.admission.Admit(...), whose own mutex (admission.go:82-83) is acquired afterward; the >= ProvisionalPoolMax comparison at admission.go:93 reads the stale argument, not live state. registerProviderSession (called at server.go:268/400, after prepareProviderAdmission returns) is what inserts the provider into the pool via s.pool.Register (server.go:599-600), so the new provider is invisible to a concurrent connectedProvisional() for the whole admission window — the window is genuinely wide. So the TOCTOU is real and the cap is soft. BUT severity is low, not medium: (1) the overshoot is bounded by the number of providers admitted within the race window, not unbounded; (2) the independent per-hour admission rate-limit still applies inside the same locked section (admission.go:96-98: len(admissions) >= ProvisionalAdmissionRatePerHour), capping sustained spray; (3) the consequence is purely resource/routing-weight over-allocation of UNTRUSTED provisional Macs that still pass through Tier2 verification and per-provider quota before serving any buyer traffic — there is no money or correctness impact, only a slightly-exceeded soft capacity knob. Confirmed as a real concurrency bug but the blast radius justifies low.

architecture.title: Admission state persisted as a full JSON blob to SQLite synchronously under a global mutex on every reserved request
architecture.lines: admission.go:133-152 (TryReserveRequest -> persistLocked while holding a.mu), admission.go:209-221, admission_store.go:61-75
architecture.description: TryReserveRequest holds a.mu (admission.go:137) and calls persistLocked (admission.go:150) inside the critical section. persistLocked marshals the ENTIRE admission state — all admissions, all ProvisionalRecords, all rejected, and all per-provider RequestWindows — to JSON and upserts the single-row admission_state table (admission_store.go:66-74) on every provisional request reservation, refund, admit, and promote, synchronously, to the shared money DB while the admission mutex is held.
architecture.impact: Every provisional inference request serializes on one mutex AND one SQLite write of an O(total-provisional-history) JSON blob. As provisional providers and request volume grow, lock hold time and write time grow, throttling all admission/quota decisions and adding write contention to the same DB the billing hot-path uses (compounding finding #2).
architecture.recommendation: Move persistence off the critical section: snapshot under the lock, release, then write; or debounce/batch persistence via a dirty flag flushed by a background ticker. Store per-provider request windows in a normalized table with incremental updates rather than rewriting the whole state blob.
architecture.evidence: CONFIRMED as described. TryReserveRequest acquires a.mu (admission.go:137-138, defer Unlock) and unconditionally calls a.persistLocked() at admission.go:150 BEFORE returning — inside the held lock. persistLocked (admission.go:209-221) builds an AdmissionState by deep-cloning admissions + ALL records (cloneAdmissionRecords) + ALL rejected + ALL requestWindows (cloneTimeWindows, admission.go:249-255) and calls store.SaveAdmissionState synchronously. SQLiteAdmissionStore.SaveAdmissionState (admission_store.go:61-75) json.Marshals the entire state and does a single-row upsert (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(key) DO UPDATE) keyed on the constant 'provisional_admission' — so the whole blob is rewritten every call. This identical pattern repeats in RefundRequest (admission.go:167), Admit (admission.go:113), Promote (admission.go:179), and Reject (admission.go:187), all under a.mu. The store is reqLogStore.DB() (main.go:58), the same pool as the billing hot-path, so this genuinely compounds finding #2's write contention. The clone-and-marshal cost is O(records + sum of all request windows), which grows with provisional-provider count and per-provider hourly request volume. Note keepAfter prunes windows to the last hour (admission.go:140) so the blob does not grow unbounded forever, but it is still O(active-provisional-fleet x requests/hour) rewritten on every single reservation while the global admission mutex is held — a real latency/throughput bottleneck on the buyer hot path. Medium upheld.

architecture.title: Provisional request-quota reservations leak (consumed without refund) on timeout/failed relay outcomes
architecture.description: forwardWS reserves a provisional quota slot via TryReserveRequest (server.go:1285) but refunds it only on a narrow set of outcomes: pre-relay error (server.go:1298-1300), streaming wsForwardProviderDisconnected (server.go:1326-1328), and non-streaming wsForwardQueueFull or wsForwardProviderDisconnected (server.go:1332-1334). Outcomes where the relay was established but the request did not successfully serve — wsForwardTimedOut, wsForwardFailed (AEAD/tier2 encoding), and wsForwardCancelled (buyer disconnect) — consume the hourly quota slot permanently.
architecture.impact: A provisional provider that times out, fails Tier2 checks, or whose buyer disconnects has its hourly request quota decremented for a request it never billably served. Accounting fails closed (over-counts usage), so it cannot exceed quota; harm is provisional providers throttled below ProvisionalQuotaPerHour after transient failures.
architecture.recommendation: Decide intended semantics explicitly: if quota should count only successfully-served requests, refund on all non-complete terminal results (timeout, failed, cancelled, unavailable) the same way disconnect/queue-full are; if it counts all attempts, document that and drop the partial refunds. Centralize the reserve/refund decision keyed off the final wsForwardResult.
architecture.evidence: CONFIRMED precisely. TryReserveRequest at server.go:1285 sets reserved = provider.Tier == TierProvisional (1289). The refund call sites are exactly the three the finding names: pre-relay err branch (1298-1300), streaming `if reserved && result == wsForwardProviderDisconnected` (1326-1328), and non-streaming `if reserved && (result == wsForwardQueueFull || result == wsForwardProviderDisconnected)` (1332-1334). The full wsForwardResult enum is at server.go:122-129. I traced the terminal returns: wsForwardTimedOut is returned at server.go:1409 (504, buyer should retry), wsForwardCancelled at 1412 (buyer disconnected), and wsForwardFailed at 1384/1393/1418/1421 (AEAD-decrypt-failed, invalid Tier2 encoding, provider-failed). NONE of these three results appears in any refund condition, so the reserved quota slot stays consumed. The leak is real and direction-correct: it fails closed (decrements quota for unserved requests, never the reverse), so it cannot be abused to exceed quota — the only harm is a provisional provider being under-served after transient timeouts/failures. The inconsistency that wsForwardProviderDisconnected and wsForwardQueueFull ARE refunded while the equally-no-fault wsForwardTimedOut is NOT confirms this is an oversight rather than deliberate count-all-attempts policy. Low upheld.

architecture.title: Billing hot-path failure silently degrades to request-log-only, deferring provider credit to the reconcile job
architecture.lines: buyer/server.go:887-897 (WriteHotPath then WriteRequestLogWithIdentity fallback), hotpath.go:31-143, recovery.go:282-310 (nightly reconcile re-derives)
architecture.description: On the money path, if WriteHotPath fails (e.g. SQLITE_BUSY per finding #2, or any tx error), the code logs a warning and falls back to WriteRequestLogWithIdentity (server.go:888-896), which writes the request_log row + identity snapshot but NOT the ledger_request_credits/operator_credits rows. Provider credit then exists only implicitly in request_log until StartNightlyReconcile/StartStartupScan re-derives it via RecoverLedger. Real-money credit creation is best-effort on the hot path; the system can run up to ~24h under-credited, recovered only if request_log row, identity snapshot, and a matching config snapshot all survive and resolve unambiguously — ambiguous/identity-missing rows are quarantined instead.
architecture.impact: Under sustained DB contention provider credits are not created in real time; they depend on the reconcile job succeeding and on rows not being quarantined for ambiguous_attempt_n / missing_provider_identity / missing_config_snapshot. A failed reconcile run records a failed status but does not retry until the next cycle; quarantined rows leave providers unpaid until manual intervention. The integrity model is eventually-consistent, not transactional, for the provider's share.
architecture.recommendation: Alarm on the hot-path fallback rate and on reconciliation runs with status='failed' or non-zero orphan/quarantine counts. Consider retrying WriteHotPath with backoff before falling back. Ensure the reconcile job retries failed runs rather than waiting a full cycle. Fixing finding #2 removes the most common trigger.
architecture.evidence: CONFIRMED end-to-end. buyer/server.go:887-896: WriteHotPath error -> Warn log -> WriteRequestLogWithIdentity fallback with NO retry/backoff between them (grep for retry/backoff in hotpath.go and the billing call site found none). WriteRequestLogWithIdentity (hotpath.go:145-172) inserts only the request_log row + ledger_provider_identity_snapshots — it never calls insertRequestCreditTx/insertOperatorCreditTx, so ledger_request_credits/operator_credits are genuinely absent, exactly as claimed. Recovery is the only backstop: StartNightlyReconcile (recovery.go:288-310) fires once at the next midnight UTC (next = time.Date(...Day()+1...), line 293), and crucially DISCARDS the RecoverLedger error with `_ =` (line 306) — a failed nightly run is not retried until the following midnight, ~24h later, confirming the no-retry-until-next-cycle claim. RecoverLedger's deferred failure handler writes a status='failed' run row (recovery.go:25-46) but performs no recovery. The quarantine paths are all real: missing_provider_identity / ambiguous_attempt_n (recovery.go:142-150), missing_config_snapshot (152-171), and ambiguous_attempt_n for attemptN>1 (201-219, 233-239) — quarantined rows are NOT credited. StartupScan (recovery.go:282-285) bounds its window to StartupReconcileWindowHours, so rows older than the window/grace are not re-scanned, confirming the survival caveat. The system genuinely creates provider credit best-effort on the hot path with an eventually-consistent (and silently-failable) safety net. The author correctly frames this as by-design-but-risky; the medium rating is justified because under-crediting is recoverable in the common case yet has real silent-failure and quarantine-stranding modes with no alarming. Medium upheld.

architecture.title: Multi-coordinator failover config is declared and validated but never used; coordinator is a hard SPOF
architecture.description: Config defines a full Coordinators[] list with Name/BaseURL/Weight/Enabled (config.go:46-51) and Validate() enforces at least one target and weight>0 per target (config.go:266-279), implying weighted routing/failover. But the only runtime consumer, coordinatorBuyerURL() (server.go:1736-1743), iterates the slice and returns the FIRST target with Enabled==true, then stops. Weight is never read; there is no health probe, no rotation, no fallback to the next enabled target on error. Every buyer-facing call (handleModels server.go:417, handleChatCompletions server.go:1341) targets that single URL. statusFromPoolz/sticky/routing-metadata calls (server.go:516, 1181, 1709) don't even use the list -- they hardwire cfg.Coordinator.OperatorURL/BuyerURL.
architecture.impact: The coordinator is an unmitigated single point of failure for all inference and money flow. The configuration surface advertises HA/failover that does not exist, so an operator who lists two coordinators believes they have redundancy but a primary outage takes the whole marketplace down. When the single coordinator is unreachable the gateway returns 503 coordinator_unavailable for 100% of paid traffic.
architecture.recommendation: Either (a) implement real failover in coordinatorBuyerURL(): iterate enabled targets weighted by Weight, track per-target health from the existing poolz probe, and retry the next target on a connection-level error/5xx with an empty pool; or (b) if single-coordinator is intentional for this phase, delete the Coordinators[]/Weight surface and the validation that implies failover, leaving only Coordinator.BuyerURL, so the config does not promise capability the code lacks.
architecture.evidence: Confirmed by reading the actual code. coordinatorBuyerURL() (server.go:1736-1743) is a plain `for _, target := range s.cfg.Coordinators { if target.Enabled { return target.BaseURL } } return s.cfg.Coordinator.BuyerURL` — returns the first enabled target, no weighting, no health, no fallback. A repo-wide grep for `Weight` outside test files matches ONLY config.go (struct field line 49, default line 146, validation line 276); Weight is never read by any router/server code. The only call sites of coordinatorBuyerURL() are the two buyer-facing endpoints: server.go:417 (handleModels -> /v1/models) and server.go:1341 (handleChatCompletions -> /v1/chat/completions). There is no retry wrapper on s.client.Do for coordinator calls — the only `retry` matches in server.go are an unrelated `X-MacProvider-Retry` header passthrough (2213-2214) and a user-facing error string (183). statusFromPoolz (1709), routing metadata (1181), and sticky purge (516) all hardwire s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorURL, bypassing the list entirely. Validate() at config.go:266-279 does enforce >=1 target and Weight>0 per target, advertising a failover capability the code does not implement.
