The SPOF and the misleading config surface are both real as described.

architecture.title: Single shared operator key spans two trust boundaries (gateway->coordinator client auth and operator->gateway admin auth)
architecture.description: cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey is overloaded as the credential for two unrelated trust relationships. As a CLIENT credential it is sent on outbound gateway->coordinator requests: poolz (server.go:1713), routing metadata (server.go:1185), sticky purge (server.go:522), and sticky-affinity forwarding (server.go:1358). As a SERVER credential it is the exact secret an operator must present in the Authorization header to invoke the gateway's own privileged endpoints -- operatorAuthorized() (server.go:1932-1938) and shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit() (server.go:1942) guard /admin/kill-switch, /admin/capacity-signal, /admin/feedback-summary, and the explorer with `Authorization == "Bearer "+OperatorKey`. So anyone/anything holding the gateway's outbound coordinator credential automatically also holds full operator/admin authority over the gateway (toggle the global kill switch that pauses all paid traffic, drive capacity tiers, read buyer explorer data).
architecture.impact: Compromise or leak of the single operator key from any of the four outbound call sites, the coordinator side, the env file, or a captured request grants the holder the ability to pause the entire public API (denial of revenue), manipulate capacity tiering, and read buyer/session explorer data. The blast radius of one secret is the union of two trust domains that should be isolated, and the key cannot be rotated on one side without breaking the other.
architecture.recommendation: Split the credential: keep Coordinator.OperatorKey strictly as the outbound client token to the coordinator, and introduce a separate Admin.OperatorKey (distinct secret, distinct env var) for operatorAuthorized()/shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit(). This isolates blast radius and allows independent rotation. Defense-in-depth already 404s /admin/ at nginx (nginx-api...conf:106-109), but the application-level coupling remains the architectural risk.
architecture.evidence: The credential overloading is real and confirmed. All four outbound call sites send `s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey` as a Bearer client credential: sticky purge (server.go:522), routing metadata (server.go:1185), sticky-affinity forwarding (server.go:1358), poolz (server.go:1713). The same secret is the SERVER admin credential: operatorAuthorized() (server.go:1933) and shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit() (server.go:1942) both compare `r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey`. So a single secret does span both trust boundaries — the architectural coupling is exactly as described. Downgraded from high to medium because the realistic blast radius is narrower than stated: (1) all four outbound uses go to the coordinator on loopback only — coordinator BaseURL/OperatorURL default to http://127.0.0.1:8443/8444 (config.go:149) and systemd places gateway and coordinator on the same host reachable on loopback (macprovider-gateway.service:4,15-16), so the key is not transmitted over an untrusted network where it could be captured; (2) the admin server endpoints are 404'd at nginx before reaching the app (nginx-api.streamvc.live.conf:106-109), and publicPaused() also exempts /admin/ paths, so an external attacker cannot present the key to the admin surface without first breaching the host. The coupling/rotation problem and same-host co-location risk are genuine, but "anyone holding the outbound credential gets admin" overstates external exploitability given both sides live behind the loopback boundary. Worth fixing for blast-radius isolation and independent rotation, but medium not high.

architecture.title: SQLite with MaxOpenConns=1 plus per-process in-memory mutable control state pins the gateway to a single non-replicable instance
architecture.description: The persistence layer is SQLite opened with SetMaxOpenConns(1)/SetMaxIdleConns(1) and busy_timeout=5000 (store.go:37-39), so all writes (every ReserveQuota/Settle/Refund/AcquireConcurrency runs BEGIN IMMEDIATE on the single connection, store.go:848-858) are globally serialized through one DB handle. On top of that, two pieces of money-relevant control state are cached in process memory and only loaded once at boot: KillSwitch (loadRuntimeKillSwitch at server.go:117, read via publicPaused/demoPaused server.go:1947-1962 under s.mu) and capacity tier is read live but the kill-switch flips are written to both memory and DB (setAllPublicPaused server.go:1981-2000). Because the DB is a local file and the kill-switch lives in per-process memory, you cannot run two gateway instances behind a load balancer: they would have divergent kill-switch state and contend on a file-locked DB. The systemd unit and nginx config confirm the single-host loopback deployment (macprovider-gateway.service:14-16, nginx...conf:60).
architecture.impact: No horizontal scale path and no hot-standby: the single gateway process is a SPOF for buyer auth, quota accounting, and the kill switch. Under write-heavy bursts all token reservations serialize on one SQLite connection (throughput ceiling); a 5s busy_timeout breach surfaces as 500 quota_reservation_failed. A second instance started for failover would silently diverge on kill-switch state (one could keep serving paused traffic) and risk SQLite lock contention. Vertical-only scaling caps the marketplace's request rate.
architecture.recommendation: Document and enforce single-instance as an explicit constraint for this phase (it is currently implicit). For the scale path, plan migration of the money ledger to a networked store (Postgres) so multiple gateway replicas can share state, and move KillSwitch/capacity tier to a short-TTL re-read from the store (or pub/sub invalidation) instead of boot-only in-memory load, so control-plane changes propagate across instances. At minimum add a startup guard/lock file to prevent a second instance from opening the same DB.
architecture.evidence: All structural claims verified. store.go:37-39 sets SetMaxOpenConns(1)/SetMaxIdleConns(1) and PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000 (line 39 also sets WAL + synchronous=NORMAL). beginImmediate (store.go:848-858) issues `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on s.db.Conn(ctx), and SettleReservation/SettleDemoReservation/RefundReservation/AcquireConcurrency all call beginImmediate (store.go:440, 500, 525), so every money write serializes on the single connection. loadRuntimeKillSwitch is invoked exactly once, in the Server constructor (server.go:117), copying DB state into s.cfg.KillSwitch (server.go:130-131); publicPaused/demoPaused (server.go:1947-1962) then read that in-memory cfg under s.mu — confirming boot-only load of kill-switch state. setAllPublicPaused (server.go:1981-2000) writes the flip to both memory (line 1984) and DB (SetKillSwitch line 1989), so a second instance would not see the change in its boot-loaded memory copy = divergence. The finding's own nuance that capacity tier is read LIVE (not cached) is also correct: GetCapacityTier is called per-request from the store at server.go:289, 492, 721, 743, 1971, never cached at boot. Single-host loopback deployment confirmed: systemd binds the gateway as a single simple service on the host (macprovider-gateway.service:8-16) and nginx proxies to 127.0.0.1:9443 (nginx-api.streamvc.live.conf:60). Severity medium is appropriate — this is a forward-looking scale/HA constraint, not an exploitable bug, and is partly inherent to the documented single-host Pearl VPS phase.

architecture.title: Settlement and refund DB writes detach from the request context (context.Background), losing cancellation/timeout bounds on the money path
architecture.description: Every ledger-mutating call on the chat path -- RefundReservation, ReleaseConcurrency, SettleReservation, SettleDemoReservation -- is invoked with context.Background() rather than the request context. This is a deliberate correctness choice (the buyer may have disconnected and you still must settle/refund the money record), and it is paired with an idempotent state machine: SettleReservation/RefundReservation both gate on status='active' (store.go:411-413, 509) so a double-settle or settle-after-refund is a safe no-op. The architectural risk is that these unbounded background writes contend for the single SQLite connection (store.go:37) with no deadline. If the DB is slow/locked, a settle started with context.Background() can block up to busy_timeout (5s) per attempt while holding the one connection, with no upstream cancellation, and there is no retry/dead-letter if SettleReservation ultimately errors -- the error is discarded (`_ =` at server.go:1427, 1465, 1530, 1609). A dropped settlement leaves the reservation 'active' until the reaper expires it (settled_tokens=0), so the buyer is under-billed for consumed tokens.
architecture.impact: Under DB contention, money-settling writes can pile up on the single serialized connection unbounded by any request deadline, amplifying tail latency for concurrent reservers. Discarded settle errors silently under-bill: a request that consumed tokens but failed to write usage_events is reaped as expired (zero settled tokens), so the account is not charged for real consumed inference -- a slow revenue leak that is invisible without reconciling provider-reported usage against usage_events.
architecture.recommendation: Use a bounded detached context (context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), settleTimeout)) for settle/refund so a stuck write cannot hold the single connection indefinitely. Add at least metrics/alerting on settle failures (the `_ =`-discarded errors at server.go:1427/1465/1530/1609) and consider a small persistent retry queue or a reconciliation job that compares provider-reported usage to settled usage_events, so dropped settlements are detected rather than silently reaped to zero.
architecture.evidence: The code facts are accurate but the impact is over-stated, so downgrade medium->low. Confirmed: settleRequest routes to SettleReservation/SettleDemoReservation with context.Background() (server.go:1605, 1609); RefundReservation/ReleaseConcurrency are also called with context.Background() throughout the chat path (verified at 1292, 1307, 1323, 1327, 1335, 1343, 1366, 1383, 1392, 1441, 1534). The detach is indeed deliberate-correctness paired with an idempotent state machine: SettleReservation gates on `if status != "active"` (store.go:411-413), RefundReservation uses `WHERE ... AND status = 'active'` (store.go:509), so double-settle/settle-after-refund is a safe no-op — exactly as the finding itself acknowledges. The discarded errors are real: every settleRequest call site uses `_ =` (e.g. server.go:1427 `_ = s.settleRequest(...,"ok")`, 1465, 1530, and settleRequest's own return at 1609 is the discarded one). Why low not medium: (1) the unbounded-context concern is bounded in practice — busy_timeout=5000 (store.go:39) caps each blocked write at ~5s, and the upstream coordinator call already runs under CoordinatorTimeout (300s) so the connection-holding window is small relative to inference time; the finding's own text concedes the 5s cap. (2) The under-billing leak is a slow, bounded revenue concern, not a correctness/security defect, and only triggers on the narrow window where the DB write itself fails AFTER tokens were consumed — most failure paths (no provider, 404, timeout) deliberately refund or settle-prompt-only by design. The recommendations (bounded detached context + settle-failure metrics + reconciliation) are sound hardening, but the realistic blast radius is a low-severity observability/revenue-hygiene gap, not a medium architectural risk.

architecture.title: Operator/admin bearer token compared with non-constant-time string equality (timing side channel)
architecture.description: operatorAuthorized() (server.go:1933) and shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit() (server.go:1942) authenticate the privileged operator by `r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey`, a plain Go string == comparison that short-circuits on the first differing byte. By contrast the buyer-facing credentials are handled correctly: API keys are looked up by HMAC hash (keys.go:60-71) and demo tokens use hmac.Equal (demo.go:53). The high-value admin/kill-switch credential is the one path that does NOT use a constant-time compare.
architecture.impact: An attacker able to reach operatorAuthorized() directly (e.g. on the loopback/host network, a co-located service, or if the nginx /admin 404 guard is ever bypassed or the gateway is exposed without nginx) could mount a remote timing attack to recover the operator key byte-by-byte, then pause all public API traffic and manipulate capacity tiers. The network 404 guard reduces but does not eliminate exposure (the same key authorizes loopback-reachable behavior).
architecture.recommendation: Replace both `==` checks with hmac.Equal/subtle.ConstantTimeCompare over the presented bearer token vs the configured key (mirroring demo.go:53). Combine with the credential-split recommendation above so the admin key is also a separate secret.
architecture.evidence: Confirmed as a real-but-low finding. operatorAuthorized() (server.go:1933) and shouldPersistInternalHeaderAudit() (server.go:1942) both use Go's `==` string comparison against `"Bearer "+s.cfg.Coordinator.OperatorKey`, which is not constant-time. The contrast is accurate: demo.go:53 uses `hmac.Equal(expected, got)` for demo tokens, and keys.go:60 (Validate -> ValidateAPIKeyHash with m.Hash, an HMAC-SHA256 at keys.go:63-71) does a hashed DB lookup rather than a raw string compare. So the admin path is genuinely the only credential check using a timing-variable `==`. Severity low is correct and unchanged: practical exploitation requires (a) reaching operatorAuthorized() directly, but /admin/ is 404'd at nginx (nginx-api.streamvc.live.conf:106-109) and publicPaused exempts /admin (server.go:1948), so the surface is loopback/co-located-process only; (b) remote timing attacks over a network with HTTP framing and Go scheduler jitter against a high-entropy secret are extremely difficult in practice. Real defect, trivially fixable with subtle.ConstantTimeCompare, but low severity given the loopback-only reachability.

architecture.title: Service-to-service contract between gateway and coordinator is implicit and unversioned (status-code and header coupling)
architecture.description: The gateway's money and routing decisions are tightly coupled to undocumented coordinator response conventions with no negotiated version. Billing branches on exact coordinator HTTP status codes -- 503 means 'no provider' (refund), 504 means provider_timeout (settle prompt only), 404 means structural rejection / no charge (server.go:1387-1419, 1445-1467). Token accounting trusts an out-of-band header X-MacProvider-Completion-Tokens (completionFromHeader server.go:2190-2200) and an in-body `usage` object. Tier-2 policy errors are detected by string-matching OpenAI error codes (coordinatorTier2PolicyError server.go:1541-1551). Pool aggregation depends on the exact /poolz JSON shape and state string vocabulary ('ready'/'degraded'/'busy'/'draining', server.go:1758-1796). None of these is guarded by a version header or contract handshake.
architecture.impact: Any coordinator-side change to a status-code meaning, the completion-tokens header name, the poolz state vocabulary, or a Tier-2 error code silently changes gateway billing or availability behavior with no compile-time or runtime signal. E.g. if the coordinator starts returning 404 for a transient no-provider case, the gateway refunds and serves a 404 'model_not_found' to a paying buyer; if the completion-tokens header is renamed, error-path requests settle at 0 completion tokens (under-billing). The coupling makes the two services impossible to deploy/upgrade independently without lockstep coordination.
architecture.recommendation: Introduce an explicit, versioned internal contract: a coordinator API version header the gateway asserts, a documented status-code/header/error-code matrix, and a contract test (the SPEC corpus is the natural home). At minimum, centralize the magic status codes, header names, and error-code strings into one documented constants block so the implicit contract is discoverable and a coordinator change forces a visible gateway diff.
architecture.evidence: Confirmed; all cited couplings exist in code. Status-code branching: forwardNonStreamingChat (server.go:1387-1419) branches on http.StatusServiceUnavailable->refund (1387-1394), http.StatusGatewayTimeout->settle prompt only (1396-1400), http.StatusNotFound->pass-through no charge (1406-1409); forwardStreamingChat mirrors it (1435-1467). Tier-2 policy detection is exact string-matching of OpenAI error codes: coordinatorTier2PolicyError (server.go:1541-1551) switches on literal codes 'tier2_hash_verified_required'/'tier2_hash_mismatch'/'tier2_encrypted_leg_required'/'tier2_attestation_required'/'tier2_hard_pin_predicate_failed' extracted via openAIErrorCode (1553-1563). completionFromHeader (server.go:2190-2200) reads the literal out-of-band header `X-MacProvider-Completion-Tokens` and returns 0 if absent/unparseable — so a rename silently under-bills error-path requests, exactly as described. Pool aggregation (aggregateStatus, server.go:1758-1796) switches on the literal state vocabulary 'ready'/'degraded'/'busy'/'draining' with a default->Unavailable bucket. None of these paths assert a coordinator API version header or perform a contract handshake (no version check exists anywhere in the forward path). Severity low is appropriate: this is a maintainability/operational-coupling risk (silent behavior change on uncoordinated coordinator deploys), not an exploitable vulnerability, and is mitigated in practice by the same-repo lockstep deployment of gateway+coordinator. Recommendation to centralize the magic codes/headers and add a version header + contract test is sound.

architecture.title: Coordinator liveness relies on a 30s app heartbeat with no WS ping/pong, no TCP keepalive, and no sleep-prevention assertion
architecture.description: The only liveness signal sent to the trusted coordinator is the application-level `heartbeat` frame, scheduled by `startHeartbeat` (lines 399-408) at an interval the coordinator dictates, defaulting to 30s when `heartbeat_interval_s` is absent (line 380: `?? 30`). The WebSocket is created with `URLSession.shared` defaults (line 46) — there is no `sendPing`/pong, no `URLSessionConfiguration` ping interval, and no TCP `SO_KEEPALIVE`. There is also no `IOPMAssertion`/`caffeinate`/`NSProcessInfo.beginActivity` no-sleep assertion anywhere in the binary. When a contributor Mac idles into sleep, the heartbeat Task is suspended with the process; the coordinator's liveness timer (documented historical 35s kill) fires and tears the session down. The reconnect loop only re-establishes after the Mac wakes. This is precisely the provider-disconnect pattern in project memory, and the in-binary mitigation (the noted 'optional no-sleep assertion') was never added.
architecture.impact: Idle providers silently drop out of the marketplace and stop earning USDC; buyers see capacity flap. The 30s heartbeat is uncomfortably close to the coordinator's kill threshold even on a healthy machine — a single GC/MLX stall or scheduler hiccup near the 30s boundary can trip an unnecessary disconnect.
architecture.recommendation: Add an IOPMAssertion (kIOPMAssertionTypePreventUserIdleSystemSleep) or NSProcessInfo.beginActivity(.idleSystemSleepDisabled) for the lifetime of the serve process so a registered provider does not sleep. Independently, send a sub-interval WebSocket ping (e.g. heartbeat_interval/2) or enable TCP keepalive on the WS socket so transport-level liveness does not depend solely on the app heartbeat, and ensure the heartbeat interval is comfortably below the coordinator kill threshold.
architecture.evidence: Every cited mechanism is verifiably absent. CoordinatorClient.swift:380 reads `let interval = max(Self.intValue(payload["heartbeat_interval_s"]) ?? 30, 1)` — 30s default confirmed. Lines 399-408 `startHeartbeat` is a plain `Task` that `Task.sleep`s for `intervalSeconds` then calls `sendHeartbeat()` — a process suspended by system sleep stops this loop, exactly as described. Line 46 creates the socket via `URLSession.shared.webSocketTask(with:)` with no configuration object. Repo-wide grep across Sources/ returned 0 files for `IOPMAssertion`, `caffeinate`, `beginActivity`, `idleSystemSleep`, `kIOPM` (sleep prevention absent), 0 files for `sendPing`/`pingInterval`/`pong` (no WS ping/pong), and 0 files for `SO_KEEPALIVE`/`keepAlive`/`tcpKeepalive` (no TCP keepalive). The only keepalive references in the codebase are debug-logging helpers (`keepaliveDebug`, line 668). The launchd plist (dist/launchd-plist-template.plist) likewise has no sleep-prevention key. Claim is accurate on all three sub-points and the sleep-while-suspended causal chain is sound; high severity retained given it reproduces a known production disconnect class on the money-moving leg.

architecture.title: Self-update boots out and replaces the live launchd job in-process with no rollback if re-bootstrap fails
architecture.description: `applyValidatedUpdate` (175-191) drains by running `launchctl bootout` on `live.streamvc.macprovider` (drainLaunchdIfInstalled, 193-201), then atomically renames the new binary over the current one (replaceCurrentBinary, 159-173), then `restartLaunchdIfInstalled` does another `bootout` followed by `bootstrap` (203-212). When `update` is run by the launchd-managed serve process itself, the `bootout` sends SIGTERM to that very process; its handler (MacProviderCLI.swift:172-183) calls `drainAndExit` -> `Darwin.exit(0)`. Because the plist uses `KeepAlive { SuccessfulExit: false }` (launchd-plist-template.plist:25-29), a clean exit(0) means launchd will NOT auto-restart — recovery depends entirely on the subsequent explicit `bootstrap` (line 211) succeeding. If the process is killed by exit before reaching `bootstrap`, or `bootstrap` fails (stale plist, GUI domain not loaded, throttle), the provider is left permanently offline. There is no post-replace health gate and no rollback to the prior binary on failed restart.
architecture.impact: A self-update on a remote contributor Mac can brick the provider with no operator present: binary replaced, job booted out, re-bootstrap fails or never runs, provider stays down until manual intervention.
architecture.recommendation: Run the update from a detached helper process (not the launchd-managed serve process) so the SIGTERM-driven exit cannot abort the replace/bootstrap sequence. Keep the previous binary staged and, after bootstrap, poll the local /v1/status (LocalStatusClient already exists) to confirm the new binary came up healthy; on failure, rename the old binary back and re-bootstrap. Make `restartLaunchdIfInstalled` failures fatal-and-rolled-back rather than best-effort.
architecture.evidence: The mechanism is real and accurately described: applyValidatedUpdate (SelfUpdate.swift:175-191) calls drain->replace->restart in that order; drainLaunchdIfInstalled (193-201) runs `bootout` with allowFailure:true; replaceCurrentBinary (159-173) does an atomic rename over Bundle.main.executableURL; restartLaunchdIfInstalled (203-212) does `bootout` (allowFailure:true) then `bootstrap` (NOT allowFailure, so a bootstrap failure throws). Plist confirmed at dist/launchd-plist-template.plist:25-29 `KeepAlive{SuccessfulExit:false}` plus `ThrottleInterval=10` (line 48), so a clean exit(0) does not trigger relaunch and bootstrap is the only recovery path. SIGTERM handler confirmed: MacProviderCLI.swift:172-183 installs a SIGTERM source calling `drainAndExit`, and CoordinatorClient.swift:454-468 `drainAndExit` ends in `Darwin.exit(exitCode)` (default 0). LocalStatusClient exists (SelfUpdate.swift:390) but grep confirms it is referenced only by StatusCommand (MacProviderCLI.swift:115), never in the update path — so 'no post-replace health gate / no rollback' is accurate. HOWEVER three mitigations the finding understates lower the realistic blast radius from high to medium: (1) update runs through a self-test gate `runProcess(newBinary.path, arguments: ["self-test"])` at SelfUpdate.swift:92 before any replace, so a structurally-broken binary cannot reach the live-job swap; (2) the in-process SIGTERM->exit race is the finding's own worst case, but the more common invocation is an operator running `macprovider-cli update` from a separate shell (UpdateCommand, MacProviderCLI.swift:152-170), which is NOT the launchd-managed process and so does not self-SIGTERM — the bricking race only applies when update is somehow triggered from within the serve process, which no code path in this binary does (there is no auto-update timer, per finding 3); (3) drainLaunchdIfInstalled/the first bootout in restart are allowFailure:true and bootstrap is throttled (ThrottleInterval=10) rather than permanently blocked. The 'permanently offline until manual intervention' worst case requires bootstrap to hard-fail after the binary is already replaced, which is plausible but not the default path. Real reliability gap (no rollback, best-effort restart, in-process drain), but exploitability/likelihood is lower than 'high' — medium.

architecture.title: auto_update_enabled and warmup_enabled config keys are parsed but never consumed — advertised behavior does not exist
architecture.description: `autoUpdateEnabled` and `warmupEnabled` are declared on AppConfig (Config.swift:26, 34) and populated from YAML/env (lines 174, 180, 197, 204), but grepping the entire macprovider-cli source shows neither is ever read. There is no timer, no launchd periodic job, and no code path that invokes `SelfUpdate.run` automatically — updates only happen when an operator manually runs `macprovider-cli update` (MacProviderCLI.swift:152-170). Likewise no code consumes `warmupEnabled`; warm-up is driven solely by a coordinator `warm_up` message (CoordinatorClient.swift:279-281). The config surface implies a self-maintaining fleet that the binary does not actually implement.
architecture.impact: Operators who set `auto_update_enabled: true` get a false sense of security; the fleet silently stays on whatever binary was last manually installed. Stale binaries mean security fixes and provider-disconnect fixes do not propagate.
architecture.recommendation: Either wire `auto_update_enabled` to a periodic in-process check that calls the (hardened) self-update path with operator-controlled opt-in, or remove the dead config keys and document that updates are manual/coordinator-driven so the config contract does not over-promise. Same for `warmup_enabled`.
architecture.evidence: The dead-config claim is factually correct. Grep for `autoUpdateEnabled`/`auto_update_enabled` across Sources/ returns matches ONLY in Config.swift (declaration line 26, default line 48, YAML assign line 174, env assign line 197) — zero read sites anywhere else. Grep for `warmupEnabled`/`warmup_enabled` returns matches ONLY in Config.swift (line 34, 56, 180, 204) — zero read sites. SelfUpdate.run is invoked only from UpdateCommand.run (MacProviderCLI.swift:168), confirming no automatic/periodic invocation. warm-up handling is indeed coordinator-driven: CoordinatorClient.swift:279-281 handles the `warm_up` message and never consults config.warmupEnabled. So 'parsed but never consumed' is verified. Severity downgraded medium->low because this is a config-contract / documentation defect, not a code-execution vulnerability: there is no incorrect behavior at runtime, only an unimplemented opt-in. The security framing ('false sense of security', 'stale binaries') is a real but indirect operational risk, and notably the config default is `autoUpdateEnabled: nil` (Config.swift:48), so nothing is silently disabled that an operator would expect on by default — the key simply does nothing if set. Low severity is the accurate altitude for an inert/dead config flag.

architecture.title: Inference path does not re-verify model_hash; provider can serve a swapped/poisoned model under an attested session
architecture.description: The model identity is captured once at startup: ModelRuntime computes `modelHash` from the on-disk safetensors manifest at init (ModelRuntime.swift:67, 294-325) and the provider advertises it in hello/auth and the attestation `claimed.model_hash` (Tier2Attestation.swift:154, CoordinatorClient.swift:584/610). But the actual inference path (InferenceRelay.process, 186-208) only validates `request.model == loadedModelID` by string match (ChatCompletionRequest.validateModelMatches) — it never re-checks that the weights still hash to the attested value, and the long-lived MLX ModelContainer is loaded once and reused. On an untrusted contributor Mac, the operator controls the model directory and process; nothing in the binary detects post-attestation weight tampering or a model directory swapped after the hash was measured.
architecture.impact: A malicious provider can pass attestation advertising a clean model_hash, then serve responses from a different/poisoned model for the life of the session. Because the coordinator trusts the attested model_hash, buyers pay for inference from a model that is not the one attested.
architecture.recommendation: Accept that an untrusted-host binary cannot self-attest weight integrity and move the trust to the coordinator: have it periodically challenge the provider to prove the live weights (e.g. signed hash-over-nonce of the loaded artifact) and/or rely on output-sampling verification. At minimum, document explicitly that model_hash is a startup-time claim, not a per-request guarantee, so the coordinator does not over-trust it.
architecture.evidence: The code facts are accurate. ModelRuntime.swift:67 sets `self.modelHash = try? Self.modelWeightArtifactManifestHash(in: directory)` once in init; modelWeightArtifactManifestHash (294-325) hashes the safetensors manifest; the container is loaded once (line 57, `loadContainer`) and reused via `container.perform` in every complete/stream. The inference path InferenceRelay.process (186-189) calls `ChatCompletionRequest.parse` then `request.validateModelMatches(loadedModelID)`, and validateModelMatches (ChatCompletionRequest.swift:101-108) is a pure ASCII case-insensitive STRING compare of model id — no re-hash. modelHash is advertised in hello (CoordinatorClient.swift:610-611), auth initial (584-586) and attestation claimed (Tier2Attestation.swift:154). So the 'startup-time claim, never re-verified per request' description is correct. HOWEVER this is fundamentally a documented trust-model limitation, not a defensible-but-broken control, which is why it is correctly only medium and I downgrade to low: (1) the recommendation itself concedes 'an untrusted-host binary cannot self-attest weight integrity' — any in-binary re-hash on a host the operator controls is trivially bypassable (the operator can patch the hashing too), so the absent check would provide near-zero security even if present; the real fix lives coordinator-side, which is out of this component's scope. (2) Once the model is loaded into the MLX container, the weights are in process memory; swapping files on disk after load does not change what is being served unless the process reloads — so the concrete 'swap the directory mid-session' vector does not actually change served outputs without a restart (which re-runs init and re-measures the hash). The genuine residual risk is a provider that ships a poisoned model from the start while presenting a forged/clean model_hash, but that is a trust-anchor problem the binary structurally cannot solve and the finding's own recommendation acknowledges. Net: real architectural note worth documenting, low security severity within this component.

architecture.title: Tier-2 AEAD nonce safety depends on a per-session counter that silently wraps and is reset on every reconnect
architecture.description: AES-GCM nonces are built as 4-byte session base + 8-byte big-endian per-direction counter (nonce(), 341-349), with `c2pCounter`/`p2cCounter` incrementing per frame (112-123, 133-151). Two structural notes: (1) the counters are plain UInt64 with no overflow guard — at 2^64 frames this would crash/wrap, which is astronomically unlikely but is an unhandled invariant rather than an enforced one; more importantly (2) a fresh Tier2ProviderSession (and thus fresh ECDH keys, fresh derived AEAD keys, and counters reset to 0) is created on every reconnect (CoordinatorClient.swift:162-176). Nonce-reuse safety therefore relies entirely on the per-reconnect key being unique. That holds because each Tier2AuthAttempt generates a new Curve25519 keypair (Tier2ProviderSession.swift:9-13), so the derived keys differ — but this safety property is implicit and undocumented at the call site, making it fragile against a future refactor that reuses a session across reconnects.
architecture.impact: Today the design is safe (new keys per reconnect => counter reset is fine). The risk is latent: any change that caches/reuses a Tier2 session or its keys across reconnects while resetting counters would cause catastrophic AES-GCM nonce reuse.
architecture.recommendation: Add an explicit assertion/comment that the AEAD key MUST be unique per session and counters MUST start at 0 only with a fresh key, and consider a counter ceiling that forces session renegotiation well before 2^64. This pins the invariant so it survives refactors.
architecture.evidence: The finding self-certifies 'Today the design is safe', so this is a latent/maintainability note, not a present vulnerability — info is the correct altitude. The code confirms the design is in fact safe: each connect builds a fresh `Tier2AuthAttempt()` (CoordinatorClient.swift:156) whose init generates a new `Curve25519.KeyAgreement.PrivateKey()` (Tier2ProviderSession.swift:9-13); makeTier2Session (CoordinatorClient.swift:162) derives the session, and the session is reconstructed every connectAndRunTier2 call. The derived keys come from `sharedSecret.hkdfData(...)` over a transcript that includes both ephemeral public keys (Tier2ProviderSession.swift:74-95, 306-314), so the c2p/p2c keys differ per reconnect even though counters reset to 0 (lines 29-30) — no (key, nonce) pair ever repeats. nonce() (341-349) is a correct 4-byte-base || 8-byte-BE-counter construction. The UInt64 overflow concern is purely theoretical: 2^64 frames per single session is unreachable. Additionally there IS already a defensive layer the finding omits: openEnvelope (275-289) enforces `seqValue == expectedSeq` and recomputes/compares the nonce, and seal/open bind seq into the AAD (Tier2FrameAAD.seq), so a counter desync is detected and rejected rather than silently producing a reused nonce. No code today reuses a session across reconnects. Downgraded low->info: valid hardening suggestion (pin the invariant with a comment/assert and a counter ceiling), zero current security impact.

architecture.title: Local HTTP server binds 127.0.0.1 with no auth and shares the single inference gate with coordinator traffic
architecture.description: The local server binds 127.0.0.1 (line 35) and exposes /v1/chat/completions with no authentication (handleChatCompletions, 180-227). Both the loopback HTTP path and the coordinator WS relay path ultimately funnel through the same ModelRuntime, which serializes all generation behind a single-permit AsyncSemaphore (ModelRuntime.swift:31, inferenceGate value:1; maxConcurrency advertised as 1 in MacProviderCLI.swift:67-70). The two ingress paths do not coordinate at the relay level: the InferenceRelay enforces maxActiveRequests=1 (CoordinatorClient.swift:65) for WS, but a local loopback caller bypasses that relay queue entirely and contends for the same gate. Any local process (or anything that reaches loopback) can occupy the single inference slot and starve paid coordinator-routed requests.
architecture.impact: On a shared/multi-user Mac, any unprivileged local process can issue free inference and, more importantly, monopolize the single generation slot, degrading or stalling revenue-generating coordinator traffic. It also means local and remote request accounting (ProviderStatus.beginRequest with vs without requestID) are tracked inconsistently.
architecture.recommendation: Either bind the local server only when explicitly enabled, gate it behind a loopback token, or route all local requests through the same InferenceRelay queue/accounting so coordinator-paid traffic is not starved by unmetered local calls. At minimum document that the loopback endpoint is unauthenticated and shares capacity with paid traffic.
architecture.evidence: All structural claims verified. HTTPServer.swift:35 binds `bootstrap.bind(host: "127.0.0.1", port: config.port)` — loopback only. handleChatCompletions (180-227) parses the body and dispatches to modelRuntime.complete/stream with NO auth/token check anywhere in RouterHandler. ModelRuntime.swift:31 `private let inferenceGate = AsyncSemaphore(value: 1)` and every complete/stream/preflight wraps generation in `inferenceGate.withPermit { ... }` (lines 77, 96, 150) — a single global generation slot shared by ALL callers. The WS relay independently caps concurrency at the relay layer: InferenceRelay enforces `active.count < maxActiveRequests` (InferenceRelay.swift:70) with maxActiveRequests=1 set at CoordinatorClient.swift:65, but the loopback path in HTTPServer never goes through InferenceRelay — it calls modelRuntime directly (HTTPServer.swift:199, 266), so a long local generation holds the gate and any concurrent WS inference blocks on `inferenceGate.withPermit` until released. Accounting inconsistency confirmed: HTTPServer.swift:197 and :239 call `providerStatus.beginRequest()` with no requestID, while InferenceRelay.swift:182 calls `beginRequest(requestID:)`; ProviderStatus.beginRequest (ProviderStatus.swift:130) only inserts into activeRequestIDs when a requestID is supplied, so local requests are counted in requestsInFlight but not in activeRequestIDCount. Severity kept at low: the listener is loopback-bound (not network-exposed), so the attacker must already have local code execution on the Mac, and the 'starvation' is bounded serialization of a single slot rather than data exposure or fund loss. Real defect (unauthenticated loopback endpoint sharing the paid capacity gate + split accounting), correctly rated low.

architecture.title: Reconnect/drain loop has no max-attempt ceiling or surfaced unhealthy state after sustained coordinator loss
architecture.description: runReconnectLoop (93-125) retries forever with exponential backoff capped at 60s, only printing a WARN after 3 failed attempts (118-120). There is no upper bound, no escalation, and crucially the provider's locally reported health (ProviderStatus) is set to coordinatorConnected=false but the `status` remains .ready — so /v1/health and /v1/status keep reporting a healthy provider that is in fact orphaned from the coordinator indefinitely. The CoordinatorDrainComplete grace path (105-114) resets backoff to 1 each cycle, so a coordinator stuck in a drain/restart flap will be hammered at 1s intervals indefinitely.
architecture.impact: An orphaned provider looks healthy to local monitoring while earning nothing, and a flapping coordinator gets a tight-loop reconnect storm from every provider (post-drain backoff resets to 1s), amplifying load during the coordinator's most fragile window (restart). Observability gap delays operator detection of a stuck provider.
architecture.recommendation: Cap or jitter the post-drain reconnect (do not reset backoff to 1s on every drain cycle), and reflect prolonged coordinator loss in the locally reported health/status (e.g. degraded after N minutes disconnected) so monitoring and the operator can detect orphaned providers.
architecture.evidence: Two of three sub-claims are correct; one is overstated. CONFIRMED: runReconnectLoop (93-125) loops `while !Task.isCancelled` with no attempt ceiling; backoff is `min(backoffSeconds * 2, 60)` (line 122) capped at 60s; WARN only after `failedAttempts >= 3` (118-120). CONFIRMED observability gap: cleanupConnection (214-223) calls `setCoordinatorSession(connected: false)` but never changes `status`; ProviderStatus.setCoordinatorSession (ProviderStatus.swift:167-178) only touches coordinator fields, leaving status at .ready, and statusResponse/healthResponse (HTTPServer.swift:347-395) report `coordinator.connected=false` yet top-level `status: ready` — so /v1/health returns HTTP 200 (HTTPServer.swift:160-165 maps .ready->ok) while orphaned. So 'looks healthy locally while orphaned' is accurate. OVERSTATED: the 'hammered at 1s intervals indefinitely' claim. On CoordinatorDrainComplete the loop FIRST sleeps `reconnectGraceNanoseconds` (lines 110-112), which is 10s by default (init default at line 44: `10 * 1_000_000_000`), THEN sets backoff=1. The 1s value only applies to the NEXT connect attempt's failure-sleep, and on a genuine connect-fail flap backoff immediately re-grows 1->2->4->...->60 via the generic catch (115-122). A true 1s tight loop requires the coordinator to keep sending fresh `drain` frames (each gated by the 10s grace), not a connect-fail flap — so the worst realistic cadence is ~once per 10s grace, not 1s. The backoff-reset-on-every-drain is a real inefficiency worth fixing (jitter/no-reset), but the described 'reconnect storm at 1s' is mitigated by the 10s grace the finding omits. Net severity stays low: the observability/health-reporting gap is the substantive issue and is real; the storm impact is smaller than claimed.

architecture.title: Provider self-reported token usage drives real-USDC payout with no independent verification
architecture.description: The provider Mac is explicitly untrusted, yet its self-declared token counts are the sole billing input. In the WS path, tokenPointersFromUsageObject(end.Usage) reads prompt_tokens/completion_tokens straight from the provider's inference_response_end.usage JSON (an untrusted frame). Those values are passed verbatim into ComputeCredits, whose default usage_source is provider_reported, and become provider_credits -> payout. The only guards are range/overflow checks. The coordinator never tokenizes the prompt or counts the streamed output to cross-check. RecoverLedger re-reads the SAME request_log.prompt_tokens/completion_tokens (provider-sourced) and reconcileExistingCreditTx only verifies rate-card arithmetic consistency, so inflated counts reconcile cleanly.
architecture.impact: A malicious or modified provider binary reports inflated completion_tokens on trivially cheap requests and is paid maximum per-request completion credit. This drains operator USDC, and reconciliation/settlement/the delta metric all pass, making the theft invisible to integrity tooling.
architecture.recommendation: Treat provider token reports as untrusted input. (1) Independently count completion tokens server-side (it already buffers full non-streaming output and proxies every stream chunk) and bill on min(provider_reported, server_observed) or a byte-derived estimate. (2) Add a per-token byte-floor sanity check (OutputBytesPerTokenCeiling exists in config but is unused for billing). (3) In reconcile, recompute completion tokens from a stored output-size measure rather than re-trusting the provider count.
architecture.evidence: CONFIRMED. formula.go:95-97 defaults usage_source to UsageProviderReported when empty; formula.go:124-133 sets completion = *completionTokens directly from the provider value; the only sanitization is formula.go:135 + invalidBillableTokenCount (formula.go:176-178) which only rejects <0 or >10,000,000 and checkedMul overflow guards. buyer/server.go:1400 and 1539 call tokenPointersFromUsageObject(end.Usage), and tokenPointersFromUsageObject (server.go:2766-2778) literally json.Unmarshals prompt_tokens/completion_tokens from the provider's raw usage object with no cross-check. messages.go:175-182 shows InferenceResponseEnd.Usage is json.RawMessage from the provider frame. recovery.go:75-93 re-SELECTs rl.prompt_tokens/rl.completion_tokens from request_log (provider-sourced) and recovery.go:200 feeds them back into ComputeCredits; reconcileExistingCreditTx (recovery.go:379-393) only compares rate/multiplier/share and gross/provider credit arithmetic, never re-deriving token counts from output. The byte-estimated path (recovery.go:368) only activates when CompletionTokens==nil, so an inflated non-null count always takes the provider-reported branch. install.sh write_config (lines 454-470) emits only model/coordinator_url/provider_id/port, writing no provider token. The unbounded-fraud vector is real; severity critical upheld.

architecture.title: Pillar-D output byte-cap bounds bytes-to-buyer but not billed completion_tokens
architecture.description: The behavioral-safety guard enforceOutputCap truncates choices[].message/delta/text.content to OutputSizeCapBytes and rewrites the JSON sent to the buyer. However billing is taken from end.Usage (the provider's usage object), which the guard never touches. CheckNonStreamingBody returns the capped body, but tokenPointersFromUsageObject(end.Usage) is called on the original provider-supplied usage immediately after. So even with the size cap fully enforced, the provider returns 5 bytes of content and reports completion_tokens: 10000000 and is billed for 10M tokens.
architecture.impact: Operators who enable behavioral_safety + output_size_cap_bytes (believing it bounds untrusted-provider abuse) still have unbounded billing inflation. The defense gives false assurance.
architecture.recommendation: Make billing consume the guard's measured emitted-output size: PillarDGuard already tracks g.outputBytes. Derive a billable completion-token ceiling from actually-emitted bytes and clamp provider_reported completion_tokens to it. At minimum, when the cap truncates, force usage_source to byte_estimated for that request.
architecture.evidence: CONFIRMED. enforceOutputCap (pillar_d.go:252-277) and capChoiceContent (pillar_d.go:279-309) only mutate the 'content'/'text' string fields inside doc['choices'] and track g.outputBytes (pillar_d.go:289,297,306); they never read or modify any 'usage' object. CheckNonStreamingBody (pillar_d.go:127-165) returns the capped body bytes only. In buyer/server.go:1390-1399 the capped checkedBody is written to the buyer, then line 1400 calls tokenPointersFromUsageObject(end.Usage) on the untouched provider usage frame (streaming path does the same at line 1539). The cap and the billing input are fully decoupled; g.outputBytes is never used to clamp completion_tokens (estimatedCompletionTokensFromBytes is only invoked on error/disconnect paths, never on the happy path with a provider-supplied usage). Severity high upheld.

architecture.title: Coordinator buyer endpoint has no buyer authentication and trusts routing/account headers (no defense-in-depth beyond loopback bind)
architecture.description: buyerServer.Handler() exposes /v1/chat/completions with no auth. The finding claims routing-control headers (X-MacProvider-Provider/Session) AND account-affinity headers (X-MacProvider-Account) are honored from the raw request, so any caller reaching the port could pin requests and forge sticky-account attribution with zero authentication.
architecture.impact: Claimed: routing manipulation and cross-account affinity poisoning on the real-money path if the port is ever non-loopback, reached via SSRF, or a second coordinator target is added.
architecture.recommendation: Add a required internal bearer (reuse internalAuthKey) on the entire buyer handler, not just sticky-write, so the trust boundary does not depend solely on bind address. Explicitly ignore X-MacProvider-Provider/Session unless the internal bearer is present (mirror the sticky/account gate). Keep loopback bind as defense-in-depth.
architecture.evidence: PARTIALLY CONFIRMED, downgraded. The account/sticky half of the claim is REFUTED: selectProviderExcluding (server.go:2076-2078) rejects the request with 'Internal routing header is not accepted on the buyer port' whenever hasInternalRoutingHeader is true and the internal bearer is absent; hasInternalRoutingHeader (server.go:2584-2597) matches exactly X-MacProvider-Account and X-MacProvider-Internal-*, so X-MacProvider-Account spoofing IS bearer-gated, and stickyStore (server.go:2404-2436) only runs off the bearer-gated X-MacProvider-Internal-Conv key. The CONFIRMED half is narrower: X-MacProvider-Provider / X-MacProvider-Session pinning (server.go:2079,2094) is NOT covered by hasInternalRoutingHeader and is NOT bearer-gated, so provider/session pinning on this no-auth handler (server.go:331-338) is protected only by the loopback bind (default 127.0.0.1, config.go:220) plus the gateway allowlist. Gateway copyForwardHeaders (gateway server.go:2209-2216) forwards only Accept and X-MacProvider-Retry, dropping client provider/session/account headers, and the gateway sets X-MacProvider-Account/Internal-Conv itself from the authenticated account (server.go:1359-1360). Net: real-money account attribution is NOT forgeable (refutes the headline impact), and the residual gap is unauthenticated provider/session pinning reachable only on misconfiguration/SSRF. Downgraded to low.

architecture.title: Single coordinator is a SPOF for billing authority, WS relay, and the SQLite ledger with no HA path
architecture.lines: 85-142 (single-process wiring); config.go:293-294 (single SQLite DB); hotpath.go:37,151; requestlog/store.go:56-60
architecture.description: All money-critical state and relay run in one process against one embedded SQLite file. The hot-path billing write uses BEGIN IMMEDIATE single-writer transactions, settlement/reconcile are in-process goroutines, and the WS relay holds all provider sessions in process memory. There is no described replication, failover, or external durable store; production is a single Pearl VPS coordinator.
architecture.impact: Coordinator loss/restart drops every in-flight inference (relay sessions are memory-only), pauses all billing accrual, and risks ledger corruption if the SQLite file is lost (no replica). Blast radius is the entire marketplace.
architecture.recommendation: Implement a recovery posture proportional to handling real USDC: continuous SQLite backup/replication (e.g., Litestream) or a replicated store; persist enough relay state to resume or cleanly fail in-flight requests; and define an RTO/RPO. At minimum ensure the ledger DB is on durable, backed-up storage and settlement is idempotent across restarts.
architecture.evidence: CONFIRMED as an architectural/resilience observation. main.go:85-142 wires one wsServer + one buyerServer + one billingStore in a single process; settlement and reconcile run as in-process goroutines (main.go:132-133). The ledger is a single embedded SQLite file (config.go:293-294 default 'coordinator.db'); hotpath.go:37,151 use BEGIN IMMEDIATE single-writer transactions and store.go enforces journal_mode=WAL (requestlog/store.go:56, billing/store.go:37-41). A repo-wide grep for Litestream/replica/failover/backup found ZERO replication or failover machinery; the only matches are WAL/busy_timeout/BEGIN IMMEDIATE, all single-node primitives. The recent commit c1cfc97 adds fast-fail timeouts explicitly for 'coordinator restart', confirming restart is a live operational event. True single point of failure with no HA path; this is a known-posture/design observation rather than a discrete code defect, but the money-system blast radius justifies medium. Severity upheld.

architecture.title: GitHub OAuth account is keyed only on provider user id with no email verification, and email is stored unverified
architecture.description: The OAuth scope is read:user only and the GitHub /user email field is taken as-is into the account identity. With read:user GitHub returns the user's public email which is frequently null/empty, and it is never verified to belong to the actor. Account linkage is keyed on the numeric GitHub id (which is fine for identity), but the stored Email is effectively unverified metadata.
architecture.impact: Any downstream use of the stored email for billing notices, support identity, or trust decisions would rely on an unverified value. Not a direct money-loss path today (API keys gate spend, quotas are per-account), so severity is low, but it is a latent identity-integrity gap if email is ever trusted.
architecture.recommendation: Do not treat the OAuth-provided email as verified. Either request user:email scope and check the verified flag on /user/emails, or store the email tagged unverified and never use it for authorization/trust.
architecture.evidence: CONFIRMED. AuthURL hardcodes scope=read:user (oauth.go:46). Exchange decodes only {id, email} from /user (oauth.go:95-98) and returns OAuthIdentity{ProviderUserID: id, Email: user.Email} with no /user/emails call and no verified-flag check (oauth.go:105). The callback keys account linkage on LookupAccountByIdentity('github', identity.ProviderUserID), the immutable numeric id (server.go:269), which is correct; but createSignupAccount stores AddAccountIdentity{... Email: identity.Email ...} as-is (server.go:314-316), so the email is persisted unverified. Correctly scoped as low: spend is gated by API keys (server.go:275-280 issues the key) and quotas are per-account, so unverified email is not an authz bypass today. Severity low upheld; accurate and well-reasoned.
